How to Use This Book Most coding-interview problems are not new. They are a small number of patterns wearing different costumes . A candidate who has memorised 300 solutions still freezes on problem 301; a candidate who can recognise "this is a monotonic quantity, so two pointers" or "this is a feasibility check over a sorted answer space, so binary search on the answer" solves problems they have never seen. This handbook teaches that recognition skill. Every chapter follows the same ten-part structure, so you always know where to look. P A R T I Array & Index-Based Patterns Eleven patterns that replace nested loops with a single, well-reasoned pass. Arrays are the substrate of most interview problems; mastering how indices move is the fastest way to move from O(n²) to O(n). PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 01 Two Pointers Two indices, one pass: turn O(n²) pair searches into O(n). A. Pattern Overview Two Pointers keeps two indices into the same sequence and moves them according to a rule, so that each step permanently rules out a set of candidates. Instead of testing every pair (i, j) with a nested loop, the pointers walk a path through the pair space and the rule guarantees that nothing you skipped could have been the answer. The pattern exists because many array and string problems ask about a pair, triplet or partition whose quality changes monotonically as an index moves. When moving an index in one direction can only make a quantity larger (or only smaller), you always know which pointer to move, and the quadratic search collapses to a linear scan. Flavour Pointers start They move Typical problems Opposite direction left = 0 , right = n-1 toward each other Two Sum II, 3Sum, Container With Most Water, Trapping Rain Water, valid palindrome Same direction read = write = 0 both forward, read Remove Duplicates, Move Zeroes, Remove (reader / writer) leads Element, in-place filtering and partitioning Fast and slow slow = fast = start forward at different speeds Cycle detection, middle of a list, Find the Duplicate Number (Floyd) Three-way partition low , mid , high mid scans, the others fence zones Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag), partition around a pivot KEY IDEA A two-pointer solution is really an elimination argument . Before you code it, be able to finish the sentence: "when the pointers are at (L, R) and the condition says X, every pair involving L (or R) and anything still inside the window is useless, so I can move that pointer." How it differs from neighbours. Sliding window also uses two indices, but both only move forward and the pointers delimit a contiguous subarray whose contents you maintain. In two pointers the indices usually represent two separate elements (a pair), often at opposite ends. Binary search discards half the range per step; two pointers discards one element per step, but needs no mid and works on pair conditions that binary search cannot express. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals The input is sorted , or sorting it first costs only O(n log n) and does not destroy the answer (pair sums, triplets, closest values). The question asks for a pair / triplet / quadruplet with a target sum, difference or product, or a best pair under a formula such as (j-i) * min(h[i], h[j]) . You are told to modify the array in place with O(1) extra space (remove, compact, partition, reorder). The brute force is a double loop over i < j , and you can argue that increasing i (or decreasing j ) changes the evaluated quantity in one known direction. A palindrome-like or symmetric check: compare the front with the back, moving inward. Linked structures or implicit graphs where you need the middle, a cycle , or the k-th from the end (fast/slow, covered again in Part IV). CONSTRAINT HINT Constraints such as n ≤ 10 ⁵ rule out O(n²) and hint at O(n) or O(n log n) . Combined with the word sorted or in-place , two pointers should be your first guess. If the array is unsorted and you need the original indices , reach for a HashMap instead (Part III). A 20-second interview checklist Is the data sorted, or can I sort it without losing information I need? Can I name a rule that says which pointer to move after looking at the current pair? Can I justify why the discarded candidates cannot be optimal? (If not, it is not two pointers.) C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Take the sorted array [2, 3, 5, 8, 11, 15] and target = 16 . Start with the widest pair. The sum 2 + 15 = 17 is too big. Because the array is sorted, 15 paired with any element at or to the right of left is at least 17 , so 15 can never be part of the answer: move right inward. Next, 2 + 11 = 13 is too small, and 2 paired with anything at or left of right is at most 13, so 2 is useless: move left . Figure 2. Each comparison removes one element from consideration. Grey cells are provably not part of the answer. A second picture shows why this is correct. Every cell below is one candidate pair (L, R) and shows its sum. The four visited cells (solid colour) eliminate every other cell in their row or column without ever computing it. Figure 3. Four evaluations rule out all 15 pairs. A red cell prunes the cells below it in its column; a blue cell prunes the cells to its left in its row. INTUITION Why the discard is safe (exchange argument). Suppose nums[L] + nums[R] > target and the optimal pair were (i, R) with i ≥ L . Then nums[i] ≥ nums[L] gives nums[i] + nums[R] ≥ nums[L] + nums[R] > target : contradiction. So no optimal pair uses R . The symmetric argument handles < . Sortedness is what makes the sum monotone in each pointer. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: 3Sum (LeetCode 15) Find all unique triplets with sum 0. Brute force: three nested loops, plus a Set of sorted triplets to deduplicate. O(n³) time and O(k) extra space for the set. For n = 3000 that is 4.5×10⁹ operations: too slow. Bottleneck: the innermost loop searches for -(a+b) . Searching a sorted array is what two pointers does in O(n) for a whole row of answers. Step up: fix one element a[i] and solve Two Sum II on the suffix a[i+1..] with target -a[i] . Time drops to O(n²) . Alternative: fix a[i] , store seen values in a HashSet while scanning j . Also O(n²) , but needs O(n) space and awkward duplicate handling. Two pointers handles duplicates by skipping equal neighbours in a sorted array. Optimal: sort + anchor + two pointers. O(n log n + n²) = O(n²) time, O(1) extra space (ignoring the output and sort). Figure 4. Why the brute force fails. On log-log axes, each step from O(n³) to O(n²) to O(n) buys orders of magnitude at n = 10⁴–10⁵. E. G. Variations of the Pattern Container With Most Water (opposite pointers + greedy discard) Choose two lines to maximise (j - i) * min(h[i], h[j]) . Start with the widest container. The shorter wall caps the height, so any container that keeps that wall but is narrower is strictly no better; the shorter wall can be thrown away. Move the pointer at the shorter wall. Figure 5. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 02 Sliding Window Maintain a moving contiguous range and update its summary in O(1) per step. A. Pattern Overview A sliding window is a contiguous subarray (or substring) [left, right] whose summary (sum, character counts, distinct count, number of zeros) is updated incrementally as the window moves, instead of being recomputed from scratch. Each element enters the window once and leaves at most once, so a search over O(n²) subarrays costs O(n) . Type Window size Right pointer Left pointer Goal Fixed size exactly k advances every step right - k + 1 , implied best / count over every window of size k Variable, longest grows and advances every moves only when maximise right - left + 1 valid shrinks step invalid Variable, shortest grows and advances every moves while still valid minimise right - left + 1 valid shrinks step Counting (at most K) grows and shrinks advances every step moves while count > K add right - left + 1 per step; exactly-K = atMost(K) − atMost(K−1) KEY IDEA The pattern is valid when the window's validity is monotone : if [l, r] is valid then every sub-window is also valid (for a longest search over a constraint ), or if it is invalid then every larger window is invalid. This is why sums with negative numbers break it, while counts, distinct values and non-negative sums work. Versus two pointers: both indices move forward and never backward here, and the pair (left, right) is a range whose interior you summarise. Versus prefix sums: prefix sums answer any range query in O(1) after preprocessing and tolerate negatives; a sliding window needs no extra array and handles conditions that are not subtractable (distinct count, "at most k replacements"). B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals The words substring, subarray, contiguous, consecutive appear together with longest, shortest, maximum, minimum, at most, exactly. The condition is about the contents of the range: distinct characters, frequency match, number of zeros, sum ≥ target with positive numbers. A fixed k is given, or the question is "for every window of size k". The brute force enumerates all (i, j) and recomputes a summary of a[i..j] ; you realise the summary of [i, j+1] follows from [i, j] in O(1) . Input is a string or array with n up to 10 ⁵ – 10 ⁶ and the target complexity is O(n) . THE MOST COMMON TRAP Negative numbers and a sum constraint = not a sliding window. For sum == k or sum ≥ k with negatives, use prefix sums + HashMap (Chapter 3) or a monotonic deque (Chapter 8). C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Fixed window. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 03 Prefix Sum Pay O(n) once, answer every range question in O(1), and turn subarray sums into a lookup. A. Pattern Overview A prefix sum array stores prefix[i] = nums[0] + … + nums[i-1] . Because the sum of any range is a difference of two prefixes ( sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] ), a range query costs O(1) after an O(n) build. Combine it with a HashMap and it solves "how many subarrays satisfy X" questions in one pass, even with negative numbers. Variant Idea Used for Basic prefix sum prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] Range sum queries, pivot index, equilibrium 2D prefix sum Inclusion–exclusion over rectangles Submatrix sums, image integral Prefix + HashMap of first Earliest equal prefix gives the longest Longest subarray with sum k, Contiguous index subarray Array, Continuous Subarray Sum Prefix + HashMap of Number of earlier prefixes equal to Subarray Sum Equals K, divisible-by-K, binary counts prefix - k subarrays Prefix / suffix products Combine left and right aggregates without division Product of Array Except Self Versus sliding window. A window maintains one moving range and needs monotone validity. Prefix sums describe all ranges at once and work with negatives, but they require the quantity to be subtractable (sums, counts, XOR, remainders), not arbitrary properties such as "distinct count". B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Many range-sum (or range-count) queries on a static array: "sum between i and j", answered repeatedly. "Number of subarrays with sum / XOR / balance equal to k" , especially when the array has negative numbers or zeros. "Longest subarray with equal 0s and 1s" or another balance condition: map the values to ±1 and look for sum 0. "Divisible by k" subarray sums: equal prefix remainders mean the difference is divisible by k . You catch yourself computing sum(nums[i..j]) inside two loops. An answer at index i needs an aggregate of everything to the left and everything to the right (product except self, pivot index). DECISION RULE If a problem says "subarray" and "sum equals" and the numbers can be negative, think prefix sum + HashMap first and sliding window never. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 11. The teal range sums to 4 + 1 + 5 = 10. Subtracting two prefixes cancels everything outside the range. The HashMap idea. A subarray nums[i..j] sums to k exactly when prefix[j+1] - prefix[i] = k , i.e. when an earlier prefix equals prefix[j+1] - k . Scan left to right keeping a map prefixValue → how many times seen ; at each index look up currentPrefix - k . INTUITION Seed the map with {0: 1} . It represents the empty prefix, which makes subarrays that start at index 0 countable. Query before you insert the current prefix, or a subarray of length 0 would be counted when k = 0 . 2D prefix sums: inclusion–exclusion Figure 12. The amber rectangle sum = big block − strip above − strip to the left + the doubly-subtracted corner. D. Reformulate: sum(i..j) = P[j+1] - P[i] . We need pairs (i, j+1) with P[j+1] - P[i] = k . That is a two-sum on prefix values. Optimal: one pass with Map<prefix, count> : O(n) time, O(n) space. E. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 04 Difference Array Apply a thousand range updates in O(1) each, then read the final array once. A. Pattern Overview A difference array diff stores how much each position changes relative to its left neighbour: diff[i] = value[i] - value[i-1] . Adding v to every element in [l, r] then needs only two writes, diff[l] += v and diff[r+1] -= v , regardless of the range length. A single prefix-sum pass at the end reconstructs the real values. KEY IDEA Difference array is the inverse of prefix sum. Prefix sum turns point values into running totals (fast reads of ranges). Difference array turns range writes into point changes. Prefix-summing a difference array gives the original array back. Operation Naive array Difference array Add v to [l, r] O(r − l + 1) O(1) : diff[l] += v; diff[r+1] -= v Read final array O(n) O(n): one prefix-sum pass Read one element between O(1) O(n): needs a pass (use a Fenwick tree if you need updates this) Use it when updates come first and reads come at the end (offline). If reads are interleaved with updates, you need a Fenwick or segment tree (Part XII). B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals A list of range updates (left, right, delta) followed by a request for the final array, a maximum, or a feasibility check. Bookings, reservations, flights, trips, meetings with a start and end that each add a load over an interval. "How many intervals cover point x?", "peak occupancy", "capacity never exceeded": counting overlaps. Naive solution is for each update: for i in [l, r]: a[i] += v , giving O(q · n) with q, n ≤ 10 ⁵ . Updates are additive (can be undone by subtraction). Non-invertible updates such as max= do not work. KEYWORD Whenever the statement says "for each booking add seats to flights first through last ", the O(1) endpoint trick is the intended solution. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Think of diff as marking where the level steps up and where it steps down . A +v at l raises the "water level" for everything to the right; a −v at r+1 lowers it back. The prefix sum is the running level. Figure 13. Three range updates cost six array writes. One sweep recovers [10, 55, 45, 25, 25]. INTUITION Why does it work? After the prefix sum, result[i] = Σ _{j ≤ i} diff[j] . An update (l, r, v) contributes +v to every i ≥ l and −v to every i ≥ r+1 ; the two cancel for i > r , leaving +v exactly on [l, r] . D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Corporate Flight Bookings (LeetCode 1109) Brute force: for each of q bookings loop over its flights: O(q · n) . With q = n = 2·10 ⁴ that is 4·10⁸ additions. Bottleneck: every booking redoes work that is identical for each flight inside its range. Idea: record only the boundaries of each range. Interior values are implied by the running sum. Optimal: O(q + n) time, O(n) space. E. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 05 Kadane's Algorithm Best subarray ending here: extend it or restart. A 1-state DP in one pass. A. Pattern Overview Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in O(n) time and O(1) space. It is dynamic programming with a single state: best[i] = the largest sum of a subarray that ends at index i . The recurrence has only two choices: extend the best subarray ending at i-1 , or start fresh at i . best[i] = max(nums[i], best[i-1] + nums[i]) and answer = max over i of best[i] INTUITION Why "start fresh" is correct. If best[i-1] is negative, attaching it to nums[i] can only lower the sum, so any optimal subarray ending at i should drop that prefix. Equivalent view: a negative-sum prefix of any optimal subarray can always be removed. Variant State kept Twist Maximum Subarray bestEndingHere Classic With indices plus start of the current run Restart updates start ; improvement updates answer bounds Circular max and min Kadane max(maxKadane, total − minKadane) , guard the all-negative case Max product max and min ending here A negative factor swaps their roles Stock profit / abs sum disguised Kadane Differences of prices; run max and min together B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Maximum / minimum sum (or product) of a contiguous subarray." Array contains negatives; otherwise the answer is trivially the whole array. An optimisation over all subarrays where the value of a subarray ending at i depends only on the best one ending at i-1 . Phrases such as best time to buy and sell once, maximum profit, largest gain over consecutive differences. Circular array with a contiguous segment that may wrap around. A constraint of n ≤ 10 ⁵ and the brute force is O(n²) over all (i, j) . SANITY CHECK If the problem allows only non-negative numbers for "max subarray", the answer is the entire array: the problem is a trick or a different one. Kadane earns its keep exactly when negatives are present. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 14. Bars are the inputs; the navy line is bestEndingHere . Whenever the line would dip below the next bar it restarts. The highlighted range [4, -1, 2, 1] = 6. Read the navy line as a running balance: it climbs while the stretch is profitable and resets to the current element when the previous balance is a liability. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Brute force: enumerate all (i, j) and compute the sum: O(n³) ; with a running sum O(n²) . Prefix-sum view: sum(i..j) = P[j+1] - P[i] . For each j we want the minimum earlier prefix : answer = max_j (P[j+1] - min_{i ≤ j} P[i]) . This is already O(n) . Kadane's compression: P[j+1] - min P[i] equals best ending at j ; maintaining it needs just one variable instead of the prefix array. Divide and conquer ( O(n log n) ) also exists but is never the right answer here. E. Java Implementation MaxSubarray.java — LeetCode 53 Java 17+ /** LeetCode 53 - Maximum Subarray. Requires a non-empty array. */ public static int maxSubArray(int[] nums) { int bestEndingHere = nums[0]; // best sum of a subarray that ends at i int best = nums[0]; for (int i = 1; i } /** Returns {sum, startIndex, endIndex} of one maximum subarray. */ public static int[] maxSubArrayWithBounds(int[] nums) { int bestEndingHere = nums[0]; int best = nums[0]; int start = 0; // start of the current run int bestStart = 0; int bestEnd = 0; for (int i = 1; i best) { best = bestEndingHere; bestStart = start; bestEnd = i; } } return new int[]{best, bestStart, bestEnd}; } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(1) Initialise from nums[0] , not 0 , or an all-negative array returns 0 (an empty subarray that is not allowed). PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 06 Cyclic Sort When values are 1..n, the array is its own hash table: send every value to its home index. A. Pattern Overview Cyclic sort applies when an array of length n holds values from a known contiguous range such as 1..n (or 0..n ). Each value v has a natural home index ( v - 1 , or v ). Walk the array; while the current value is not at home, swap it into its home slot . Every swap places at least one value permanently, so the whole array is sorted in O(n) swaps with O(1) extra space. After one pass, any index holding the wrong value reveals a missing or duplicate number. KEY IDEA The array is the hash table: index = key, value = presence. You get the effect of a boolean[] seen without allocating it. Value range Home index of v Skip when Typical outcome 1..n v - 1 nums[i] == nums[v-1] Missing / duplicate numbers 0..n (one slot short) v v == n or already home Missing number Arbitrary integers, answer v-1if1≤v≤n v ≤ 0 , v > n , or already home First Missing Positive in 1..n+1 B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals The array has n elements with values in [1, n] (or [0, n] ) and the statement asks for missing, duplicate , or misplaced numbers. The constraint demands O(1) extra space and O(n) time : a HashSet or counting array is explicitly ruled out. "Find the smallest missing positive" : the answer must lie in 1..n+1 by the pigeonhole principle. You may modify the input (or you can clone it, and say so). KEY ARGUMENT Pigeonhole thinking: with n slots, the first missing positive is at most n + 1 . So values outside [1, n] are irrelevant and can be ignored. CONSTRAINT If the array must not be modified , use Floyd's cycle detection (Chapter 1, LeetCode 287), XOR (missing number), or sums. Cyclic sort destroys the original order. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Sort [3, 1, 5, 4, 2] . At index 0 the value 3 belongs at index 2, so swap; the value that arrives at index 0 (5) is checked next, and so on. The index i advances only when nums[i] is already home. Figure 16. Each swap sends one value home permanently; the array is sorted after 3 swaps and one final scan. INTUITION Why O(n) with a while inside? Each swap puts at least one value in its final position and a placed value is never moved again, so there are at most n - 1 swaps. The pointer i itself advances at most n times. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: First Missing Positive (LeetCode 41) Brute force: for x = 1, 2, … scan the array: O(n²) . Sorting: sort, then scan for the gap: O(n log n) time. Misses the required O(n) . HashSet: put everything in a set, try 1, 2, … : O(n) time but O(n) space. Misses the required O(1) . Observation: the answer is in [1, n + 1] . Use the array itself as the set: place each v in [1, n] at index v - 1 . Optimal: cyclic sort; the first index with nums[i] != i + 1 gives answer i + 1 , else n + 1 . O(n) time, O(1) space. E. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 07 Monotonic Stack Keep a stack in sorted order so each element is pushed once and popped once. A. Pattern Overview A monotonic stack is a stack whose elements are kept in strictly increasing or decreasing order. Before pushing a new element you pop everything that violates the order . The pop is the interesting event: the new element is the answer for every element it pops . Because each element is pushed once and popped once, a whole scan costs O(n) even though a single step may pop many items. Order kept (bottom → top) Pop while… Answers the question… Decreasing (top is smallest) stack.top < current Next greater element of each popped item Increasing (top is largest) stack.top > current Next smaller element of each popped item Stack below an element after — Previous smaller / greater element of the popping current item KEY IDEA Each element asks one question: "who is the first element to my right (or left) that beats me?" The monotonic stack answers it for all elements in one pass, because elements still on the stack are exactly the ones whose answer is still unknown. Versus a normal stack: a normal stack stores pending items (brackets, calls) and pops on a match . A monotonic stack pops on a comparison and exists to find nearest greater/smaller neighbours, or to find the span in which an element is the maximum or minimum. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Next greater / next smaller / previous greater element" , or how many days until a warmer temperature. The problem asks for the largest rectangle, area , or span where one element is the limiting height. "Sum of subarray minimums / maximums" : count the subarrays in which each element is the minimum. Greedy digit / letter removal to obtain the smallest or largest result (Remove K Digits, Remove Duplicate Letters). Online queries such as stock span : each new element needs the distance to the previous larger one. A brute force that scans left or right from every index until it finds something larger or smaller: O(n²) hiding a linear algorithm. ONE-LINE TEST If the brute force is "for each i, scan right until arr[j] > arr[i]" , it is a monotonic stack. If it is "for each window of size k find the max" , it is a monotonic deque (Chapter 8). C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Daily Temperatures. T = [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73] . The stack holds the indices of days that are still waiting for a warmer day, so their temperatures are decreasing from bottom to top. Figure 17. At i = 5 the 72 pops days 4 and 3; at i = 6 the 76 pops days 5 and 2. Each pop answers that day in one step. INTUITION Amortised O(n). Each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the total number of pops ≤ n . The while inside the for does not make it quadratic. Largest Rectangle in Histogram. For bar h , the widest rectangle of height h extends left and right until it meets a strictly shorter bar. A stack of increasing heights finds both borders when a bar is popped: the right border is the bar that caused the pop; the left border is the new stack top. Figure 18. The dashed rectangle is the maximum (area 10). Bar 1 (height 1) on the left and bar 4 (height 2) on the right are the strictly shorter borders. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Largest Rectangle in Histogram (LeetCode 84) Brute force 1: every pair (i, j) , track the minimum height in between: O(n²) . Brute force 2: for each bar, expand left and right while neighbours are ≥ it: O(n²) worst case (sorted input). Bottleneck: the expansion repeats work that neighbouring bars have already done. Insight: the left border of bar i is the previous smaller bar and the right border is the next smaller bar. Both come from a monotonic stack. Optimal: one pass, a sentinel 0 at the end flushes the stack. O(n) time, O(n) space. E. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 08 Monotonic Queue / Deque A monotonic stack with an expiry date: the window maximum in O(1) amortised. A. Pattern Overview A monotonic deque keeps a window's candidates in sorted order and lets elements leave from both ends : from the back when a new element makes them useless (same rule as a monotonic stack) and from the front when they slide out of the window . The front of the deque is always the current window's maximum (or minimum), readable in O(1) ; every element is added once and removed once, so the total is O(n) . KEY IDEA Dominance argument. If an older element a is ≤ a newer element b , then a can never again be the maximum: b is larger and will outlive it. So a is discarded the moment b arrives. What remains is a decreasing sequence whose front is the maximum. Operation End Reason Remove expired index front Oldest index left the window Remove dominated values back Smaller-or-equal and older than the new element Insert new index back Newest element Read window max (or min) front Largest surviving candidate Versus monotonic stack: the stack has no expiry; it answers nearest greater/smaller neighbour . The deque answers extreme of a moving window . Versus a heap: a priority queue gives the same answer in O(n log n) with lazy deletion; the deque is O(n) and simpler to reason about. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Maximum (or minimum) of every sliding window of size k." A window whose validity depends on both max and min ( max - min <= limit ): use two deques. Subarray sum ≥ K with negative numbers where a sliding window fails: prefix sums plus a deque of increasing prefix values. A DP transition over a sliding range : dp[i] = nums[i] + max(dp[i-k .. i-1]) (Jump Game VI, Constrained Subsequence Sum). The sliding-window code almost works but needs the extreme element of the window, not just a sum or a count. DECISION RULE "Window" + "maximum/minimum" → deque. "Window" + "negatives" + "sum at least K" → prefix sums + deque. "DP over the last k states" → deque to get the best previous state in O(1) . C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 19. The blue deque is decreasing from front to back. Its front is the window maximum; smaller older values are evicted when a bigger one arrives. INTUITION Store indices , not values: you need the index to detect when the front has left the window ( front <= i - k ), and the value is one lookup away ( nums[front] ). D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Sliding Window Maximum (LeetCode 239) Brute force: scan each window for its maximum: O(n · k) . With n = 10 ⁵ and k = 5·10 ⁴ that is about 2.5·10⁹ steps: far too slow. Heap: push (value, index) , lazily pop the top while its index is outside the window: O(n log n) , O(n) space. Observation: an element that is both older and not larger than a newer one can never be a maximum again. Discard it immediately. Optimal: deque of indices with decreasing values: O(n) time, O(k) space. E. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 09 Array Techniques Voting, in-place reversal and single-pass greedy: the small tricks that turn O(n) space into O(1). A. Pattern Overview Not every array problem needs a named algorithm. A large family of screening-round questions is solved by one of four compact ideas, each replacing extra memory or a second pass with a clever invariant: Technique Idea Classic problems Time / Space Boyer-Moore voting Pair off different elements; whatever survives is the only possible majority Majority Element (169), Majority Element II (229) O(n) · O(1) Reversal trick A rotation is three reversals Rotate Array (189), Reverse Words in place O(n) · O(1) Greedy single pass Local decisions on adjacent elements add up to the global optimum Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II (122), Jump-style scans O(n) · O(1) Running best-so-far Carry the best left partner while scanning right partners Best Sightseeing Pair (1014), Increasing Triplet (334) O(n) · O(1) Run counting A run of length L contributes L(L+1)/2 subarrays, or L per element Zero-Filled Subarrays (2348) O(n) · O(1) KEY IDEA Each technique maintains a tiny summary of the prefix (a candidate and a count, the two smallest values, the best left partner, the current run length). If you can say what must be remembered about everything before index i in one or two variables, you have an O(1) -space single pass. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "More than ⌊n/2⌋ (or ⌊n/3⌋) times" with a space limit of O(1) : Boyer-Moore voting. "Rotate by k" in place, or a reversal that must preserve order inside segments: three reversals. "Unlimited transactions" , or a profit that is the sum of positive adjacent differences: collect every rise. Pair or triple conditions with ordering ( i < j , a < b < c ) where a hash set or DP table is too heavy : carry the best partner so far. Counting subarrays made of identical values (all zeros, all ones): count per run, not per pair. The constraints say n ≤ 10 ⁵ and the brute force is O(n²) or O(n) extra memory. SPACE-LIMIT HINT The phrase "in O(1) extra space" plus a counting or ordering property almost always points to one of these five techniques. Think "what do I need to remember about the prefix?" before reaching for a map. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Boyer-Moore voting. Imagine a vote where each different pair of ballots cancels out. If an element is a strict majority, it outnumbers all other elements combined, so it cannot be cancelled completely . Keep a candidate and a count : matching ballots add one, different ballots remove one, and when count hits 0 the next ballot starts a fresh candidate. Figure 20. Green cells vote for the current candidate. The candidate can change, but the true majority always survives to the end. Rotation by three reversals. Rotating right by k moves the last k elements to the front without changing the order inside either block. Reversing the whole array puts the blocks in the right places but backwards; reversing each block restores their order. Figure 21. Reverse everything, then reverse the first k and the remaining n − k elements. INTUITION Why Boyer-Moore needs a second pass for "n/3". The voting phase only guarantees that if an element exceeds the threshold it is among the candidates. A candidate that survives may still be below the threshold ( [1, 2, 3] ), so verify with a counting pass . For Majority Element I the problem guarantees existence and the check is skipped. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Majority Element (LeetCode 169) Brute force: count every element against every other: O(n²) . Sorting: the majority element sits at index n / 2 after sorting: O(n log n) , O(1) to O(n) space. HashMap of counts: O(n) time, O(n) space. Good, and the right answer when space is not constrained. Randomised: pick random elements and verify; expected O(n) but not deterministic. Boyer-Moore voting: O(n) time and O(1) space, deterministic. The same ladder applies to Rotate Array : copy into a new array ( O(n) space), rotate one step k times ( O(nk) time), cyclic replacements ( O(n) time but fiddly with gcd(n, k) cycles), and finally the three-reversal solution. E. Java Implementation Boyer-Moore voting: Majority Element I and II MajorityElement.java — LeetCode 169 and 229 Java 17+ import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Boyer-Moore voting: LeetCode 169 (majority > n/2) and LeetCode 229 (elements > n/3). */ public class MajorityElement { /** The majority element is guaranteed to exist. */ public static int majorityElement(int[] nums) { int candidate = 0; int count = 0; for (int x : nums) { if (count == 0) { // previous votes cancelled out: adopt a new candidate candidate = x; } count += (x == candidate) ? 1 : -1; } return candidate; } /** Every element that appears more than n / 3 times: at most two such elements exist. */ public static List majorityElementII(int[] nums) { int cand1 = 0, cand2 = 1; // distinct dummy candidates int count1 = 0, count2 = 0; for (int x : nums) { if (x == cand1) { count1++; } else if (x == cand2) { count2++; } else if (count1 == 0) { cand1 = x; count1 = 1; } else if (count2 == 0) { cand2 = x; count2 = 1; } else { count1--; // x votes against both candidates count2--; } } // Second pass: the voting phase only finds candidates, it does not prove the threshold. int c1 = 0, c2 = 0; for (int x : nums) { if (x == cand1) c1++; else if (x == cand2) c2++; } List result = new ArrayList<>(); if (c1 > nums.length / 3) result.add(cand1); if (c2 > nums.length / 3) result.add(cand2); return result; } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(1) For n/3 keep two candidates and two counts; a different third element cancels one vote from each. Always verify in a second pass for the n/3 variant. Rotate Array: three reversals RotateArray.java — LeetCode 189 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 189 - Rotate Array. Three reversals rotate right by k in O(n) time and O(1) space. */ public class RotateArray { public static void rotate(int[] nums, int k) { int n = nums.length; if (n == 0) return; k %= n; // k may exceed n if (k == 0) return; reverse(nums, 0, n - 1); // [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] -> [7,6,5,4,3,2,1] reverse(nums, 0, k - 1); // reverse the first k: the new head reverse(nums, k, n - 1); // reverse the rest } private static void reverse(int[] a, int lo, int hi) { while (lo int tmp = a[lo]; a[lo++] = a[hi]; a[hi--] = tmp; } } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(1) k %= n is mandatory ( k can exceed n ); each element is moved at most twice. It appears 4 times out of 7, a strict majority. Increasing Triplet: nums = [2, 1, 5, 0, 4, 6] i x first second Action 0 2 2 ∞ x ≤ first → first = 2 1 1 1 ∞ x ≤ first → first = 1 2 5 1 5 x ≤ second → second = 5 3 0 0 5 x ≤ first → first = 0 4 4 0 4 x ≤ second → second = 4 5 6 0 4 x > second → triplet found first = 0, second = 4, x = 6 proves a triplet exists (for example 2 < 5 < 6). Note that first and second need not belong to the same triplet: only their existence matters. G. Variations of the Pattern Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II: sum of rises With unlimited transactions, any climb from a low to a high equals the sum of its daily increases, so collect every positive difference prices[i] − prices[i−1] . Number of Zero-Filled Subarrays: count per run A maximal run of L zeros contains L(L+1)/2 zero-filled subarrays. Equivalently, each zero at run position p adds p new subarrays ending there. Related one-pass ideas Majority in a stream or very large data: Boyer-Moore works online with O(1) memory (verify with a second pass if allowed). Rotate a linked list or a string : the reversal trick generalises (reverse words in place: reverse the whole string, then each word). Jump-style greedy scans (Jump Game, Gas Station): carry the farthest reach or running tank; developed in the Greedy chapters. H. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 10 String Patterns Strings are arrays of characters with extra rules: same pointers, plus the cost of immutability. A. Pattern Overview String problems reuse array patterns (two pointers, sliding window, hashing) but add three recurring concerns: immutability (every concatenation copies), character sets (case, digits, Unicode, ASCII-only?), and construction (build the answer without quadratic copying). This chapter covers the pointer and simulation patterns that appear in nearly every screening round. Windows over substrings are in Chapter 2, frequency maps in Part III, and string-matching algorithms (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Z, Manacher) in Part XII. Pattern Idea Problems Time / Space Subsequence check Greedy: match each pattern character at the earliest possible spot in the text Is Subsequence (392) O(n) · O(1) Opposite-end Compare s[l] and s[r] , skipping Valid Palindrome (125) O(n) · O(1) palindrome check unwanted characters One-deletion On the first mismatch, try skipping the left Valid Palindrome II (680) O(n) · O(1) palindrome or the right character Vertical scan Compare column by column and stop at the first mismatch Longest Common Prefix (14) O(total chars) Expand around centre Every palindrome has a centre; grow outwards while the ends match Longest Palindromic Substring (5), Palindromic Substrings (647) O(n²) · O(1) Row/cursor simulation Walk with a direction variable and append to the right row Zigzag Conversion (6) O(n) · O(n) Word-level scan Walk from the end, detect word boundaries, append with one space Reverse Words in a String (151) O(n) · O(n) Reader / writer Consume a run with read , emit it with write String Compression (443) O(n) · O(1) compression in the same array B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Is s a subsequence of t ?" : one pass over t with a pointer into s . "Palindrome" in the statement: compare from both ends, or expand from a centre. Longest or count of palindromic substrings suggests expansion ( O(n²) ) before Manacher ( O(n) ). "Ignore case / non-alphanumeric" means two pointers that skip characters rather than building a cleaned copy. "In place" on a char[] : reader / writer pointers, as in Chapter 1. A conversion that follows a geometric rule (zigzag, spiral of characters): simulate with a cursor and direction. "Reverse the words" : scan from the end or reverse twice; never split in a space-limited setting. CLARIFY FIRST Before writing code, answer three questions: (1) which alphabet? (2) is case relevant? may I allocate? The answers decide between int[26] , int[128] , char[] in place, or a StringBuilder . C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Expand around the centre. A palindrome is symmetric, so it is determined by its centre. A string of length n has 2n − 1 centres: n letters (odd-length palindromes) and n − 1 gaps between letters (even length). For each centre, grow l--, r++ while s[l] == s[r] . Figure 22. Each centre costs up to O(n) ; all 2n − 1 centres cost O(n²) with O(1) space. Zigzag by cursor. Instead of computing indices with formulas, keep a row and a step ( +1 going down, −1 going up); append each character to rows[row] , flipping step at the top and bottom rows. Figure 23. Concatenating the rows gives PAHNAPLSIIGYIR . INTUITION Immutability tax. In Java s += c inside a loop is O(n²) because each concatenation copies. Use StringBuilder (or a char[] ) for any loop that builds output, and substring carefully: since JDK 7u6 it copies, so repeated slicing is also O(n) each. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Longest Palindromic Substring (LeetCode 5) Brute force: check every substring (i, j) for palindromicity: O(n³) . DP: dp[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] && dp[i+1][j-1] : O(n²) time and O(n²) space (or reversed-string LCS). Expand around centre: same O(n²) time, O(1) space, and short to write: the interview default. Manacher's algorithm: O(n) time. Rarely expected in interviews; covered in Part XII. For Valid Palindrome II the brute force deletes each character and re-checks ( O(n²) ). The key observation is that only the first mismatch matters: the deleted character must be one of the two mismatching characters, so try both once, O(n) total. E. PART I · ARRAY & INDEX-BASED PATTERNS 11 Matrix Traversal and Manipulation Four shrinking boundaries, a transpose, and bits in the cells: grids without extra grids. A. Pattern Overview A matrix is an array with two indices, and most interview matrix problems are not about search but about systematic traversal and in-place transformation . Four ideas cover the majority of them: Technique Idea Problems Time / Space Boundary shrinking Keep top, bottom, left, right ; walk the four sides, then move each boundary inward Spiral Matrix (54, 59) O(mn) · O(1) Geometric identity A rotation is a transpose followed by a row reversal Rotate Image (48) O(n²) · O(1) Borrowed marker Use the first row and column of the matrix Set Matrix Zeroes (73) O(mn) · O(1) storage itself as flag arrays State encoding Store old and new state in different bits of one cell Game of Life (289) O(mn) · O(1) Index invariants Rows r , columns c : anti-diagonal = r + c ; 3×3 box = (r/3, c/3) Diagonal Traverse (498), Valid Sudoku (36) O(mn) KEY IDEA Grid traversal gets easy when you pick an invariant that names a position: top/bottom/left/right for rings, r + c for anti-diagonals, r - c for diagonals, (r / * 3 + c / 3 for sudoku boxes, (index / cols, index % cols) to flatten. Write the invariant in a comment before the loop. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Return the elements in spiral / diagonal / zigzag order" : boundary shrinking or an index invariant. "Rotate / flip / transpose the matrix in place" : combine transpose and reversal; do not allocate a second grid if the statement forbids it. "If a cell is 0, set its row and column to 0" , or any update that must not see its own changes : separate marking from applying , using spare storage inside the matrix. Simultaneous cell updates (cellular automata, Game of Life): encode both states in a cell. Validate a board (Sudoku, N-Queens placement): one set or bitmask per row, column, and box. m, n ≤ 200 and a requirement of O(1) extra space. SQUARE VS RECTANGLE Beware non-square inputs. Transposing in place only works for n × n (rotating a rectangular matrix needs a new n × m grid), and boundary-shrinking spirals need the "does a row/column remain?" guards. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Spiral = peel the outer ring, repeat. Walk the top row left to right, the right column downward, the bottom row right to left, the left column upward, then shrink all four boundaries by one. Two guards ( top <= bottom before the bottom row, left <= right before the left column) handle the last single row or column. Figure 24. Visit order 1 → 12: the outer ring is peeled first, then the remaining inner row. Rotate 90° clockwise = transpose, then reverse every row. The cell at (i, j) ends up at (j, n−1−i) ; the transpose sends it to (j, i) and the row reversal mirrors the column index. Original Transposed Rows reversed = rotated [1, 2, 3] [1, 4, 7] [7, 4, 1] [4, 5, 6] [2, 5, 8] [8, 5, 2] [7, 8, 9] [3, 6, 9] [9, 6, 3] INTUITION Counter-clockwise rotation: transpose then reverse each column (or reverse each row first, then transpose). 180° : reverse rows, then reverse each row. Memorise the 90° case and derive the rest by composition. Set Zeroes in O(1) space. If you zero rows immediately, later cells see fake zeros. Instead, record zeros in the first row and first column (they act as per-column and per-row flags), apply from the inside out, and use two booleans to remember whether the first row and column originally contained a zero. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Set Matrix Zeroes (LeetCode 73) Copy the matrix: read from the copy, write to the original: O(mn) space. Two boolean arrays zeroRow[m] , zeroCol[n] : O(m + n) space. Markers inside the matrix: reuse the first row and column as those arrays: O(1) space. The first row/column need their own two booleans because they double as storage. Apply order matters: inner cells first (using the markers), then the first row and column last. The same ladder appears in Rotate Image : allocate a new grid ( rotated[j][n−1−i] = m[i][j] , O(n²) space), then rotate four cells at a time in cycles ( O(1) ), or transpose-then-reverse ( O(1) , the easiest to remember). P A R T II Binary Search Patterns Six patterns built on one idea: keep an invariant and halve the search space. Binary search is not only for sorted arrays; it works on any monotone predicate, including the space of possible answers. PART II · BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS 12 Classic Binary Search Halve the search space every step by keeping an invariant: O(log n) from a sorted order. A. Pattern Overview Binary search finds a position in a sorted (more generally, monotone ) sequence by comparing the middle element with the target and discarding the half that cannot contain the answer. Each step halves the search space, so n = 10 ⁹ needs at most 30 comparisons. Everything in Part II is a variation of one idea: keep an invariant that says where the answer must be, and shrink the range while preserving it. KEY IDEA Think of binary search as finding the boundary of a predicate. For a sorted array and a target t , the predicate nums[i] >= t is false … false true … true . The first true is the lower bound. Exact search, insert position, first/last occurrence and sqrt are all "find the first true" in disguise. Variant Question answered Result when absent Exact search (704) Some index with nums[i] == t -1 Lower bound First index with nums[i] >= t n Upper bound First index with nums[i] > t n First / last occurrence (34) lowerBound(t) and upperBound(t) - 1 [-1, -1] Search insert position (35) Where t keeps the array sorted = lower bound Insert index Count of t upperBound(t) - lowerBound(t) 0 B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals The input is sorted (or sorted after a cheap pre-step) and the statement asks to find, locate, count or insert. The required complexity is O(log n) , or n is so large ( 10 ⁹ +) that a linear scan is impossible. You can define a yes/no question about an index whose answer flips exactly once: false … false true … true . Phrases: "first/last position", "smallest index such that", "insert position", "closest to", "how many times does x appear". Linear search works but the interviewer says "can you do better?" on sorted data. DECISION RULE Sorted input + O(log n) hint → binary search. No sorted input but a monotone yes/no answer over a numeric range → binary search on the answer (Chapter 13). C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 25. Each step compares nums[mid] with the target and removes half of the remaining range, including mid itself. For duplicates, the predicate view is clearer. Searching 4 in [1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 7] : the predicate nums[i] >= 4 flips at index 2 (lower bound) and nums[i] > 4 flips at index 5 (upper bound). The occurrences are exactly [2, 5) . Figure 26. Red = predicate false, green = true. The occurrences of the target are [lower, upper) . INTUITION Choose the loop shape to match the question. Closed range [lo, hi] with while (lo <= hi) suits exact match (the answer may be mid , and we exclude it when wrong). Half-open range [lo, hi) with while (lo < hi) suits boundary search ( mid can still be the answer, so hi = mid , never mid - 1 ). D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: First and Last Position of an Element (LeetCode 34) Brute force: scan once, record the first and last index equal to t : O(n) . Correct, but the statement demands O(log n) . Binary search then expand: find any occurrence and walk outwards. Looks fast, but with n equal elements it degrades to O(n) . Observation: the first occurrence is the first index with nums[i] >= t ; the last occurrence is the first index with nums[i] > t , minus one. Optimal: two boundary searches sharing one helper: O(log n) time, O(1) space. E. PART II · BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS 13 Binary Search on Answer No sorted array? Search the range of possible answers with a feasibility check. A. Pattern Overview In binary search on the answer the sorted thing is not the input but the space of candidate answers . You guess a value x , ask "is x feasible?" with a greedy or counting check in O(n) , and use the fact that feasibility is monotone (if speed 5 works, speed 6 works; if capacity 10 fails, capacity 9 fails) to discard half of the candidates. Total cost: O(n · log(range)) . KEY IDEA The recipe: (1) define feasible(x) ; (2) prove it is monotone; (3) bound the answer: lo = smallest conceivable, hi = a value that is surely feasible; (4) binary search for the first feasible (minimise) or the last feasible (maximise). Family Reads as Feasible region Loop shape Minimise the maximum "smallest capacity / speed / largest-sum such that …" F F F T T T (large values work) hi = mid on success; lo = mid + 1 on failure Maximise the minimum "largest minimum distance / sweetness such that …" T T T F F F (small values work) lo = mid on success ( upper mid); hi = mid - 1 on failure Kth / count-based "kth smallest value in a structure" count(≤ x) ≥ k is monotone Search the value range, count with a staircase B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Minimise the maximum" or "maximise the minimum" appears in the statement: the unmistakable fingerprint. The answer is a number in a bounded range (speed, capacity, days, distance, limit), and given a candidate you can verify it greedily in O(n) . A brute force tries every answer 1, 2, 3, … ; the feasibility pattern suggests answers are ordered by difficulty. Constraints: values up to 10 ⁹ or 10¹ ⁵ (a linear sweep of the answer range is impossible) but the array has n ≤ 10 ⁵ . Splitting, partitioning or scheduling into at most k groups / days / workers. TWO-QUESTION TEST Ask: "If I told you the answer was x , could I check it quickly, and would a bigger (or smaller) x be at least as easy?" Two yeses mean binary search on the answer. CHECK MONOTONICITY If feasibility is not monotone (for example, "is there a subarray of length exactly L with sum S " with negatives), binary search is invalid. Check monotonicity before coding. C. A bad lo can skip the answer; a bad hi can make the search return an infeasible value. D. Observation 2: if capacity c works, any c' > c works too, so feasibility is monotone. Optimal: binary search c over that range, checking each with a greedy packing: O(n · log Σ w) , O(1) space. E. PART II · BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS 14 Binary Search in Rotated Arrays One half is always sorted: use it to decide where to go, even when the whole array is not. A. Pattern Overview A rotated sorted array is a sorted array whose prefix was moved to the back: [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] becomes [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] (the last four elements moved to the front, i.e. a right rotation by 4). It is no longer globally sorted, but it consists of two sorted runs joined at a single "drop" (the pivot , which is also the minimum). Binary search still works because, for any mid , at least one of [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] is fully sorted , and a sorted half lets you test in O(1) whether the target lies inside it. KEY IDEA Two flavours: (1) find the minimum / pivot by comparing nums[mid] with nums[hi] ; search a target by identifying the sorted half and checking membership. With duplicates the sorted half can be unidentifiable, and the worst case becomes O(n) . Task Compare Rule Time Find minimum (distinct) nums[mid] vs nums[hi] > → lo = mid + 1 ; else hi = mid O(log n) Search target (distinct) nums[lo] vs nums[mid] Left sorted if nums[lo] <= nums[mid] O(log n) Find minimum (duplicates) nums[mid] vs nums[hi] Equal → hi-- O(n) worst case Search target (duplicates) three-way equality nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] → lo++, hi-- O(n) worst case Rotation count index of the minimum Distinct values only O(log n) B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals The statement says "sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot" and asks to search , find the minimum , or count rotations. Required complexity O(log n) on data that is almost sorted: two ascending runs with one drop. A circular sorted structure (ring buffer, log files that wrap) where the logical start is unknown. Follow-up flavour: "what if there are duplicates ?" (a classic interviewer escalation). KEY QUESTION Whenever the array "is sorted except for one wrap-around", ask: which half of [lo, hi] is sorted right now? The answer drives every decision. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 28. The pivot can lie in only one of the two halves; the other half is therefore a plain sorted range. Searching 0 : the left half [4..7] is sorted but 0 is not in [4, 7) , so go right. Finding the minimum: if nums[mid] > nums[hi] , the drop lies strictly to the right of mid ; otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left. Comparing with hi (not lo ) is what makes the minimum search correct for non-rotated input as well. INTUITION Why compare with nums[hi] and not nums[lo] ? If the array is not rotated , nums[mid] >= nums[lo] always holds and says nothing about the pivot; nums[mid] <= nums[hi] correctly reports "no drop on the right". D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Search in Rotated Sorted Array (LeetCode 33) Brute force: linear scan: O(n) . Ignores the structure. Two-step: find the pivot with one binary search, then binary search the correct run: O(log n) with two loops and index arithmetic. Single pass: at each step decide which half is sorted; if the target lies in that half's value range, go there, else go to the other half. O(log n) with one loop. With duplicates: when nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] no half can be proved sorted; shrink both ends by one. Worst case O(n) (for example [1,1,1,1,1,0,1] ). E. PART II · BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS 15 Binary Search in 2D Matrices Flatten it when it is one sorted list; walk the staircase when only rows and columns are sorted. A. Pattern Overview Two matrix shapes look alike but need different algorithms. The fully ordered matrix (each row sorted, and each row starts after the previous row ends) is one sorted array in disguise: binary search the virtual index 0 … rows·cols − 1 . The row-and-column-sorted matrix (rows ascend left to right, columns ascend top to bottom, but rows overlap) has no single order, so use the staircase walk from a corner that gives an unambiguous decision at every step. Matrix property Algorithm Time Space Rows sorted and row i+1 starts after row i Binary search on flattened index; (mid / O(log(m·n)) O(1) ends (LC 74) cols, mid % cols) Rows sorted, columns sorted, rows overlap (LC Staircase from top-right (or bottom-left) O(m + n) O(1) 240) Same as above, but need the kth smallest (LC Binary search on the value range with O(n · log O(1) 378) staircase counting range) Only rows sorted Binary search each row O(m log n) O(1) B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals A matrix described as "sorted" : read the exact sentence . "First integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row" means flatten. "Each row sorted left to right and each column sorted top to bottom" means staircase (flattening would be wrong). Constraints suggest O(log(mn)) or O(m + n) , not O(mn) . "Kth smallest in a sorted matrix" with memory limits that forbid copying everything: value-range binary search. MOST COMMON TRAP Do not flatten a matrix whose rows overlap ( [[1,4,7],[2,5,8]] ). Index order is not value order, so the monotone predicate does not exist. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Flatten: with cols columns, virtual index k maps to row k / cols and column k % cols . Searching 16 in the fully ordered matrix probes virtual indices 5, 8, 6 and finds it at index 6 = (1, 2) . Figure 29. Probes (1,1) → (2,0) → (1,2) : three comparisons for 12 virtual positions. Staircase: start at the top-right corner. It is the largest value in its row and the smallest in its column, so comparing it with the target eliminates a whole row or a whole column. Figure 30. The walk visits at most m + n − 1 cells. INTUITION Why the corner? From the top-right , the two moves are unambiguous: left decreases the value, down increases it. From the top-left both moves increase the value, so no decision is possible. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Search a 2D Matrix II (LeetCode 240) Brute force: scan all m·n cells: O(mn) . Row-wise binary search: binary search each row: O(m log n) . Better, but ignores the column order. Skip impossible rows: only search rows where row[0] <= t <= row[n-1] . Still O(m log worst case. Optimal: staircase from a corner, discarding a row or column per step: O(m + n) . (A divide-and-conquer binary search also exists, O(m log n) or better, but is harder to write.) For the fully ordered matrix (LC 74) the improvement goes further: one binary search over m·n elements is O(log(mn)) = O(log m + log n) , which beats the staircase. E. PART II · BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS 16 Unbounded and Unknown-Size Search No length? Double the boundary until it overshoots, then binary search the bracket. A. Pattern Overview Binary search needs a right end. When the array length is unknown (a stream, a paged API, an ArrayReader with no length() ) or the domain is unbounded ("smallest x such that f(x) ≥ target " with no upper limit), first find a bracket [lo, hi] that must contain the answer by doubling hi , then run an ordinary binary search inside it. This is exponential search (also called galloping or doubling search). KEY IDEA Two phases: (1) Grow: lo = hi; hi *= 2 until get(hi) >= target . (2) Shrink: binary search [lo, hi] . If the answer is at position p , phase 1 takes O(log p) probes and the bracket has size O(p) , so phase 2 also takes O(log p) . Total O(log p) , independent of the (possibly enormous or infinite) array size. Situation What you do Cost Sorted array, unknown length (LC 702) Double the index until the value passes the target O(log p) Monotone f(x) over [1, ∞ ) Double x until f(x) >= goal , then binary search O(log answer) Target near the front of a huge sorted Galloping beats plain binary search ( O(log p) vs O(log p) array O(log n) ) Merging a tiny list into a huge one Gallop through the big list (the idea behind TimSort's galloping mode) O(k log(n/k)) B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals The statement says "unknown size", "infinite", "you cannot call length()" , or hides the array behind an interface with get(i) . Out-of-range reads return a sentinel ( Integer.MAX_VALUE , null , an error code) instead of throwing. The search domain is all positive integers and a monotone function decides if a candidate is too small. You need O(log p) where p is the answer's position, not the container size. DECISION RULE Sorted + "no right bound" → first manufacture the right bound by doubling. Then it is Chapter 12 again. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 31. Grey cells are never read. Four probes found the bracket [4, 8] ; the second phase needs only about log ₂ 5 more. INTUITION Out-of-range handling is the trick. If reads past the end return Integer.MAX_VALUE , they behave like an enormous value, so the doubling loop stops and the binary search steers left. If the real API throws, catch it (or call a bounds check) and treat it as "too large". D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Search in a Sorted Array of Unknown Size (LeetCode 702, premium) Brute force: scan get(0), get(1), … until found or the sentinel appears: O(p) . Fixed big right bound: set hi = 10 ⁴ and binary search. Works only because the constraints cap the size; reads O(log 10 ⁴ ) always, and fails if the cap is wrong. Optimal: doubling to find the bracket ( O(log p) ), then binary search ( O(log p) ): correct for any size. E. Galloping merge To merge a short sorted list into a very long one, advance in the long list by exponentially growing strides, then binary search the last stride. PART II · BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS 17 Peak Finding and Bitonic Search Follow the slope: a local comparison tells you which side must contain a peak. A. Pattern Overview Binary search does not need a sorted array; it needs a local test that tells you which half to keep . In a peak-finding problem the test is the slope at mid : if nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] the ground rises to the right, so a peak must exist on the right (the array eventually ends, treating nums[n] = − ∞ ); otherwise a peak exists at mid or to its left. A bitonic (mountain) array increases strictly to one peak and then decreases strictly; it is the special case with exactly one peak, and searching it means find the peak, then binary search each side. KEY IDEA Slope rule: compare nums[mid] with its neighbour nums[mid + 1] and move toward the higher neighbour. A peak is guaranteed in that direction because the boundary is treated as − ∞ . Task Test at mid Move Time Find any peak (LC 162) nums[mid] < nums[mid+1] True → lo = mid + 1 ; false → hi = mid O(log n) Peak of a mountain (LC 852) same same O(log n) Find target in a mountain (LC 1095) peak first, then ascending and descending searches Left side first O(log n) Peak in a 2D grid (LC 1901) Max of the middle column vs its neighbours Move to the larger side O(m log n) B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Find a peak element" where any peak is acceptable and neighbours differ ( nums[i] != nums[i+1] ). The array is described as a mountain, bitonic , "increases then decreases" , or has a single maximum. Required complexity O(log n) for a non-sorted array: the only structure available is the slope. The comparison of mid with its neighbour can reveal a direction (unimodal functions, hill climbing in one dimension). Limited access (a MountainArray interface with a call budget): you must reuse reads carefully. DECISION RULE Unsorted + O(log n) + "peak / maximum / local" → compare with the neighbour, not with a target. For a unimodal function you can also use ternary search, but the neighbour comparison on integers is simpler and exact. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 32. Rising slope: peak to the right. Falling slope: the peak is mid or to the left. The range always contains a peak. INTUITION Why a peak must exist in the kept half. Suppose nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] . Walk right from mid + 1 : either the values keep rising until the array ends (the last element is a peak because nums[n] = − ∞ ), or they eventually fall, and the point where they first fall is a peak. Either way, a peak lives in [mid + 1, hi] . The same argument works to the left when the slope falls. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Find in Mountain Array (LeetCode 1095) Brute force: read every element: O(n) calls, which exceeds the allowed budget of 100 get() calls for n up to 10⁴. Find the peak: binary search with the slope rule: about log ₂ n iterations, 2 reads each. Search the ascending side [0, peak] with ordinary binary search. If found, return immediately: the smaller index wins. Otherwise search the descending side [peak + 1, n − 1] with the comparison flipped. Total: three binary searches, O(log n) time and reads, O(1) space. E. Because the mountain has a single peak, the answer is unique and also the maximum value: FindPeakElement.findPeakElement solves it unchanged. Search in a Mountain Array with a read budget FindInMountainArray above performs about 3 · log ₂ n reads. To cut reads further, cache get(mid) and get(mid + 1) in local variables instead of re-reading. Find a peak in a 2D grid (LeetCode 1901) Pick the middle column, find its row maximum, compare with the left and right neighbours, and move toward the larger neighbour (a peak must exist there). That halves the columns each step: O(m log n) . Unimodal functions and ternary search For a unimodal real function, ternary search narrows [lo, hi] by thirds. For integer arrays prefer the neighbour comparison: it is exact, simpler, and needs one comparison per step. Related hard problem: Median of Two Sorted Arrays (LeetCode 4) binary searches the partition point of the shorter array in O(log(min(m, n))) ; it uses the same "local test decides direction" reasoning. Equal neighbours break the guarantee If nums[i] == nums[i+1] is allowed (plateaus), the slope test can be ambiguous and the worst case degrades to O(n) . LeetCode 162 guarantees distinct neighbours; confirm that in an interview. H. PART III · HASHING & FREQUENCY PATTERNS 18 HashMap and HashSet Patterns Trade O(n) memory for O(1) lookups: complements, groups, and membership. A. Pattern Overview A hash table maps a key to a bucket in O(1) expected time. Three jobs cover most interview use: Job Question it answers Structure Classic problems Complement lookup "Have I already seen the partner of this element?" HashMap<value, index> Two Sum (1), 4Sum II (454), Subarray Sum Equals K (Chapter 3) Membership / "Is this value present? Have I seen HashSet Longest Consecutive Sequence deduplication it?" (128), Contains Duplicate II (219) Grouping by canonical "Which items are equivalent?" HashMap<key, Group Anagrams (49), key List<item>> Isomorphic Strings (205) Counting "How many of each?" HashMap<item, count> or an array Valid Anagram (242), Ransom Note (383); more in Chapter 19 KEY IDEA The hashing bargain. A nested loop asks "is there a j such that …?" in O(n) per element. If the condition can be rewritten as " key(j) equals something I can compute from i " , a hash lookup answers it in O(1) . Every pattern in this chapter is that rewrite: find the key. Collection add / get / remove Ordered? Use when HashMap / HashSet O(1) expected No Default choice LinkedHashMap / LinkedHashSet O(1) Insertion order Deterministic output, LRU (Part V) TreeMap / TreeSet O(log n) Sorted by key Floor / ceiling, range queries int[] / boolean[] O(1) worst By index Small, dense key domain (letters, digits, 0..n ) B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Find two (or four) elements that add to / differ by a target" on unsorted data, and indices matter or sorting is unwanted: complement lookup. "Have we seen this before?" , duplicate, first repeated, within distance k : a set (a window of a set for the distance variant). "Group / categorise / bucket the items" where equivalent items differ only in arrangement: canonical key. "Longest sequence of consecutive integers" , order-independent: a set plus only start counting at sequence starts. A nested loop whose inner test is an equality after algebra ( a + b == t → b == t − a ). Constraints around n ≤ 10 ⁵ and the brute force is O(n²) ; memory is not tight. CHOOSING THE TOOL Sorted input and no indices needed → two pointers (Chapter 1) beats a map ( O(1) space). Unsorted input or indices required → hash map . Range or nearest-neighbour queries → TreeMap /binary search (Part II). C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Complement lookup. For nums = [2, 7, 11, 15] and target = 9 : at each element ask the map "is target − x already stored?" If yes, the pair is complete; otherwise store x → i . Looking up before inserting guarantees an element is never paired with itself. Figure 33. The map stores what has been seen; each element asks a single O(1) question. Longest consecutive sequence. Put all numbers in a set. A number x starts a run only if x − 1 is absent ; walk upward from starts only. Each element is visited a constant number of times, so the loop is O(n) even though it contains a while . Figure 34. Elements such as 2, 3, 4 are skipped immediately because their predecessor exists. INTUITION Why the "is it a start?" test matters. Without it, every element starts a walk and [1, 2, 3, …, n] costs O(n²) . With it, each run is walked exactly once from its first element: total O(n) . Under the hood. A bucket index is hash(key) & (capacity − 1) . Keys that collide share a bucket, chained as a linked list (Java 8+ converts a long chain into a balanced tree). Good hashing and a load factor around 0.75 keep chains short, giving O(1) expected time. Key Bucket (key & 3) Chain after insert (head first) 5 1 5 9 1 9 → 5 1 1 1→9→5 Key Bucket (key & 3) Chain after insert (head first) 13 1 13→1→9→5 6 2 6 Capacity 4: keys 5, 9, 1, 13 all land in bucket 1 (a collision chain); 6 lands in bucket 2. Resizing at load factor 0.75 spreads them out. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Group Anagrams (LeetCode 49) Brute force: compare every pair of words for anagram-ness ( O(n² · L) ), then merge groups. Sorted-letters key: sort each word's characters and use it as the map key: O(n · L log L) . Count-signature key: for lowercase letters, a 26 -slot count array rendered as a string ( 1#0#0#… ) is the key: O(n · L) . Optimal in practice: the count signature; mind the separator so [1, 11] and [11, 1] do not collide. The same "find the canonical key" step applies to Isomorphic Strings (key = pattern of first occurrences, or two-way maps), Find Duplicate File (key = content), Group Shifted Strings (key = difference sequence). MyHashMap.java — LeetCode 706 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 706 - Design HashMap: separate chaining, power-of-two table, resize at load factor * 0.75. */ public class MyHashMap { private static final class Node { final int key; int value; Node next; Node(int key, int value, Node next) { this.key = key; this.value = value; this.next = next; } } private Node[] table = new Node[16]; private int size; private int indexFor(int key, int length) { // spread high bits into the low bits (as java.util.HashMap does) int h = key ^ (key >>> 16); return h & (length - 1); // length is a power of two, so & replaces % } public void put(int key, int value) { int i = indexFor(key, table.length); for (Node n = table[i]; n != null; n = n.next) { if (n.key == key) { n.value = value; // overwrite return; } } table[i] = new Node(key, value, table[i]); // insert at the head of the chain if (++size > table.length * 3 / 4) resize(); } public int get(int key) { for (Node n = table[indexFor(key, table.length)]; n != null; n = n.next) { if (n.key == key) return n.value; } return -1; } public void remove(int key) { int i = indexFor(key, table.length); Node prev = null; for (Node n = table[i]; n != null; prev = n, n = n.next) { if (n.key == key) { if (prev == null) table[i] = n.next; else prev.next = n.next; size--; return; } } } private void resize() { Node[] bigger = new Node[table.length * 2]; for (Node head : table) { for (Node n = head; n != null; ) { Node next = n.next; // save before relinking int i = indexFor(n.key, bigger.length); n.next = bigger[i]; bigger[i] = n; n = next; } } table = bigger; } public int size() { return size; } } TIME O(1) expected per operation SPACE O(n) hash ^ (hash >>> 16) mixes high bits so that power-of-two masks still distribute well, as in java.util.HashMap . PART III · HASHING & FREQUENCY PATTERNS 19 Frequency-Based Patterns Count first, then select: Top K by bucket sort, heap, or counting sort. A. Pattern Overview Many problems reduce to two steps : (1) build a frequency map in O(n) , (2) select, sort or compare by frequency. The interesting design choice is step 2, because the number of distinct values d and the requested k change which tool wins. Selection tool Time Space Best when Sort the entries by frequency O(d log d) O(d) Simplicity; d small Min-heap of size k O(d log k) O(d + k) k � d , streaming data Bucket sort by frequency O(n) O(n) Frequencies are bounded by n : the interview-optimal answer for Top K Counting sort over a small O(n + σ ) O( σ ) Letters, digits, small ranges alphabet Quickselect on the entries O(d) average O(d) Only the kth boundary is needed, order within the top k is free (Part XII) KEY IDEA Frequencies are bounded by n . That single fact lets you replace comparison sorting by an array of buckets indexed by frequency : bucket f lists the values that occur exactly f times. Reading the buckets from n down to 1 yields values in descending frequency, with no sorting. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Top K frequent / most common / least common" : map + heap or buckets. "Sort by frequency" of characters, words or integers: map + custom comparator or counting sort. "Rearrange so no two adjacent items are equal" (reorganize, task scheduler): greedy on the most frequent item with a max-heap. "Majority / more than n/k " with relaxed space: counting map (strict O(1) space leads to Boyer-Moore, Chapter 9). "Longest subsequence where values differ by at most 1" and similar value-pair constraints: only neighbouring values matter, so look at count[x] + count[x + 1] . Ties specified ("alphabetical order if equal"): the comparator must have two keys. DECISION RULE "Top K" + "frequent" + O(n) required → bucket sort . "Top K" + data stream or huge n + small k → size-k heap . "Sorted by frequency, ties by value" → map + two-key comparator. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Figure 35. Bucket index = frequency. The array has n + 1 slots because a value can appear at most n times. Size-k min-heap. Keep the k best candidates seen so far in a min-heap keyed by frequency. When a new entry makes the heap exceed k , remove the smallest : it can never belong to the top k . Why a min-heap for a top-k problem? Because the element you need fast access to is the weakest one currently kept , the one to evict. INTUITION Tie-breaking in the heap comparator. For Top K Frequent Words (higher frequency first, alphabetical on ties) the heap is a min-heap whose top is the worst kept word: lowest frequency, and for equal frequency the alphabetically larger word. Reverse the comparison for the second key; that inversion is the usual bug. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Example: Top K Frequent Elements (LeetCode 347) Brute force: for each distinct value, count it by scanning ( O(n·d) ), then pick the k largest. Map + sort: count in O(n) , sort the d entries by count: O(n + d log d) . The statement asks for better than O(n log n) . Map + size-k min-heap: O(n + d log k) . Good, and it works on streams. Map + bucket sort: index buckets by frequency ( ≤ n ), scan from high to low: O(n) time and O(n) space. E. Reduce fractions, normalise signs, sort or count letters, subtract the shared part of an equation. If you can compute the key in O(1) or O(L) , the rest is a HashMap<key, count> . B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Pairs (i, j) satisfying an equation where you can move all i terms to one side and all j terms to the other: hash the key of one side ( a + rev(b) = b + rev(a) → a − rev(a) = b − rev(b) ). normalise the sign; use squared distances instead of square roots. "Points on the same line / same distance" : reduce the slope to lowest terms with gcd and Values bounded by a small constant (digits, 0..1000 , ASCII): a counting array replaces both sorting and hash maps. Fixed-length windows over a small alphabet (DNA, binary strings, lowercase letters): pack into an integer so equal windows have equal ints. "Line / cut that crosses the fewest items" : maximise coincident boundaries with a gap map. A comparison that uses floating point (slopes, ratios): replace it with an exact integer key. NO FLOATING POINT KEYS Never hash a double slope. 1/3 and 2/6 may not compare equal in floating point, and 1e-9 differences create false classes. Always use a reduced integer pair or a cross-product test. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Counting sort. For values in 0..9 , count each value, take prefix sums to learn the end position of each value in the output, then place elements right to left so equal keys keep their relative order (stability). PART IV · LINKED LIST PATTERNS 21 Fast and Slow Pointers Two runners at different speeds: middle, cycles, and n-th from the end. A. Pattern Overview A singly linked list has no random access: to reach the middle you must walk there. The fast and slow pointer pattern (also called the tortoise and hare , after Floyd) moves two references through the structure at different speeds, or with a fixed gap, so that their relative position answers a question about the whole list in one pass and O(1) extra space. Every list in this part uses the node below. It is shown once; later chapters refer to it as ListNode and never redefine it. After t steps, fast has travelled exactly twice as far as slow . When fast falls off the end, slow is halfway. If the structure loops, fast gains one node per step on slow inside the loop, so it must catch it. Both facts follow from the speed ratio alone. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Find the middle" of a list whose length is unknown, or "split the list in half" : slow lands there when fast finishes. "Detect a cycle" , "where does the cycle begin", "is the sequence eventually periodic" : Floyd's algorithm, O(1) space instead of a HashSet . " n -th node from the end" , "remove the k -th last" : a gap of n nodes between two pointers, one pass. "Do two lists meet" , "first common node" : switching heads so both pointers travel lenA + lenB . A function f applied repeatedly to a value (digit squares, nums[i] , next index ) and a question about repetition : the sequence is a linked list in disguise. The constraint says O(1) extra space and the obvious answer uses a set, a counter pass, or an array copy.
