Floyd's cycle detection: why the pointers must meet Suppose the list has a tail of a nodes before the cycle, and the cycle has c nodes. Once slow enters the cycle, fast is already somewhere inside it. Each step fast moves one node closer to slow (it gains 2 − 1 = 1 node of distance), so the gap shrinks by one per step and reaches zero within c steps. They cannot jump over each other, because the gap changes by exactly one. Figure 38. Floyd's meeting on a tail-3, cycle-6 list: the pointers meet at G, three nodes past the entrance D. Finding the entrance. Let b be the distance from the entrance to the meeting point. When they meet, slow has walked a + b , and fast has walked a + b + k·c for some k ≥ 1 (it completed k extra laps). Since fast is twice as fast, 2(a + b) = a + b + k·c , so INTUITION a = k·c − b = (k − 1)·c + (c − b) . Walking a nodes from the head and walking a nodes from the meeting point therefore lands both pointers on the entrance : the second walk goes c − b nodes to reach the entrance, then (k − 1) full laps. Phase 2 of the algorithm is exactly this: one pointer back to the head, both move one node at a time until they meet. In the figure a = 3 , b = 3 , c = 6 , k = 1 , so a = c − b = 3 : the head pointer and the meeting-point pointer both reach D after three steps. A fixed gap finds the n-th node from the end Advance lead by n nodes, then move both pointers until lead is on the last node. lag is then exactly n nodes behind the end, so lag.next is the target. Starting both at a dummy head handles the case where the head itself is removed. Figure 39. The gap between the pointers never changes, so lag stops exactly before the target. An array is a linked list: Find the Duplicate Number For nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2] treat index i as a node whose next is nums[i] . Because every value is in 1..n , node 0 is never the target of an edge, and some node has two incoming edges : that node is the duplicated value, and it is the entrance of a cycle. Figure 40. Two edges (3 → 2 and 4 → 2) point at node 2, so 2 is both the cycle entrance and the duplicated value. D. PART IV · LINKED LIST PATTERNS 22 Linked List Reversal Flip arrows in place: whole lists, sublists, and blocks of k nodes. A. Pattern Overview Reversing a linked list means re-pointing each next arrow to the previous node . No values move and no nodes are allocated: the same nodes end up in the opposite order in O(n) time and O(1) space. The pattern has three sizes, and each larger one is built from the smaller one. Level What is reversed Technique Classic problems Whole list Every node prev / cur / next loop (or recursion) Reverse Linked List (206) Sublist Positions left..right Walk to the node before left ; head-insertion or reverse-and-reconnect Reverse Linked List II (92) Blocks Every full block of k nodes Check k nodes exist; reverse the block; reconnect with the previous tail Reverse Nodes in k-Group (25), Swap Nodes in Pairs (24) As a subroutine The second half, or a copy of the list Middle + reverse + merge / compare Palindrome (234), Reorder List (143), Maximum Twin Sum (2130) Ring / cut Not a reversal, but the same pointer surgery Close the tail to the head, cut at a computed node Rotate List (61) KEY IDEA Three-step rule for any pointer change: (1) save the node you are about to lose ( next ), (2) re-link the arrow, (3) advance . Forgetting step 1 is the cause of nearly every linked-list bug: after cur.next = prev , the rest of the list is unreachable unless you saved it. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Reverse the list" , "reverse between positions", "reverse in groups of k ", "swap every two nodes". "Read the list backwards" or "compare the first half with the second half" with an O(1) space limit: reverse one half in place. "Pair the first with the last" , "twin" nodes, interleave front and back : reverse the second half, then walk two pointers. "Add two numbers stored as digit lists" with most significant digit first: reverse both (or use stacks). "Rotate by k " : not a reversal but a ring cut, and the same n -minus- k index arithmetic as the array version (Chapter 9). The statement says "do not modify the node values, only the nodes themselves" : relinking is expected. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations The three-pointer dance Keep prev (the already-reversed part, starting as null ), cur (the node being processed), and a temporary nxt (the rest). Each step flips one arrow and slides all three one node to the right. Figure 41. Green arrows are the flipped ones. When cur falls off the end, prev is the head of the reversed list. Recursion: trust the rest Assume reverseRecursive(head.next) returns the reversed rest, whose tail is head.next . Then head.next.next = head hangs head after that tail, and head.next = null ends the list. The recursion depth is n , so very long lists risk StackOverflowError : prefer the iterative version in production. Reverse a sublist by head-insertion To reverse positions 2..4 of 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 , stand on node before (position 1). Node cur (position 2) stays put and becomes the tail of the reversed segment. Each step takes the node after cur and inserts it right after before . After right − left moves the segment is reversed, and no reconnection step is needed. Figure 42. cur never moves in the list; it simply ends up as the segment's tail as nodes are inserted in front of it. Blocks of k For each block: (1) walk k nodes from groupPrev to find kth ; if it is null, fewer than k nodes remain, so stop and leave them untouched. (2) Reverse the k nodes, making the first node point to groupNext (so the tail already links to the rest). (3) Point groupPrev.next at the new block head ( kth ) and move groupPrev to the old first node, now the block's tail. Figure 43. Blocks are reversed independently; only a short final block is left alone. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Brute force (copy): push all values on a stack or into an array, then rewrite the node values in reverse. O(n) time and O(n) space, and it breaks when the task forbids changing values. Recursion: elegant, O(n) time, but O(n) call-stack space. Iterative three-pointer: O(n) time, O(1) space: the standard answer. Sublist / blocks: the same loop restricted to a window, plus reconnection of the window to its neighbours. Head-insertion folds the reconnection into the loop. For blocks of k , the naive plan reverses every k nodes without checking that k remain; the correct plan locates the k -th node first, so a short tail is left untouched. E. PART IV · LINKED LIST PATTERNS 23 Merge and Partition Weave sorted lists, split by a pivot, sort in O(1) extra space, and add digit lists. A. Pattern Overview Arrays are easy to sort and merge because you can index them. Linked lists are the opposite: merging is O(1) space (relink nodes, never copy), and indexing is impossible . That makes them the natural home of merge-based algorithms. This chapter covers the family: merge two lists, merge k lists, partition around a value, merge sort a list, and add two numbers digit by digit. Task Core move Cost Classic problems Merge two sorted lists Compare heads, append the smaller to a tail on a dummy O(m + n) , O(1) Merge Two Sorted Lists (21), Merge In Between (1669) Merge k sorted lists Min-heap of k heads, or merge pairwise (tournament) O(N log k) Merge k Sorted Lists (23) Partition Two dummy-headed chains, concatenated O(n) , O(1) , stable Partition List (86), Odd Even List (Chapter 24) Sort a list Split at the middle, sort halves, merge O(n log n) Sort List (148), Insertion Sort List (147) Add numbers Walk both lists, carry between columns O(max(m, n)) Add Two Numbers (2), Add Two Numbers II (445) KEY IDEA The dummy-head idiom. Create dummy = new ListNode(0) and a tail = dummy . Append by tail.next = node; tail = node . Return dummy.next . It removes the "is this the first node?" branch from every merge, partition and filter in this part of the book. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Merge two (or k ) sorted lists" : dummy head plus comparison; heap or divide and conquer for k > 2 . "Sort a linked list in O(n log n) ", especially with constant extra space (bottom-up) or no array copy : merge sort. "Rearrange so that all nodes less than x come before the others, preserving relative order" : two chains, then concatenate. "Numbers stored as lists of digits" : simulate column addition; carry may outlive both lists. "Merge sorted data from k sources / streams / files" : the k -way merge, the heart of external sorting. The input is already sorted in pieces: merging is cheaper than re-sorting. QUICK RULE Sorted + linked list + O(1) extra space almost always means relinking with a dummy head . k sorted inputs means heap (online) or divide and conquer (offline). C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Merge two sorted lists Maintain tail , the last node of the merged list. Compare the two heads and steal the smaller node: no node is copied. When one list is exhausted, attach the other in one step , because the remainder is already sorted. Figure 44. The result is built from the original nodes; teal nodes came from a , amber from b . Merge k sorted lists: heap or tournament With k lists and N nodes in total, merging them one after another costs O(kN) , because the accumulated list is re-walked k times. Two efficient plans: Plan Idea Time Space Prefer when Min-heap of heads Poll the smallest head, push its successor O(N log k) O(k) Streaming input, or k is small Divide and conquer Merge lists pairwise like a tournament, log k rounds O(N log k) O(log k) stack Offline, no heap needed, cache-friendly Sequential merge merge(merge(l1, l2), l3) … O(kN) O(1) Only for tiny k Collect and sort Dump all values into an array and sort O(N log N) O(N) Never in an interview Partition: two chains Walk the list once; append each node to the less chain or the greater-or-equal chain, each with its own dummy head. Finally attach the second chain to the first and null-terminate the second : its last node may still point into the old list. Figure 45. Both chains keep their original order (stable), which is why this is not quicksort's partition step. Merge sort fits linked lists Merge sort needs split and merge . On an array, merging needs O(n) scratch space; on a list, merging is relinking. The split uses the fast / slow pointers of Chapter 21 (first-middle form, so both halves are non-empty). Total O(n log n) time, O(log n) recursion stack; a bottom-up version removes the stack and uses O(1) space. Figure 46. Splitting is O(n) by walking, merging is O(n) by relinking; there are log n levels. Adding numbers: column by column With digits in reverse order (least significant first), the list order is the column order: add digit by digit with a carry. Keep looping while either list has nodes or the carry is non-zero: [9, 9] + [1] ends with a new node for the final carry. D. Sequential merge: fold the lists with merge : the answer list is walked up to k times: O(kN) . Min-heap: only the k current heads can be next, so keep them in a heap: O(N log k) , O(k) space. Divide and conquer: log k rounds of pairwise merges, each round touching every node once: O(N log k) , O(log k) stack, no heap overhead. PART IV · LINKED LIST PATTERNS 24 In-Place List Manipulation Dummy heads, pointer surgery, deep copies and design: the toolkit for everything else. A. Pattern Overview The previous three chapters taught named techniques. Most remaining list problems are pointer surgery : delete nodes, regroup them, copy a structure with extra pointers, flatten a nested one, or build the list class itself. They share one toolkit: a dummy head , the save / relink / advance rule, and, when a problem looks hard, a composition of the earlier patterns. Task Technique Cost Classic problems Delete by value Dummy head; prev.next = prev.next.next and do not advance after a deletion O(n) , O(1) Remove Linked List Elements (203), Remove Duplicates from Sorted List (83, 82) Delete a given node Copy the next node's value into it, then unlink the next node O(1) Delete Node in a Linked List (237) Regroup by position Two interleaved chains (odd / even), then concatenate O(n) , O(1) Odd Even Linked List (328) Compose patterns Middle (Ch. 21) + reverse half (Ch. 22) + interleave O(n) , O(1) Reorder List (143) Deep copy with extra Map original → copy, or weave copies into O(n) , O(n) or Copy List with Random pointers the list O(1) Pointer (138) Flatten a nested list At each child, splice its list between the parent and the parent's next O(n) , O(1) Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List (430) Design a list Sentinel node and a size counter; helper before(index) O(n) per index op Design Linked List (707), LRU Cache (Chapter 29) KEY IDEA The sentinel principle. A dummy node in front of the head (or a sentinel at each end of a doubly linked list) means every real node has a predecessor . Deleting or inserting at the head, in an empty list, or at the tail is then identical to the general case. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Remove all nodes with value x " , remove duplicates, remove a node : dummy head and a prev pointer. "Group the odd-indexed nodes together" , segregate, split into parts : independent chains, then concatenate (like Partition in Chapter 23). "Rearrange as L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 … ": it is Fast / Slow + Reverse + Merge: recognise the composition. "Deep copy" of a structure whose nodes have extra pointers ( random , child ): you need an original → copy mapping , in a map or in the structure itself. "Flatten" a list whose nodes may carry nested lists: splice, do not copy. "Implement a linked list / LRU / queue" : write the node class and the sentinel-based operations. DECOMPOSE FIRST If you can name the three earlier patterns hiding in a hard-looking list problem (fast / slow, reverse, merge), the problem usually becomes three short loops. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations A dummy head makes deletion uniform When the head itself may be deleted (for example removing 6 from 6 → 6 → 1 → 6 ), a bare head pointer needs a special loop first. With dummy → head , the same prev.next = prev.next.next handles every position. Do not advance prev after a deletion : the new prev.next has not been examined yet. Figure 47. Grey nodes are skipped by the arc. The head (a 6 ) was deleted without any special case. Compose patterns: Reorder List 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 becomes 1 → 5 → 2 → 4 → 3 . Find the first middle, reverse the second half , then interleave the two halves. Each step is a pattern you already know. Figure 48. Two halves, one reversed, then zipped: O(n) time and O(1) space. Deep copy by weaving To copy a list whose nodes also have a random pointer, you must know, for any original node, where its copy is . A HashMap<Node, Node> answers that in O(n) space. The O(1) -space trick stores the answer inside the list : place each copy right after its original, so original.next is its copy. Figure 49. The next pointer doubles as the original-to-copy map. The third pass must restore the original list. Flatten: splice the child between a node and its next For each node with a child , find the tail of the child list, connect tail.next to the node's old next , connect the node to the child, and null the child pointer . Nested children are handled automatically because the loop continues into the spliced nodes. D. Java Implementation Delete by value, with a dummy head RemoveDuplicates.java: LeetCode 203, 83, 82 /** LeetCode 203 / 83 / 82 - delete nodes by value with a dummy head. */ public class RemoveDuplicates { /** 203: remove every node whose value equals val. */ public static ListNode removeElements(ListNode head, int val) { ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), prev = dummy; while (prev.next != null) { if (prev.next.val == val) { prev.next = prev.next.next; // unlink; stay on prev } else { prev = prev.next; } } return dummy.next; } /** 83: keep one copy of each value in a sorted list. */ public static ListNode keepOne(ListNode head) { for (ListNode cur = head; cur != null && cur.next != null; ) { if (cur.val == cur.next.val) { cur.next = cur.next.next; } else { cur = cur.next; } } return head; } /** 82: drop every value that appears more than once in a sorted list. */ public static ListNode removeAllDuplicated(ListNode head) { ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), prev = dummy, cur = head; while (cur != null) { if (cur.next != null && cur.next.val == cur.val) { int v = cur.val; while (cur != null && cur.val == v) { cur = cur.next; // skip the whole run } prev.next = cur; } else { prev = cur; cur = cur.next; } } return dummy.next; } } Java 17+ TIME O(n) SPACE O(1) In 203 stay on prev after unlinking. In 82 skip the whole run, then decide whether to keep cur using the next node. Odd Even Linked List OddEvenList.java: LeetCode 328 Java 17+ /** LeetCode 328 - Odd Even Linked List: group by POSITION (not value), keeping order. */ public class OddEvenList { public static ListNode oddEvenList(ListNode head) { if (head == null || head.next == null) return head; ListNode odd = head, even = head.next, evenHead = even; while (even != null && even.next != null) { odd.next = even.next; // odd chain skips an even node odd = odd.next; even.next = odd.next; // even chain skips an odd node even = even.next; } odd.next = evenHead; // append the even chain return head; } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(1) Positions, not values. Remember evenHead before the loop: it is lost otherwise. Reorder List ReorderList.java: LeetCode 143 Java 17+ /** LeetCode 143 - Reorder List: L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 ... = middle + reverse + interleave. */ public class ReorderList { public static void reorderList(ListNode head) { if (head == null || head.next == null) return; ListNode slow = head, fast = head; while (fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; } ListNode second = reverse(slow.next); // reverse the second half slow.next = null; // detach it from the first half ListNode first = head; while (second != null) { // the second half is never longer ListNode n1 = first.next, n2 = second.next; first.next = second; second.next = n1; first = n1; second = n2; } } private static ListNode reverse(ListNode head) { ListNode prev = null; while (head != null) { ListNode nxt = head.next; head.next = prev; prev = head; head = nxt; } return prev; } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(1) slow.next = null before interleaving: without the cut, the first half still points into the reversed half. Copy List with Random Pointer CopyRandomList.java: LeetCode 138 Java 17+ import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; /** * LeetCode 138 - Copy List with Random Pointer: hash map version and O(1)-space interleaving. */ public class CopyRandomList { public static class Node { public int val; public Node next, random; public Node(int val) { this.val = val; } } /** O(n) time, O(n) space: map every original node to its copy. */ public static Node copyWithMap(Node head) { Map copyOf = new HashMap<>(); for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) copyOf.put(c, new Node(c.val)); for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) { copyOf.get(c).next = copyOf.get(c.next); // get(null) is null: handles the tail copyOf.get(c).random = copyOf.get(c.random); } return copyOf.get(head); } /** * O(n) time, O(1) extra space: weave A -> A' -> B -> B' ..., set randoms, then unweave. */ public static Node copyInterleaved(Node head) { if (head == null) return null; for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next.next) { Node twin = new Node(c.val); twin.next = c.next; c.next = twin; // A -> A' -> B } for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next.next) { if (c.random != null) c.next.random = c.random.next; // twin of the random target } Node copyHead = head.next; for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) { Node twin = c.next; c.next = twin.next; // restore the original chain twin.next = (c.next != null) ? c.next.next : null; } return copyHead; } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(n) map version, O(1) weave version The map version relies on get(null) == null . The weave version restores the original list in the third pass. Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List FlattenMultilevel.java: LeetCode 430 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 430 - Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List (children spliced in after their * parent). */ public class FlattenMultilevel { public static class Node { public int val; public Node prev, next, child; public Node(int val) { this.val = val; } } public static Node flatten(Node head) { for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next) { if (cur.child == null) continue; Node child = cur.child, tail = child; while (tail.next != null) { tail = tail.next; // last node of the child list } tail.next = cur.next; // child list ... -> parent's old next if (cur.next != null) cur.next.prev = tail; cur.next = child; // parent -> child list child.prev = cur; cur.child = null; } return head; } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(1) Repair prev pointers on both splice points, and set child = null : the problem requires it. Design Linked List A singly linked list with get , addAtHead , addAtTail , addAtIndex , deleteAtIndex . A sentinel node plus a size counter and one helper, before(index) , make every operation a two-line method. MyLinkedList.java: LeetCode 707 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 707 - Design Linked List: singly linked with a sentinel node and a size counter. */ public class MyLinkedList { private static class Node { int val; Node next; Node(int val) { this.val = val; } } private final Node sentinel = new Node(0); // its next is the real head private int size; /** The node BEFORE position index (the sentinel when index == 0). */ private Node before(int index) { Node p = sentinel; for (int i = 0; i = size) ? -1 : before(index).next.val; } public void addAtHead(int val) { addAtIndex(0, val); } public void addAtTail(int val) { addAtIndex(size, val); } public void addAtIndex(int index, int val) { if (index > size) return; // out of range: ignored Node prev = before(Math.max(index, 0)); Node node = new Node(val); node.next = prev.next; prev.next = node; size++; } public void deleteAtIndex(int index) { if (index = size) return; Node prev = before(index); prev.next = prev.next.next; size--; } } TIME O(index) per operation, O(1) for head operations SPACE O(n) before(index) returns the sentinel when index == 0 . Pattern Overview A stack gives you the most recent unfinished thing in O(1) . Whenever a problem has nesting (a closer must match the nearest opener), cancellation (a new element may destroy the previous one), or backtracking context (return to the state before a bracket), a stack is the natural model. This chapter covers the non-monotonic uses; the monotonic stack (next greater element) is Chapter 7. At every moment the stack holds exactly the unresolved part of the input, ordered from oldest (bottom) to newest (top). A well-formed solution states in one sentence what is on the stack; if you cannot say it, the algorithm is not clear yet. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Nested structure: brackets, tags, parentheses in expressions, k[encoded] strings, function call / return logs. "The most recent unmatched …" , "the nearest enclosing …", "undo the last …" : LIFO in plain words. Adjacent cancellation repeated until nothing changes: process left to right and let the top of the stack absorb the new item. "Remove the fewest characters to make the string valid" : mark unmatched positions with an index stack. A path or token stream with a back command ( .. , back , undo ): the stack is the history. Collisions where only one direction pair interacts (right-moving meets left-moving). RECURSION VS STACK A recursion that is only used to remember where you were is a stack in disguise. Write it iteratively with an explicit stack when depth could reach 10 ⁵ (Java's default call stack overflows near 10 ⁴ – 10 ⁵ frames). C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Push the expected closer For {[()]} : each opener pushes the closer it will need. A closer is valid only if it equals the top. This removes the separate map from opener to closer and makes the check a single comparison. Figure 50. The stack always holds the closers still owed, newest on top. Index stack with a wall: Longest Valid Parentheses Store indices of unmatched ( . After popping at a ) , the new top is the index just before the current valid run, so the run length is i − top . When the stack becomes empty, the ) itself is unmatched: push it as the new wall . Seeding the stack with −1 makes the first run work with no special case. Figure 51. Indices on the stack make run lengths a subtraction. Cancellation: the stack is the answer so far In Remove All Adjacent Duplicates the stack is the string built so far. A new character equal to the top cancels it; otherwise it is appended. For runs of k , keep (char, count) pairs and pop when the count reaches k . Context save: Decode String At [ you must remember two things about the outer level: the repeat count and the text built so far . Push both, start a fresh buffer, and at ] pop them, repeat the inner buffer, and append it to the restored text. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Brute force (repeated deletion): repeatedly remove () , [] , {} (or equal neighbours) until nothing changes: O(n²) , because each pass is O(n) and up to n/2 passes are needed. Stack: one left-to-right pass; each character is pushed and popped at most once: O(n) time, O(n) space. Constant space for one bracket type: a counter is enough for Valid Parentheses with ( only ; for Longest Valid Parentheses two scans (left-to-right, then right-to-left) with open and close counters give O(1) space. With several bracket kinds, the stack is unavoidable. The O(n²) repeated-deletion method is exactly what the book's test suite uses as an oracle for these solutions. E. CHAPTER SUMMARY A stack holds the unresolved part of the input, oldest at the bottom. Say in one sentence what it holds before coding. Brackets: push the expected closer; a closer must equal the top; the stack must be empty at the end. Use ArrayDeque , not Stack . Index stack + wall ( −1 ) turns run lengths into subtraction (Longest Valid Parentheses) and marks the unmatched positions to delete (Min Remove). Cancellation (adjacent duplicates, asteroids): compare with the top, so cascades are handled automatically; pop at most once per push gives O(n) . Context save ( k[...] ): push the outer state at an opener, pop and combine at the closer. Counts can have several digits.

PART V · STACK, QUEUE AND DESIGN 26 Expression Parsing and Evaluation Precedence, parentheses and postfix: calculators from stacks. A. Pattern Overview Evaluating 3 + 2 * 2 - (4 / 2) requires respecting precedence ( * and / bind tighter than + and - ), associativity ( 8 - 3 - 2 is (8 - 3) - 2 ) and parentheses . Three techniques cover every interview variant, in increasing generality: Technique Handles State Classic problems Sign + result stack + - and parentheses (no * / ) Saved (result, sign) per open bracket Basic Calculator (224) Term stack + - * / , no parentheses A stack of terms to be summed; * / merge into the top Basic Calculator II (227) Recursive descent + - * / , parentheses, any nesting One function per precedence level Basic Calculator III (772) Shunting-yard + RPN Anything; separates parsing from evaluation Operator stack, then a value stack Evaluate RPN (150), expression trees, compilers KEY IDEA Precedence is nesting in disguise. An expression is a sum of terms , a term is a product of factors , a factor is a number or a parenthesised expression. That three-level grammar is the whole parser: expr → term (± term)* , term → factor (× factor)* , factor → number | ( expr ) . B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Evaluate the expression string" with + - * / , spaces, and possibly parentheses. "Reverse Polish / postfix notation" , "convert infix to postfix", "build an expression tree". "Do not use eval ": the constraint is the exercise. "Add parentheses to maximise / count results" : interval DP (Different Ways to Add Parentheses, 241), not a stack. Operators with different priority , or unary minus, or a custom operator table: precedence climbing. CHOOSING THE TOOL No parentheses → term stack (one pass, O(1) extra beyond the terms). Parentheses but only + - → sign + result . Everything → recursive descent or shunting-yard. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Terms: * and / merge into the previous term Treat the expression as a sum of terms. When you read + 3 , push 3 ; for - 3 , push −3 ; for * 3 or / 3 , pop the last term, combine, push the result . At the end, sum the stack. Division is applied as soon as it is read, so 8 / 3 * 3 is (8 / 3) * 3 = 6 , as left-to-right evaluation requires. Parentheses: save and restore the context For + - only, keep result (the sum so far in the current bracket) and sign (the sign of the next operand). At ( , push result and sign , reset to 0 and +1 . At ) , finish the inner sum, then compute outer result + saved sign × inner . A leading − before ( is just the saved sign, so unary minus before a bracket needs no extra code. Shunting-yard: operators wait on a stack until something weaker arrives Read tokens left to right. Numbers go straight to the output. An operator first pops every stacked operator that binds at least as tightly (left-associativity), then is pushed. ( is pushed; ) pops to the output until ( . At the end, pop everything. The output is postfix , which needs no precedence rules to evaluate. Figure 52. The operator stack keeps lower-precedence operators waiting; the output is the postfix form. Postfix evaluation: operators pop two values Scan postfix tokens: push numbers; on an operator, pop the right operand first , then the left, apply, and push the result. After the last token, the single value left on the stack is the answer. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Brute force: find the innermost parentheses with a regex, evaluate the sub-expression, substitute, repeat: O(n²) and fragile. Two-pass precedence: first evaluate all * / , then all + - : works, but needs a token list and does not nest. Term stack (no parentheses): one pass, O(n) , and the precedence rule is a single case per operator. Recursive descent (with parentheses): one pass, O(n) , O(depth) stack; the code mirrors the grammar and extends to ^ , unary minus, functions. Shunting-yard + RPN: separates parsing from evaluation , which is how real compilers and calculators work, and lets you reuse the postfix form for expression trees. E. No brackets: a term stack ; * / merge into the top, + - push ±num , then sum. Apply the previous operator when the next one arrives, and flush at the end. PART V · STACK, QUEUE AND DESIGN 27 Queue Patterns and Conversions First in, first out: ring buffers, windows and stack-queue duality. A. Pattern Overview A queue serves the oldest item first. Interview problems use it in four ways: (1) simulation of turns or rounds, (2) a time window that evicts expired entries, (3) building the structure itself from other structures, and (4) level-by-level exploration (BFS), which arrives in Part VII and Part VIII. If fairness, arrival order, or a sliding time horizon appears in the statement, think queue. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Process in the order they arrived" , round-robin, each person takes a turn, the first to act bans the next : queue of indices. "In the last t seconds / last k elements" over a stream: a queue with eviction; keep a running aggregate so each query is O(1) . "Fixed capacity buffer" , wrap around, circular : ring buffer with head and size . "Implement a queue using stacks" (or the reverse): you are asked about amortisation. "First unique / first non-repeating" in a stream: a queue plus a count map, lazily discarding duplicates from the front. "Level by level" , shortest number of steps : BFS (Parts VII and VIII). JAVA CHOICE In Java use ArrayDeque for both queues and stacks. LinkedList allocates a node per element and allows null ; java.util.Queue is the interface, ArrayDeque the implementation. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations A queue from two stacks: lazy transfer Pushes go onto in . Pops and peeks use out , whose top is the oldest element. When out is empty, move everything from in to out (this reverses the order, turning newest-first into oldest-first). Never move while out is non-empty, or the order breaks. Each element moves at most once, so every operation is amortised O(1) , although one pop can cost O(n) . Figure 53. Transferring only when out is empty keeps the order correct and the cost amortised. The ring buffer Store the queue in an array of capacity k , with head (index of the front) and size . The next free slot is (head + size) % k ; the rear is (head + size − 1) % k . Tracking size (instead of two indices) removes the classic ambiguity that empty and full look the same when head == tail . Figure 54. Indices wrap with the modulo; size distinguishes empty from full. A sliding time window Append each timestamp. Before answering, evict from the front every timestamp older than t − 3000 . The queue size is the answer. Each timestamp is added and removed once, so a million pings cost O(10 ⁶ ) , not O(10 ⁶ · window) . For Moving Average keep a running sum : add the new value, subtract the evicted one. Turn-based simulation with indices In Dota2 Senate , each senator, on their turn, bans the next opponent. Put each side's indices in its own queue. Compare the fronts: the smaller index acts first, removes the other front, and re-enters its queue with index + n (its turn in the next round). The side whose queue empties loses. D. CHAPTER SUMMARY A queue serves the oldest item first: use it for arrival-order simulation, time windows with front eviction, and ring buffers. Two stacks make a queue: push to in ; move to out only when out is empty ; each element moves once, so operations are amortised O(1) . PART V · STACK, QUEUE AND DESIGN 28 Designing Data Structures Augment a stack, array or map so that one extra operation is also O(1). A. Pattern Overview Design problems ask for a class with a specified API and a complexity target (usually O(1) or O(log n) per operation). They are rarely about a clever algorithm; they are about choosing the right pair of structures and keeping them consistent. Nearly every answer is one of five moves: Move Idea Classic problems Remember with each Store extra data next to each element (the Min Stack (155), Max Stack (716) entry minimum so far, the previous state) Two coordinated A list for random access + a map for value → Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) (380) structures position Bucket by a key One stack / list per frequency, per key, per level Maximum Frequency Stack (895), Time Based Key-Value Store (981) Lazy work Record an update now, apply it when the data is touched Stack with Increment (1381) Cursor over history An array plus an index; truncate on a new action Browser History (1472), Undo / Redo KEY IDEA Read the API as a contract. For every method write the target complexity next to it. Then ask: which operation is the bottleneck for the naive structure? The fix is the extra structure that makes exactly that operation O(1) , at the price of maintaining it on every other operation. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Design a class that supports push , pop , and getMin in O(1) ": add a method that a plain structure lacks. " insert , remove , getRandom in O(1) ": random access needs an array; membership needs a hash map; deletion needs a swap-with-last trick. "Return the value at or before time t " : per-key history with binary search (timestamps arrive in order). "Pop the most frequent element, ties broken by recency" : a stack per frequency level. "Apply an operation to the bottom k elements" : tag the boundary lazily instead of looping. "Back / forward", "undo / redo" : a list with a cursor. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Min Stack: every entry knows the minimum beneath it A single min variable breaks when the minimum is popped. Store, with each element, the minimum of the stack up to and including it . Popping an element automatically restores the previous minimum. Figure 55. The second row is the answer to getMin() for each possible stack height. Insert / Delete / GetRandom in O(1): swap with the last An array gives O(1) random access, but deleting the middle shifts elements. Swap the element to delete with the last one, then remove the last : order is irrelevant for a set, so this is O(1) . A hash map from value to index lets you find the element and fix the moved element's index. Figure 56. Order is sacrificed, which a set does not need; getRandom stays uniform. Frequency Stack: a stack per frequency The element to pop is the one with the highest frequency , and among those the most recent. Keep freq[x] and a map level → stack . Pushing x for the f -th time puts it on the stack for level f ; the element stays on the stack for level f − 1 too, which is exactly what makes the next pop correct: after popping x from level f , its earlier push at level f − 1 is still there. Figure 57. Each element appears on one stack per occurrence; the highest non-empty level holds the answer. Lazy increments increment(k, val) adds val to the bottom k elements. Instead of looping, put val on lazy[k − 1] . When an element is popped, add its lazy value to the result and pass the tag down to the element below. Every operation is O(1) . D. Java Implementation Min Stack MinStack.java: LeetCode 155 import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** * LeetCode 155 - Min Stack: every entry remembers the minimum of the stack up to and * including it. */ public class MinStack { private final Deque stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); // {value, minimum so far} public void push(int val) { int min = stack.isEmpty() ? val : Math.min(val, stack.peek()[1]); stack.push(new int[]{val, min}); } public void pop() { stack.pop(); } public int top() { return stack.peek()[0]; } Java 17+ public int getMin() { return stack.peek()[1]; // O(1): no scan needed } } TIME O(1) per operation SPACE O(n) Alternative: a second stack of minima, pushed only when the value is <= the current minimum. The pair version is simpler and has the same asymptotics. Maximum Frequency Stack FreqStack.java: LeetCode 895 Java 17+ import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; /** * LeetCode 895 - Maximum Frequency Stack: one stack per frequency level; pop from the * highest. */ public class FreqStack { private final Map freq = new HashMap<>(); private final Map > levels = new HashMap<>(); private int maxFreq; public void push(int x) { int f = freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum); maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, f); levels.computeIfAbsent(f, k -> new ArrayDeque<>()).push(x); // x joins level f } public int pop() { Deque top = levels.get(maxFreq); int x = top.pop(); // most recent among the most frequent if (top.isEmpty()) maxFreq--; // that level is now empty freq.merge(x, -1, Integer::sum); return x; } } TIME O(1) per operation SPACE O(n) maxFreq only ever decreases by one on a pop , because the level below is non-empty whenever a higher one was. Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) RandomizedSet.java: LeetCode 380 import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Random; /** Java 17+ * LeetCode 380 - Insert Delete GetRandom O(1): array for random access, map for value -> * index. */ public class RandomizedSet { private final List items = new ArrayList<>(); private final Map indexOf = new HashMap<>(); private final Random random = new Random(); public boolean insert(int val) { if (indexOf.containsKey(val)) return false; indexOf.put(val, items.size()); items.add(val); return true; } public boolean remove(int val) { Integer idx = indexOf.remove(val); if (idx == null) return false; int last = items.remove(items.size() - 1); // O(1): removing the tail if (last != val) { // move the tail into the hole items.set(idx, last); indexOf.put(last, idx); } return true; } public int getRandom() { return items.get(random.nextInt(items.size())); } } TIME O(1) expected SPACE O(n) When the removed value is the last element, do not re-insert it into the map: the last != val guard prevents a stale entry. Time Based Key-Value Store TimeMap.java: LeetCode 981 Java 17+ import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * LeetCode 981 - Time Based Key-Value Store: per key, timestamps are increasing; binary * search them. */ public class TimeMap { private static class Entry { final int time; final String value; Entry(int time, String value) { this.time = time; this.value = value; } } private final Map > history = new HashMap<>(); /** Timestamps passed to set() for one key are strictly increasing. */ public void set(String key, String value, int timestamp) { history.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(new Entry(timestamp, value)); } /** Value with the largest timestamp list = history.get(key); if (list == null) return ""; // find the first entry with time > timestamp int lo = 0, hi = list.size(); while (lo TIME set O(1), get O(log n) SPACE O(n) The binary search finds the first time greater than the query; the answer is the entry just before it, or "" if there is none. Design Browser History BrowserHistory.java: LeetCode 1472 Java 17+ import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * LeetCode 1472 - Design Browser History: an array plus a cursor; visiting truncates the * forward pages. */ public class BrowserHistory { private final List pages = new ArrayList<>(); private int cur; public BrowserHistory(String homepage) { pages.add(homepage); } public void visit(String url) { // drop the forward history while (pages.size() > cur + 1) pages.remove(pages.size() - 1); pages.add(url); cur++; } public String back(int steps) { cur = Math.max(0, cur - steps); return pages.get(cur); } public String forward(int steps) { cur = Math.min(pages.size() - 1, cur + steps); return pages.get(cur); } } TIME amortised O(1) SPACE O(n) visit discards the forward pages; back and forward clamp the cursor with max / min . Stack with increment CustomStack.java: LeetCode 1381 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 1381 - Design a Stack With Increment Operation: lazy increments make inc() O(1). */ public class CustomStack { private final int[] stack; private final int[] lazy; // lazy[i] is owed by elements 0..i private int size; public CustomStack(int maxSize) { stack = new int[maxSize]; lazy = new int[maxSize]; } public void push(int x) { if (size 0) lazy[i - 1] += lazy[i]; // pass it down to the element below lazy[i] = 0; return value; } public void increment(int k, int val) { int i = Math.min(k, size) - 1; if (i >= 0) lazy[i] += val; // tag the top of the affected prefix } } TIME O(1) per operation SPACE O(maxSize) Apply the tag to the popped value, then pass it to the element below: otherwise the increment is lost. PART V · STACK, QUEUE AND DESIGN 29 LRU and LFU Cache Design A hash map plus ordered lists: O(1) lookup, O(1) update, O(1) eviction. A. Pattern Overview A cache keeps a bounded number of entries and must decide what to evict when it is full. Two policies dominate interviews and real systems: Policy Evicts Good when Structure for O(1) LRU (Least Recently The entry untouched for Recent access predicts HashMap<key, node> + doubly Used) the longest time future access (temporal locality) linked list ordered by recency LFU (Least Frequently The entry used the fewest A stable set of hot keys; HashMap + a bucket per Used) times; ties: least recently scans should not flush them frequency (ordered sets) + minFreq FIFO The oldest inserted entry Simple, predictable Queue + map TTL / expiry Entries older than a deadline Staleness matters Map + min-heap on expiry (or lazy check on read) KEY IDEA Why two structures? A hash map finds an entry in O(1) but has no order. A list keeps order but needs O(n) to find an entry. Storing the list node in the map gives both: find in O(1) , then move or remove that exact node in O(1) because a doubly linked list can unlink itself. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Design a cache with capacity k " , "get and put in O(1) ", "evict the least recently / frequently used". "Maintain items in order of recent use" and be able to move any item to the front in O(1) . "Ties broken by recency" inside a frequency class: ordered sets per frequency. Real-world cues: page replacement, CDN edge caches, database buffer pools, memoisation with bounded memory, @Cacheable with Caffeine (size-bounded, W-TinyLFU). ONE-LINE TEST Whenever a statement demands O(1) eviction in a stated order , it is a hash map pointing into an ordered linked structure. The order is the policy. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations LRU: most recent at the head, least recent at the tail Two sentinel nodes ( head , tail ) remove every empty-list and boundary case. The most recently used entry sits right after head ; the eviction victim is tail.prev . get and put on an existing key both unlink the node and re-insert it after head . A put on a new key inserts at the front and, if the cache is over capacity, removes tail.prev and its map entry. Figure 58. Each operation touches a constant number of pointers; the map locates the node directly. The three pointer operations • unlink(n): n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; addFirst(n) : n.next = head.next; n.prev = head; head.next.prev = n; head.next = n; evict() : lru = tail.prev; unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key); (so the node must store its key). Order matters in addFirst : read head.next before overwriting it. LFU: buckets by frequency Each key has a count . Keep buckets[f] = the keys with count f , in insertion-into-bucket order (a LinkedHashSet ), and minFreq . A touch moves the key from buckets[f] to buckets[f + 1] ; if buckets[f] becomes empty and f == minFreq , then minFreq++ . Eviction removes the first key of buckets[minFreq] (least frequent, then least recent). A new key has count 1 , so minFreq = 1 . Figure 59. Within a bucket the leftmost key is the least recently used; the lowest non-empty bucket is evicted first. Java ships an LRU: LinkedHashMap new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) orders entries by access (the true ), and overriding removeEldestEntry to return size() > capacity evicts automatically. It is five lines and perfectly acceptable in production code. In an interview, implement the list yourself first, then mention this. D. Java Implementation LRU cache with a hand-written doubly linked list LRUCache.java: LeetCode 146 Java 17+ import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; /** * LeetCode 146 - LRU Cache: HashMap for O(1) lookup + doubly linked list for O(1) recency * order. */ public class LRUCache { private static class Node { int key, value; Node prev, next; } private final int capacity; private final Map map = new HashMap<>(); // sentinels: MRU after head, LRU before tail private final Node head = new Node(), tail = new Node(); public LRUCache(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; } public int get(int key) { Node n = map.get(key); if (n == null) return -1; unlink(n); addFirst(n); // a read makes it most recently used return n.value; } public void put(int key, int value) { Node n = map.get(key); if (n != null) { n.value = value; unlink(n); addFirst(n); return; } if (map.size() == capacity) { Node lru = tail.prev; // evict the least recently used unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key); } n = new Node(); n.key = key; n.value = value; map.put(key, n); addFirst(n); } private void unlink(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; } private void addFirst(Node n) { n.next = head.next; n.prev = head; head.next.prev = n; head.next = n; } } TIME O(1) per operation SPACE O(capacity) The node stores its key , so eviction can remove the map entry. Sentinels mean unlink and addFirst have no null checks. LRU cache with LinkedHashMap LRUCacheLinkedHashMap.java: the idiomatic Java version Java 17+ import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; /** * LRU in six lines: LinkedHashMap in access order, evicting the eldest entry (what Java gives * you). */ public class LRUCacheLinkedHashMap extends LinkedHashMap { private final int capacity; public LRUCacheLinkedHashMap(int capacity) { // true = access order (get() reorders) super(16, 0.75f, true); this.capacity = capacity; } public int getOrDefault(int key) { return super.getOrDefault(key, -1); } @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest) { return size() > capacity; // called by put() after insertion } } TIME O(1) per operation SPACE O(capacity) accessOrder = true makes get reorder entries. This class is not thread-safe; wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap if needed. LFU cache with frequency buckets LFUCache.java: LeetCode 460 Java 17+ import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.LinkedHashSet; import java.util.Map; /** * LeetCode 460 - LFU Cache in O(1): a bucket per frequency, each bucket ordered by recency. */ public class LFUCache { private final int capacity; private final Map values = new HashMap<>(); private final Map counts = new HashMap<>(); // freq -> keys, oldest first private final Map > buckets = new HashMap<>(); private int minFreq; public LFUCache(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } public int get(int key) { if (!values.containsKey(key)) return -1; touch(key); return values.get(key); } public void put(int key, int value) { if (capacity == 0) return; if (values.containsKey(key)) { values.put(key, value); touch(key); return; } if (values.size() == capacity) { LinkedHashSet lowest = buckets.get(minFreq); int victim = lowest.iterator().next(); // least frequent, then least recent lowest.remove(victim); values.remove(victim); counts.remove(victim); } values.put(key, value); counts.put(key, 1); buckets.computeIfAbsent(1, f -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key); // a new key always has the lowest frequency minFreq = 1; } /** Move key from bucket f to bucket f + 1 and keep minFreq correct. */ private void touch(int key) { int f = counts.get(key); LinkedHashSet old = buckets.get(f); old.remove(key); if (old.isEmpty() && f == minFreq) minFreq++; counts.put(key, f + 1); buckets.computeIfAbsent(f + 1, x -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key); } } TIME O(1) per operation SPACE O(capacity) LinkedHashSet provides insertion order and O(1) removal by key. Capacity 0 must ignore every put . F. At put(4, 4) both remaining keys have count 2; key 1 was used less recently than key 3, so key 1 is evicted. G. Variations of the Pattern LRU with TTL Store an expiry time per entry. Lazy expiry checks on get ; active expiry uses a min-heap (or a timer wheel) keyed by expiry. Redis does both: lazy on access plus a periodic sampling of keys. Thread-safe LRU A single lock around get and put is correct but contended, since even a read mutates the list. Production caches (Caffeine, Guava) buffer reads and apply the reordering in batches, trading strict recency for throughput. Beyond LRU: LRU-K, ARC, and TinyLFU LRU is vulnerable to scans : one large sequential read flushes the whole cache. LRU-K (evict by the K-th most recent access), ARC (adaptive, balances recency and frequency) and W-TinyLFU (Caffeine's policy: a frequency sketch admits a new key only if it is hotter than the victim) resist scans. Memoisation with a bound LinkedHashMap with removeEldestEntry is the standard bounded memo table for recursive functions with large state spaces (Part XI): it keeps the working set and drops cold entries. Design a cache for a service Key space and size: estimate entries and bytes; choose capacity by memory, not count. Consistency: write-through, write-back or cache-aside; invalidate or expire on updates. Stampede protection: coalesce concurrent misses for one key (a per-key lock or future). Observability: hit ratio, eviction rate, load latency; a low hit ratio means the policy or the size is wrong. Interview Tips INTERVIEW Say the design in one sentence: "a hash map from key to a node of a doubly linked list ordered by recency, with sentinel head and tail". Then draw get(1) moving a node. Justify the doubly linked list: a singly linked list cannot unlink a node in O(1) without its predecessor. CHAPTER SUMMARY LRU = HashMap<key, node> + doubly linked list ordered by recency + sentinels. get and put unlink the node and re-insert it at the front; eviction removes tail.prev (and its map entry, so nodes store their key). A doubly linked list is required so that a node can unlink itself in O(1) ; the map gives direct access to that node. LFU = HashMap + LinkedHashSet per frequency + minFreq . A touch moves a key to bucket f + 1 ; bump minFreq when its bucket empties; a new key resets minFreq = 1 ; evict the first key of buckets[minFreq] . In Java, LinkedHashMap(accessOrder = true) + removeEldestEntry is a complete LRU in a few lines; know it, but be able to build the list by hand. In production, add TTL, thread-safety, stampede protection and metrics; scans defeat LRU, which is why policies like W-TinyLFU exist.

PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 30 Basic Recursion Patterns Base case, smaller problem, combine: three shapes of recursion. A. Pattern Overview A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance of the same problem. Every correct recursion has the same three parts: Base case: an input small enough to answer directly (it stops the recursion). Recursive step: reduce the input and call the function (trust that the call returns the right answer: the recursive leap of faith). Combine: turn the sub-answers into the answer for this input. The shape of the recursion (how many calls, and how fast the input shrinks) decides the cost. Almost every recursive problem in this book is one of these three shapes: Shape Calls per level Input shrinks by Depth Total work Examples Linear 1 n − 1 n O(n) Sum of a list, reverse a list, factorial Halving 1 n / 2 log n O(log n) Fast power (50), K-th Symbol (779), binary search Branching 2 or more n−1orn/2 n or log n O(2 ⁿ ) to O(n log n) Fibonacci, Hanoi, merge sort, subsets, permutations KEY IDEA Cost of a recursion = (number of calls) × (work per call). Draw the recursion tree: one node per call. Count the nodes, multiply by the work done in a node excluding its recursive calls. Everything in Part VI (subsets, permutations, N-Queens, Sudoku) is analysed this way. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals The answer for n is described using the answer for a smaller input: x^n from x^(n/2) , row n of a grammar from row n − 1 , the winner of n players from the winner of n − 1 . Self-similar structure: nested brackets, trees, folders, fractal patterns, "do the same thing to the rest". A natural halving: "divide the exponent / range / string in two" gives O(log n) depth. "Move n things using a helper" (Tower of Hanoi): the sub-problem uses the same rules with different roles. Overlapping sub-calls (the same arguments appear again and again) mean the plain recursion is exponential and the memoised version is a DP (Part XI). Core Intuition with Illustrations The call stack: recursion unwinds in reverse Each call gets its own frame on the call stack holding its parameters and local variables. Calls are pushed on the way down and popped on the way back, so the combine step of the deepest call runs first. Trace pow(2, 10) : the halving calls go 10 → 5 → 2 → 1 → 0 , and the answers are combined on the way back up. Variations of the Pattern Divide and conquer Split the input into independent parts, solve each, merge: merge sort ( T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n) ), quick select, Different Ways to Add Parentheses (241), Special Binary String (761). The parts must not overlap; otherwise memoise. Tail recursion and conversion to loops If the recursive call is the very last action ( return f(n − 1, acc * n) ), the function can become a loop. The JVM does not optimise tail calls , so a depth of 10⁵ throws StackOverflowError ; convert such recursions into loops, or use an explicit Deque as the stack. Mutual recursion Two functions call each other ( isEven / isOdd , a recursive-descent parser from Chapter 26). The same three parts apply. Recursion on structure (preview) Trees (Part VII), graphs (Part VIII, DFS) and linked lists (Part IV) are recursive structures: their natural algorithms are recursions on left / right or on next . Memoisation: when sub-calls repeat If a recursion on (i, j, …) is called twice with the same arguments, cache the result keyed by the arguments. A pure function with k distinct states and w work per state costs O(k·w) . This is top-down DP (Part XI). H. PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 31 Choose, Explore, Unchoose The backtracking template: build a path, recurse, undo. A. Pattern Overview Backtracking is recursion that builds a solution one decision at a time and undoes each decision after exploring it. The search space is a tree: every node is a partial solution (the path ), every edge is a choice. The whole technique is one three-line loop body: The universal template void backtrack(State state, List choices) { if (isComplete(state)) { record(state); return; } // base case for (Choice c : choicesAt(state)) { apply(c, state); // 1. choose backtrack(state, ...); // 2. explore undo(c, state); // 3. unchoose } } Java 17+ KEY IDEA State is shared and mutable; correctness depends on the undo. After explore returns, the state must be exactly what it was before choose . That one invariant is what makes siblings independent. Most backtracking bugs are a missing or asymmetric undo. Question to answer Examples in this chapter What is a complete solution? (when do I record?) Path length is 2n (parentheses); one letter per digit (phone); end of the string What are the choices at this node? ( or ) ; the letters on a key; keep or flip the case Which choices are illegal? (pruning) ) with nothing open; two equal adjacent letters How do I undo? deleteCharAt , remove(last) , restore the flipped bit B. Small constraints ( n ≤ 8 , n ≤ 12 , n ≤ 20 , a string of length ≤ 16): an exponential search is intended. A sequence of independent-looking decisions whose combination must satisfy a rule: balanced, no two adjacent equal, sum to target. "How many ways" with tiny n is also solvable this way; with large n it is DP. CHAPTER SUMMARY Template: if complete, record a copy ; otherwise for each legal choice: choose, explore, unchoose. The state is shared and mutable : every choose has a matching unchoose, so siblings start from the same state. Prune while choosing , not after: enforce the rule ( close < open , no equal neighbour) before recursing so that no dead prefix exists. PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 32 Subsets Every element is in or out: 2ⁿ subsets, with or without duplicates. A. Pattern Overview The subsets (power set) pattern enumerates every selection of elements, where order does not matter. For n distinct elements there are exactly 2 ⁿ subsets. There are three equivalent ways to see the search tree: View Decision at each step Tree shape Answers are Best for Include / exclude Take nums[i] or not Binary tree of depth n Leaves ( 2 ⁿ ) Counting, subset-sum style problems Pick the next element Which index ≥ start comes next Each node has n − start children Every node Duplicates, size limits, combinations Bitmask Bit j of an integer No recursion Integers 0 … n ≤ 20 , speed, small code 2ⁿ − 1 KEY IDEA Order does not matter, so impose one. Always choose indices in increasing order ( start parameter): the subset {1, 3} is generated only as 1 then 3 , never as 3 then 1 . This single rule is what separates subsets and combinations (Chapters 32, 34, 35) from permutations (Chapter 33). B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Return all possible subsets" / "power set" / "all subsequences". Each element is used at most once and order does not matter. "Return all unique …" with duplicates in the input : sort, then skip repeats at the same depth (Subsets II). n ≤ 20 and a question about every selection: subset-sum, partition, maximum of a function over subsets: bitmask enumeration. "Non-decreasing subsequences" : subsets with an order constraint and an unsortable input: dedupe each level with a set (491). ONE-LINE TEST If the answer is a set of elements (not an arrangement) and you must list all of them, it is this pattern; the tree has one node per subset when you use pick the next element. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations "Every node is an answer" In pick the next element form, the path from the root to any node is a valid subset, so we record at every node , not only at the leaves. The root is the empty set. For [1, 2, 3] the tree has 2³ = 8 nodes. Figure 65. The edge label is the element appended; children only use later indices, so no subset appears twice. Bitmask enumeration Interpret an integer mask in [0, 2 ⁿ ) as a subset: bit j set means nums[j] is chosen. Counting from 0 to 2 ⁿ − 1 visits every subset once. Useful identities: mask & (1 << j) tests membership, mask | (1 << j) adds, mask & (mask − 1) removes the lowest bit, Integer.bitCount(mask) is the size. Mask (bit 0 on the right) Decimal Subset 000 0 [] 001 1 [1] 010 2 [2] Mask (bit 0 on the right) Decimal Subset 011 3 [1,2] 100 4 [3] 101 5 [1,3] 110 6 [2,3] 111 7 [1,2,3] Duplicates: skip the repeat at the same depth, not the repeat on the same path For [1, 2, 2] , choosing the second 2 right after the first (path [1, 2, 2] ) is fine; choosing the second 2 instead of the first at the same position repeats subsets already produced. After sorting, the rule is: if (i > start && a[i] == a[i−1]) continue . The i > start part is crucial; i > 0 would also forbid [2, 2] . Figure 66. Six distinct subsets instead of eight: the skipped branches would regenerate [2] and [1, 2] . D. E. Java Implementation Subsets: three formulations Subsets.java: LeetCode 78 Java 17+ import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * LeetCode 78 - Subsets. PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 33 Permutations All arrangements: n!, with duplicates, next order, k-th order. A. Pattern Overview A permutation is an arrangement of all n elements where order matters ; there are n! of them ( n = 8 gives 40 320, n = 10 gives 3 628 800). At depth d the search chooses which unused element goes in position d , so the tree has n children at the root, n − 1 at depth 1, and so on. Task Technique Cost List all permutations of distinct values used[] flags, or swap into position O(n · n!) List all unique permutations when values repeat Sort; skip an equal value whose twin is unused O(n · n!) , fewer nodes Count sequences from tiles (with repeats) Branch on letter counts Counts without building lists The next permutation in lexicographic order Ascent, swap, reverse the suffix O(n) , O(1) space The k-th permutation Factorial number system O(n²) (or O(n log n) ), no enumeration KEY IDEA Listing needs backtracking, but finding one specific permutation (next, k-th) does not: use the structure of lexicographic order instead. Interviewers like candidates who notice the difference. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "All possible orderings / arrangements / rearrangements / permutations". Every element is used exactly once and order matters ( [1, 2] and [2, 1] are different answers). "Rearrange the numbers into the next greater arrangement" → next permutation. "Return the k-th …" over permutations → factorial number system, no enumeration. Duplicates in the input and "unique" results → sort and skip same-level repeats. ONE-LINE TEST If every element must appear and swapping two of them gives a different answer, it is a permutation problem. If the answer is a selection , it is subsets or combinations. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations The permutation tree Each level fixes one more position. For [1, 2, 3] there are 3 · 2 · 1 = 6 leaves, and the tree has 3 + 6 + 6 = 15 nodes below the root. Figure 67. Level 1 has 3 choices, level 2 has 2, level 3 has 1: the leaf count is 3! . Two ways to track what is used used[] flags: simple; a loop over all n indices at every level, skipping used ones. Output order follows the input order. Swap into place: the prefix a[0..pos) is fixed; swap each a[i] ( i ≥ pos ) into position pos , recurse, swap back. No extra array, but output order is not lexicographic. Duplicates: the leftmost unused twin goes first Sort so equal values are adjacent. When position d is filled, an element a[i] equal to a[i−1] may be used only if a[i−1] is already used on the current path ; otherwise we would be picking the right twin before the left twin , which yields the same arrangement twice. Figure 68. Three unique permutations instead of six. Next permutation: three moves To step to the next arrangement in lexicographic order: (1) find the rightmost ascent a[i] < a[i+1] ; the suffix after i is non-increasing, so it is already the largest arrangement of its elements. (2) Swap a[i] with the smallest suffix element larger than it . (3) Reverse the suffix (it is still non-increasing after the swap) to make it the smallest. If there is no ascent, the array is the last permutation: reversing the whole array gives the first. Step Detail Array 1. rightmost ascent i = 1 [1,3,5,4,2] 2. swap with next larger on the right j = 3 [1,4,5,3,2] 3. reverse the suffix from 2 [1,4,2,3,5] The k-th permutation: the factorial number system Permutations of n elements in lexicographic order split into n blocks of size (n − 1)! , one per leading digit. So the leading digit is index ⌊ (k−1) / (n−1)! ⌋ of the remaining digits, and k becomes (k−1) mod (n−1)! for the rest. Example: n = 4, k = 9 . Place Block size Index = k0 // size Digit Left 1 3! = 6 8//6=1 2 [1,3,4] 2 2! = 2 2//2=1 3 [1,4] 3 1! = 1 0//1=0 1 [4] 4 0! = 1 0//1=0 4 [] The 9th permutation of 1234 is 2314. D. PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 34 Combinations Choose k of n: increasing order, bound pruning, lexicographic iteration. A. Pattern Overview A combination is a selection of exactly k elements from n , order ignored : C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!) of them ( C(20, 10) = 184 756 ). It is the subsets pattern with a size limit, and the limit enables a powerful kind of pruning: if too few elements remain to reach size k , stop. Idea Rule Effect Increasing order Next element index ≥ last + 1 Each combination is produced once, as a sorted list Size limit Record only when size == k Leaves sit at depth k Bound pruning Loop x only up to n − (k − size) + 1 No branch is explored that cannot be completed Remaining-sum pruning Stop when the digit exceeds what is left (Combination Sum III) Cuts the tail of every loop (digits ascend) KEY IDEA Prune with the feasibility bound, not with the answer. Before recursing, ask: can this prefix still become a full answer? For combinations the test is arithmetic: need = k − size elements are still required, so the next pick can be at most n − need + 1 . B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Choose k numbers / items out of n " , order irrelevant: Combinations (77). "Find all combinations of k numbers that sum to n , using each digit at most once": Combination Sum III (216). "Iterator over combinations in lexicographic order" : Iterator for Combination (1286). Fixed-size subsets with a property (team selection, committee, k -subset with bounded sum). ONE-LINE TEST If the problem fixes the size of a selection and does not care about order, enumerate with a start index and prune when n − start + 1 < need . C. Core Intuition with Illustrations The pruned tree for C(4, 2) With n = 4 , k = 2 : after choosing the first element, need = 1 , so the second can be any of the later numbers. For the first pick need = 2 , so x stops at n − 2 + 1 = 3 : starting with 4 can never produce two elements. The ✗ shows the pruned pick. Figure 69. Without the bound the first loop would also try 4 , creating a node that dies immediately; at larger n such dead nodes dominate. How much does the bound save? For n = 20 , k = 10 the answer has 184 756 leaves. Without the bound the tree contains every prefix of every increasing sequence, including many that cannot reach length 10; with the bound, every internal node has at least one leaf below it , so the work is O(C(n, k) · k) . PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 35 Combination Sum Reuse allowed or not: target-driven search with sorted pruning. A. Pattern Overview Combination Sum problems ask for all multisets (or sequences) of numbers drawn from a list that add up to a target. Three variants differ only in two choices, reuse and duplicates in the input: Problem Input Reuse an element? Next start index Duplicate handling Combination Sum (39) Distinct Yes, unlimited i (same index) None needed Combination Sum II (40) May repeat No, once each i + 1 Sort, if (i > start && c[i] == c[i−1]) continue Combination Sum III (216) Digits 1–9 No i + 1 None needed; also exactly k digits Combination Sum IV (377) Distinct Yes Order matters (sequences) Counting: memoise, it is DP KEY IDEA Sort the candidates once, then prune with break . After sorting, if c[i] > remain then every later candidate is also too large, so the loop ends (not continue ). This is the single most effective optimisation in the whole family. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Return all unique combinations that sum to target". "The same number may be chosen an unlimited number of times" : recurse with the same index. "Each number may be used once" + duplicates in the input : i + 1 plus the same-level skip. "Number of possible combinations" where [1, 2] and [2, 1] count separately: Combination Sum IV, a DP on the remaining sum. ONE-LINE TEST Target sum + list all : backtracking over sorted candidates with remain . Target sum + count or exists : DP (coin change, subset sum), and the backtracking is the exponential baseline. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Reuse means the index does not advance For candidates [2, 3, 6, 7] and target 7 : we choose a candidate, subtract it from remain , and recurse starting at the same index , so the same value can be chosen again. Starting at i (never below) keeps combinations in non-decreasing order, so [2, 2, 3] appears once and [2, 3, 2] never. Figure 70. Each node shows the path and the remaining sum r . The two answers are [2, 2, 3] and [7] . Termination: why it cannot loop forever Candidates are positive, so each choice strictly decreases remain ; the depth is at most target / min(candidates) . With a zero or a negative candidate the recursion would never end: the problem statements rule it out, and an interviewer may ask. Each element once, with duplicates in the input For [10, 1, 2, 7, 6, 1, 5] and target 8 , sort to [1, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 10] . The same-level skip rule prevents choosing the second 1 as the first element again; the pair 1, 1 is still allowed on one path. Action Path Why break [1,1,2,5] 5 > remain 4; later values are larger break [1,1,5,6] 6 > remain 1; later values are larger found [1,1,6] break [1,1,7] 7 > remain 6; later values are larger found [1,2,5] break [1,2,6] 6 > remain 5; later values are larger break [1,5,6] 6 > remain 2; later values are larger break [1,6,7] 7 > remain 1; later values are larger found [1,7] break [1,10] 10 > remain 7; later values are larger skip [1] duplicate of c[0] at this depth break [2,5,6] 6 > remain 1; later values are larger found [2,6] break [2,7] 7 > remain 6; later values are larger break [5,6] 6 > remain 3; later values are larger break [6,7] 7 > remain 2; later values are larger break [7,10] 10 > remain 1; later values are larger break [10] 10 > remain 8; later values are larger Answers: [1,1,6], [1,2,5], [1,7], [2,6]. Java Implementation Combination Sum (reuse allowed) CombinationSum.java: LeetCode 39 Java 17+ import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; /** * LeetCode 39 - Combination Sum: candidates are distinct and each may be reused any number of * times. */ public class CombinationSum { public static List > combinationSum(int[] candidates, int target) { int[] c = candidates.clone(); Arrays.sort(c); List > out = new ArrayList<>(); build(c, 0, target, new ArrayList<>(), out); return out; } private static void build(int[] c, int start, int remain, List cur, List > out) { if (remain == 0) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur)); return; } for (int i = start; i remain) break; cur.add(c[i]); // i, not i + 1: the same value may be chosen again build(c, i, remain - c[i], cur, out); cur.remove(cur.size() - 1); } } } TIME O(N^(T/M)) SPACE O(T/M) N candidates, target T , minimum candidate M . PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 36 N-Queens One queen per row: O(1) attack tests with column and diagonal sets. A. Pattern Overview Place n queens on an n × n board so that no two attack each other (same row, column or diagonal). The N-Queens pattern shows how a good state representation turns a hopeless-looking search into a fast one: the number of boards with n queens is C(n², n) , but by placing exactly one queen per row and testing conflicts in O(1) , the search visits only a few thousand nodes for n = 8 . Idea What it does Effect for n = 8 One queen per row Rows are the recursion depth; the decision is the column 8 ⁸ ≈ 16.7M leaves instead of C(64, 8) ≈ 4.4 billion Column set cols[c] is true if column c holds a queen Rejects column conflicts in O(1) Diagonal sets Cells on a diagonal share r − c ; on an anti-diagonal share r + c Rejects diagonal conflicts in O(1) Pruning (conflicts) Never place on an attacked square Only 2 057 nodes are explored for n = 8 ; 92 solutions Bitmasks Three integers hold columns and both diagonals; free & −free picks a square Counts 14 200 solutions for n = 12 in milliseconds KEY IDEA Choose the representation so the constraint check is O(1) . The brute-force check (scan all placed queens) costs O(n) per placement; the three boolean arrays (or three bitmasks) cost O(1) . The same idea powers Sudoku (Chapter 39): rows, columns and boxes as bitmasks. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Place n items on a board so that none conflict" : queens, rooks, kings, non-attacking pieces. One decision per row (or per item) and a conflict rule between decisions. Small n ( n ≤ 9 for listing boards, n ≤ 15 for counting with bitmasks). Constraints expressible as "same line / diagonal / group" , so each can be a set or a bit. ONE-LINE TEST Assign one value per slot so that no two slots clash is a constraint-satisfaction search. PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 37 Word Search and Grid Backtracking DFS on a grid: mark the cell, explore four ways, restore it. A. Pattern Overview Grid backtracking searches for a path through a matrix in which no cell may be used twice. It is DFS (Part VIII) with one difference that makes it backtracking: the visited mark is removed when the call returns, because a cell that failed on one path may well succeed on another. Problem Goal Prune Answer type Word Search (79) Does a path spell word ? Letter mismatch, out of bounds, cell already on the path Boolean (stop at the first path) Word Search II (212) Which of many words are on the board? Prefix not in the trie List of words Unique Paths III (980) Walks that visit every empty cell once Obstacle, visited cell, end reached too early Count Path with Maximum Gold Best sum along a simple path Zero cells, visited cells Maximum (1219) KEY IDEA Visited-while-on-the-path ≠ visited-ever. Plain graph DFS marks a node visited forever (each node is processed once). Path-enumeration marks a cell only while it is on the current path and unmarks it on return. Using the permanent version here finds fewer paths; using the temporary version in a plain traversal makes DFS exponential. B. "Find all words from a dictionary on a board" → trie plus grid DFS. "Maximum gold / longest path" where a path may start anywhere and may not revisit. ONE-LINE TEST Grid + simple path (no revisits) + small size = backtracking with a temporary visited mark. Grid + reachability or shortest steps = BFS/DFS with a permanent mark. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Mark, explore, restore At cell (r, c) with index k into the word: reject if out of bounds or b[r][c] != word[k] ; accept if k is the last letter. Otherwise save the letter, overwrite the cell with a sentinel ( '#' ) so it cannot be re-entered, try the four neighbours with k + 1 , then restore the saved letter. The sentinel doubles as the visited array, saving O(mn) space. Figure 74. The path A → B → C → C → E → D visits six distinct cells. Many words at once: the trie Searching each word separately repeats work on shared prefixes. A trie (prefix tree) stores all words; one DFS carries a pointer to the current trie node and prunes the moment the current prefix has no node .
