Java Implementation Word Search WordSearch.java: LeetCode 79 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 79 - Word Search. DFS from every cell; mark a cell as used while it is on the * current path. */ public class WordSearch { private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}}; public static boolean exist(char[][] board, String word) { int rows = board.length, cols = board[0].length; for (int r = 0; r = b.length || c >= b[0].length || b[r][c] != word.charAt(k)) return false; if (k == word.length() - 1) return true; char saved = b[r][c]; b[r][c] = '#'; // choose: cell is on the path for (int[] d : DIRS) if (dfs(b, word, k + 1, r + d[0], c + d[1])) { b[r][c] = saved; return true; } b[r][c] = saved; // unchoose return false; } } TIME O(mn · 3ᴸ) SPACE O(L) L = word length. The recursion depth is at most L . The board is restored on every exit path, including the early true . Word Search II with a trie WordSearchII.java: LeetCode 212 Java 17+ import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * LeetCode 212 - Word Search II. One DFS over the grid walks a trie of all words * simultaneously. */ public class WordSearchII { private static final class Node { Node[] next = new Node[26]; String word; // non-null when a word ends here } public static List findWords(char[][] board, String[] words) { Node root = new Node(); for (String w : words) { Node cur = root; for (char ch : w.toCharArray()) { if (cur.next[ch - 'a'] == null) cur.next[ch - 'a'] = new Node(); cur = cur.next[ch - 'a']; } cur.word = w; } List out = new ArrayList<>(); for (int r = 0; r out) { if (r = b.length || c >= b[0].length) return; char ch = b[r][c]; // off the trie: prune the whole subtree if (ch == '#' || parent.next[ch - 'a'] == null) return; Node node = parent.next[ch - 'a']; // report each word once if (node.word != null) { out.add(node.word); node.word = null; } b[r][c] = '#'; dfs(b, r + 1, c, node, out); dfs(b, r - 1, c, node, out); dfs(b, r, c + 1, node, out); dfs(b, r, c - 1, node, out); b[r][c] = ch; } } TIME O(mn · 3ᴸ) SPACE O(total word length) L = longest word. Clearing node.word after reporting guarantees each word appears once. Pruning dead trie branches (removing leaves) is a further optimisation for large dictionaries. Unique Paths III: visit every empty cell once UniquePathsIII.java: LeetCode 980 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 980 - Unique Paths III. Count walks from start (1) to end (2) that visit every * empty cell (0) exactly once. */ public class UniquePathsIII { public static int uniquePathsIII(int[][] grid) { // `empty` counts the start cell too int rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length, empty = 1, sr = 0, sc = 0; for (int r = 0; r = g.length || c >= g[0].length || g[r][c] == -1) return 0; // the end is valid only after everything else is visited if (g[r][c] == 2) return left == 0 ? 1 : 0; int saved = g[r][c]; g[r][c] = -1; int total = walk(g, r + 1, c, left - 1) + walk(g, r - 1, c, left - 1) + walk(g, r, c + 1, left - 1) + walk(g, r, c - 1, left - 1); g[r][c] = saved; return total; } } TIME O(4^(mn)) SPACE O(mn) Counting empty cells first lets the end cell succeed only when left == 0 . Cells are marked -1 while on the path and restored after. Path with Maximum Gold PathWithMaximumGold.java: LeetCode 1219 Java 17+ /** * LeetCode 1219 - Path with Maximum Gold: best sum of a simple path through non-zero cells, * starting anywhere. */ public class PathWithMaximumGold { public static int getMaximumGold(int[][] grid) { int best = 0; for (int r = 0; r = g.length || c >= g[0].length || g[r][c] == 0) return 0; int gold = g[r][c]; // mined: cannot be revisited on this path g[r][c] = 0; int bestNext = Math.max(Math.max(collect(g, r + 1, c), collect(g, r - 1, c)), Math.max(collect(g, r, c + 1), collect(g, r, c - 1))); g[r][c] = gold; return gold + bestNext; } } TIME O(mn · 3^G) SPACE O(G) G ≤ 25 gold cells. The cell is set to 0 while on the path (a natural visited mark) and restored with the saved gold. F. CHAPTER SUMMARY Grid backtracking enumerates simple paths : the visited mark is temporary , set on entry and cleared on return. PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 38 Palindrome Partitioning and String Splits Cut the string: choose the next piece, recurse on the rest. A. Pattern Overview Partitioning problems split a string s into consecutive pieces so that every piece satisfies a rule . The decision at each step is where does the next piece end ; the recursion works on the suffix that remains. A string of length n has 2^(n−1) ways to be cut, so the pieces' validity test is what prunes the tree. PART VI · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING 39 Constraint-Based Backtracking Sudoku, bucket filling, operators: prune hard, choose the tightest slot. A. Pattern Overview Constraint-based backtracking assigns values to variables (cells, buckets, operator slots) under rules that couple the variables. The search tree is huge in principle ( 9 ⁵ ¹ for a Sudoku with 51 blanks), but strong pruning and a good variable ordering make it fast in practice. Four techniques recur: Technique Idea Used in Constraint sets as bitmasks Row / column / box (or used-numbers) as ints: candidates = ~(r | c | b) Sudoku (37), Beautiful Arrangement (526) Most-constrained variable Branch on the slot with the fewest candidates (fail Sudoku solver first early) Sort descending Place big items first; they fail fastest Partition to K Subsets (698), Matchsticks (473) Symmetry breaking Skip choices equivalent to ones already tried Equal items, empty buckets, interchangeable sides Running-state arithmetic Carry value and the open term last so that * can be applied without re-evaluating Expression Add Operators (282) KEY IDEA Prune with a necessary condition, not a hope. Every pruning rule here is a proof that no completion exists (sum not divisible by k , candidate set empty, bucket overflows). A rule that sometimes discards a valid branch is a bug, however fast it makes the program. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Fill the grid / assign items so that every constraint holds" (Sudoku, puzzles). "Can the array be partitioned into k groups with equal sum?" with n ≤ 16 : bucket filling with pruning (or bitmask DP). "Insert operators between digits to reach a target" : a branching of 4 choices per gap. "Count arrangements where each position satisfies a rule" ( n ≤ 15 ): permutations with pruning. Small n with a hard feasibility rule ; plain enumeration is hopeless, and DP needs a subset mask. ONE-LINE TEST A feasibility puzzle over a small set where each choice removes options from other variables is constraint backtracking. First find the pruning rules, then the branching order. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Sudoku: candidates from three bitmasks Keep row[9] , col[9] , box[9] ints; bit d − 1 is set when digit d is used. For an empty cell, candidates = ~(row[r] | col[c] | box[b]) & 0x1FF : one expression gives all legal digits. The box index is (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3 . Branch on the most constrained cell At every step scan the empty cells and pick the one with the fewest candidates ( Integer.bitCount ). A cell with 0 candidates is an immediate dead end; a cell with 1 is a forced move (no branching at all). On the classic puzzle below, all 51 moves turn out to be forced, so the solver never has to guess: the whole puzzle falls out by repeated singles. Bucket filling: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets Total S must be divisible by k ; each bucket target is S / k . Fill one bucket at a time : choose unused items until the bucket reaches the target, then start the next. Three prunings keep it fast: sort descending (large items fail early), skip equal neighbours (interchangeable items), and if the first item tried in an empty bucket fails, the whole branch fails (any other item would have to go there instead). To evaluate in one pass, keep value (the total so far) and last (the signed term that a following * would multiply). Choosing * with operand cur replaces that term: value − last + last·cur , and the new last is last·cur . Use long ; forbid operands with leading zeros. Of the 16 ways to place nothing, + , − or * in the two gaps (nothing joins digits into 12 , 23 or 123 ), only these two reach 6. D. Variations of the Pattern Exact cover and Algorithm X Sudoku, N-Queens and tiling are exact cover problems. Knuth's Algorithm X (with dancing links) always branches on the constraint with the fewest options: the formal version of most constrained first. Bitmask DP instead of search For partition problems with n ≤ 16 , dp[mask] = reachable fill state of the current bucket removes all repeated sub-searches (Part XI). Meet in the middle Split into two halves, enumerate 2^(n/2) each, combine with sorting or hashing: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference (2035). Constraint propagation After placing a value, immediately remove it from related candidate sets and apply forced moves ( naked singles ) before branching: the way human solvers and fast solvers work. CHAPTER SUMMARY Constraint backtracking = choose a variable, try its candidates, prune with proofs, undo. The ordering of variables matters as much as the pruning. Sudoku: row/col/box bitmasks; candidates = ~(r|c|b) & 0x1FF ; branch on the cell with the fewest candidates; no candidates means backtrack. Bucket problems: check S mod k , sort descending, skip equal items, and fail when the first item tried in an empty bucket fails. Expression operators: carry value and the open term last ; * becomes value − last + last·cur ; use long ; no leading zeros. If the state is a subset and you only need feasibility or a count, bitmask DP replaces the search (Part XI).

PART VII · TREE PATTERNS 40 Tree DFS One recursion per node: return a summary up, or pass a bound down. A. Pattern Overview A binary tree is a recursive structure: a node, a left subtree and a right subtree. Depth-first search (DFS) exploits that: solve the problem on left and right , then combine at the node. Nearly every tree-DFS problem is one of two shapes: Shape Information flows The function returns Examples Bottom-up (postorder) Children → parent A summary of the subtree (height, best path, is-balanced) Max depth, diameter, balanced tree, max path sum Top-down (preorder) Parent → children Usually nothing, or a boolean; the parent passes a parameter (remaining sum, bounds, path so far) Path sum, root-to-leaf paths, validate BST, good nodes Both Down, then up Pass a parameter down; return a summary up Path Sum III (prefix sums), LCA, lowest-ancestor problems KEY IDEA Ask two questions at every node: (1) what do I need from each child? (that is the return value), and (2) what do I tell each child? (that is the parameter). The answer to the problem is then either the root's return value, or a global that every node updates (diameter, best path). The three classic traversal orders differ only in when the node is visited relative to its two recursive calls: Order Visit position Typical use Preorder (root, left, right) Before both calls Copy or serialize a tree; top-down parameters Inorder (left, root, right) Between the calls Sorted order of a BST (Chapter 42) Postorder (left, right, root) After both calls Bottom-up summaries; delete a tree; evaluate expression trees B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Any question whose answer for a node depends on its two subtrees : height, size, sum, balanced, symmetric, same tree, diameter. "Root-to-leaf path" with a sum or a property: carry the running value down (Path Sum I/II). "Path between any two nodes" : bottom-up; the best path bends at some node, but only one arm continues upward (diameter, max path sum). "Count / find nodes satisfying a relation with their ancestors" : pass the ancestor information down (good nodes, validate BST). "Do it without recursion" / a very deep (skewed) tree : the same DFS with an explicit stack, or Morris traversal for O(1) space. ONE-LINE TEST A tree problem with no ordering by levels and no BST property is almost always DFS. Decide bottom-up (return a summary) or top-down (pass a parameter); if you need both, return a summary and pass a parameter. C. Preorder visits a node before its children, inorder between them, postorder after them. Iterative inorder: the stack is the call stack The recursion's call stack is simulated by an explicit Deque<TreeNode> : dive left pushing every node, pop and visit, then continue with the right child. This has no recursion-depth limit, so it survives a tree of 100 000 nodes in a chain, where recursion would overflow. That path bends at its highest node; there it uses a downward arm into each child, so its length is leftHeight + rightHeight . But the parent can only extend one arm, so the function returns 1 + max(left, right) while a global keeps the best bend. Figure 78. TreeNode cur = root; while (cur != null) { if (cur.left == null) { out.add(cur.val); cur = cur.right; } else { TreeNode pred = cur.left; while (pred.right != null && pred.right != cur) pred = pred.right; Height * returned up, best path kept in a field-free holder. */ public class DiameterOfBinaryTree { public static int diameter(TreeNode root) { int[] best = {0}; height(root, best); return best[0]; } Java 17+ /** * Returns the height (in nodes) of n; updates best with the longest path that * bends at n. */ private static int height(TreeNode n, int[] best) { if (n == null) return 0; int left = height(n.left, best); int right = height(n.right, best); // path through n uses both downward arms best[0] = Math.max(best[0], left + right); // but only one arm can continue upward return 1 + Math.max(left, right); } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(h) best is a one-element array so the recursion can update it. Heights are in nodes, so left + right is the path length in edges . Balanced binary tree BalancedBinaryTree.java: LeetCode 110 /** * LeetCode 110 - Balanced Binary Tree. A single pass returns the height, or -1 as * soon as any subtree is unbalanced. */ public class BalancedBinaryTree { public static boolean isBalanced(TreeNode root) { return height(root) != -1; } private static int height(TreeNode n) { if (n == null) return 0; int left = height(n.left); // propagate failure without visiting the right side if (left == -1) return -1; int right = height(n.right); if (right == -1 || Math.abs(left - right) > 1) return -1; return 1 + Math.max(left, right); } } Java 17+ TIME O(n) SPACE O(h) The −1 sentinel stops all further work as soon as one subtree fails. Path sums: root-to-leaf, all paths, and any downward path PathSum.java: LeetCode 112, 113, 437 import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * LeetCode 112 / 113 / 437 - root-to-leaf path sums and path sums that start and * end anywhere downward. Java 17+ */ public class PathSum { /** 112: does a root-to-leaf path sum to target? */ public static boolean hasPathSum(TreeNode root, int target) { if (root == null) return false; if (root.left == null && root.right == null) return root.val == target; return hasPathSum(root.left, target - root.val) || hasPathSum(root.right, target - root.val); } /** * 113: every root-to-leaf path with the given sum (backtracking on a shared * list). */ public static List > allPaths(TreeNode root, int target) { List > out = new ArrayList<>(); walk(root, target, new ArrayList<>(), out); return out; } private static void walk(TreeNode n, int remain, List path, List > out) { if (n == null) return; path.add(n.val); // choose if (n.left == null && n.right == null && remain == n.val) out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); walk(n.left, remain - n.val, path, out); walk(n.right, remain - n.val, path, out); path.remove(path.size() - 1); // unchoose } /** * 437: count downward paths (any start, any end) with the given sum, using * prefix sums along the current path. */ public static int countPaths(TreeNode root, int target) { Map seen = new HashMap<>(); seen.put(0L, 1); // the empty prefix return count(root, 0L, target, seen); } private static int count(TreeNode n, long prefix, int target, Map seen) { if (n == null) return 0; prefix += n.val; // paths ending here that start just below an ancestor int total = seen.getOrDefault(prefix - target, 0); seen.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum); // choose total += count(n.left, prefix, target, seen) + count(n.right, prefix, target, seen); seen.merge(prefix, -1, Integer::sum); // unchoose return total; } } TIME O(n) (113: O(n²) worst) SPACE O(h) 113 copies a path of length up to h at each qualifying leaf. In 437 , long prefix sums avoid overflow, and the map entry is decremented on return . F. PART VII · TREE PATTERNS 41 Tree BFS Process a queue one level at a time: depth, views, zigzag, width. A. Pattern Overview Breadth-first search (BFS) visits a tree level by level : all nodes at depth 0, then depth 1, and so on. A queue holds the frontier. The decisive trick is to freeze the queue size at the start of each round : exactly that many nodes belong to the current level, so the loop body knows which level it is in without storing depths. The level-order template Queue queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); queue.add(root); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int size = queue.size(); // nodes of the current level for (int i = 0; i Java 17+ Task What changes in the template Result Level order (102) Collect each level into a list List<List<Integer>> Zigzag (103) Reverse every odd level Alternating direction Right side view (199) Keep the last node of each level ( i == size − 1 ) What you see from the right Minimum depth (111) Return the depth of the first leaf found Early exit Maximum width (662) Track heap indices 2i , 2i + 1 last − first + 1 per level Level aggregates (637, 515) Sum / max over the level Averages, maxima KEY IDEA BFS finds the shallowest answer first. Whenever the question is about depth, levels, the nearest node with a property, or a view of the tree, BFS is the natural tool; DFS can answer too (pass depth down) but cannot stop early. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Level by level", "row by row", "by depth", "each level". "Minimum depth" / "nearest leaf" / "closest node with …" : the first hit in BFS order is the answer. "View from the right / left / top / bottom" : one node per level (or per column). "Zigzag", "spiral" : level order plus a direction flag. "Connect each node to its right neighbour", "width of a level" : you need to know the node's position within its level. ONE-LINE TEST If the word level (or depth, nearest, shortest ) appears in the statement, reach for the queue and the size loop. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations The queue, round by round Each round, size equals the length of the next level, which is exactly what was added during the previous round. Figure 79. Tree [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]: three levels. Depth size Queue at start Visited this level Queue for next 0 1 [3] [3] [9, 20] 1 2 [9, 20] [9, 20] [15, 7] 2 2 [15, 7] [15, 7] [ ] Why freeze the size? queue.size() changes inside the loop (children are appended). Reading it once before the loop fixes the count of nodes of this level; reading it in the loop condition would mix levels. In Java, for (int i = queue.size(); i > 0; i--) does the same. Minimum depth: stop at the first leaf BFS visits shallower nodes before deeper ones, so the first leaf it dequeues has the minimum depth, and the rest of the tree is never touched. A DFS must scan everything. On a tree with a leaf at depth 2 and a million nodes elsewhere, BFS does O(1) work. COMMON TRAP Leaf, not null. In a chain 1 → 2 → 3 the minimum depth is 3, not 1: a node with one null child is not a leaf. The recursive formula 1 + min(left, right) gets this wrong unless it handles one-child nodes. Width: count the gaps with heap indices Number the root 0 ; the children of index i are 2i and 2i + 1 , as in a heap. The width of a level is lastIndex − firstIndex + 1 , including null gaps between its end nodes. Indices double each level, so in a deep tree they overflow long : subtract the first index of the level before computing the children. (node, index) in level first last width [(1, 0)] 0 0 1 [(3, 0), (2, 1)] 0 1 2 [(5, 0), (3, 1), (9, 3)] 0 3 4 The widest level has width 4 (nodes 5 and 9, with an empty slot between them). Zigzag and views Zigzag is level order where odd levels are reversed (reverse the finished list, or insert at the front). Right side view keeps the last node of each level; a DFS variant visits right before left and records the first node seen at each new depth. D. DFS needs only O(h) ; this is the BFS vs DFS trade-off. E. import java.util.Deque; import java.util.List; import java.util.Queue; /** * Breadth-first tree patterns: level order (102), zigzag (103), right side view * (199), minimum depth (111), width (662). */ public class LevelOrder { Java 17+ /** * 102: process the queue one level at a time by freezing its size at the start * of each round. */ public static List > levels(TreeNode root) { List > out = new ArrayList<>(); if (root == null) return out; Queue queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); queue.add(root); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { // exactly the nodes of the current level int size = queue.size(); List level = new ArrayList<>(size); for (int i = 0; i > levelsDfs(TreeNode root) { List > out = new ArrayList<>(); fill(root, 0, out); return out; } private static void fill(TreeNode n, int depth, List > out) { if (n == null) return; if (depth == out.size()) out.add(new ArrayList<>()); out.get(depth).add(n.val); fill(n.left, depth + 1, out); fill(n.right, depth + 1, out); } /** * 103: left-to-right on even levels, right-to-left on odd levels (reverse the * finished level). */ public static List > zigzag(TreeNode root) { List > out = levels(root); for (int d = 1; d rightSideView(TreeNode root) { List out = new ArrayList<>(); if (root == null) return out; Queue queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); queue.add(root); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int size = queue.size(); for (int i = 0; i return out; } /** * 111: BFS stops at the first leaf, so it never visits deeper levels (DFS must * scan the whole tree). */ public static int minDepth(TreeNode root) { if (root == null) return 0; Queue queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); queue.add(root); int depth = 1; while (!queue.isEmpty()) { for (int i = queue.size(); i > 0; i--) { TreeNode n = queue.poll(); if (n.left == null && n.right == null) return depth; if (n.left != null) queue.add(n.left); if (n.right != null) queue.add(n.right); } depth++; } return depth; } /** * 662: width counts null gaps; number nodes as in a heap (children of i are 2i, * 2i+1), rebased per level to avoid overflow. */ public static long maxWidth(TreeNode root) { if (root == null) return 0; Deque nodes = new ArrayDeque<>(); Deque index = new ArrayDeque<>(); nodes.add(root); index.add(0L); long best = 0; while (!nodes.isEmpty()) { long first = index.peekFirst(), last = index.peekLast(); best = Math.max(best, last - first + 1); for (int i = nodes.size(); i > 0; i--) { TreeNode n = nodes.poll(); // rebase: the leftmost node of the level becomes 0 long id = index.poll() - first; if (n.left != null) { nodes.add(n.left); index.add(2 * id); } if (n.right != null) { nodes.add(n.right); index.add(2 * id + 1); } } } return best; } } TIME O(n) SPACE O(w) w = maximum level width. levelsDfs produces the same lists with O(h) extra space by using the depth as the list index. In maxWidth the subtraction index.poll() − first keeps indices small. F. PART VII · TREE PATTERNS 42 BST Patterns Left < node < right: search, validate and walk in sorted order. A. Pattern Overview A binary search tree (BST) keeps, for every node, all keys of the left subtree strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree strictly larger (LeetCode's definition; duplicates are not allowed unless a problem says otherwise). Two consequences drive every BST problem: Search by comparison: at each node you can discard one whole subtree, so lookup, insert and delete cost O(h) . Inorder is sorted: an inorder walk yields keys in increasing order. Kth smallest, successor, range queries, validation and recovery all reduce to inorder with a twist. KEY IDEA The BST property is global, not local. Checking left.val < node.val < right.val at each node is wrong : a node deep in the left subtree can still exceed an ancestor. Correct validation carries an open interval (lo, hi) down the tree. "kth smallest / largest", "in sorted order", "next / previous greater", "closest value": inorder or successor logic. "Validate", "two nodes swapped" : bounds, or look for inorder inversions. "Within [low, high]" : skip subtrees entirely outside the range. "Iterator over a BST" with O(h) memory: controlled inorder. ONE-LINE TEST If the tree is a BST and your solution visits every node to answer a point query, you ignored the property. A point query is O(h) . C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Validate with bounds, not with parent checks Each node must fall in the open interval inherited from its ancestors. Going left sets hi = node.val ; going right sets lo = node.val . Figure 80. Every parent-child pair is ordered, yet the tree is not a BST. Node Allowed open interval Check 5 (−∞, +∞) inside 1 (−∞, 5) inside 6 (5, +∞) inside 3 (5, 6) OUTSIDE → invalid Node 3 must lie in (5, 6) , which excludes it, so the tree is invalid although every parent-child pair is ordered. Use long bounds (or null ) so Integer.MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE as node values are handled. Kth smallest: stop the inorder walk early The iterative inorder stack pops nodes in sorted order; the k -th pop is the answer, and we stop right there: O(h + k) . Visited Rank so far State 1 1 k left = 2 2 2 k left = 1 3 3 k left = 0 → answer Answer for k = 3 : 3. For many queries on a changing tree, augment each node with its subtree size and descend by rank ( O(h) per query). Inorder successor: the last node where we went left The successor of p is the smallest key greater than p . Walk from the root: if p < node , this node is a candidate and the answer lies to the left (maybe a smaller candidate); otherwise go right. No parent pointers are needed. Node Decision 5 p < node: candidate = 5, go left 3 p ≥ node: go right 4 p ≥ node: go right Successor of 4 is 5. If p has a right child, the successor is that subtree's leftmost node; the descent above covers both cases. Deleting a node Case Action Leaf Return null One child Return that child Two children Replace the value by the inorder successor (leftmost of the right subtree) and delete that node from the right subtree Recover Binary Search Tree Two nodes were swapped. In the inorder sequence this creates one or two descents ( a[i] > a[i+1] ). If the swapped nodes are adjacent there is one descent: swap that pair. Otherwise there are two: the first element of the first descent and the second element of the second descent are the culprits. Example: 1 3 2 4 (one descent: 3, 2) and 3 2 1 (descents 3 > 2 and 2 > 1: swap 3 and 1). D. Two children: copy the inorder successor's value up, * then delete that successor. */ public static TreeNode delete(TreeNode root, int key) { if (root == null) return null; if (key root.val) root.right = delete(root.right, key); else { // 0 or 1 child: splice the node out Java 17+ if (root.left == null) return root.right; if (root.right == null) return root.left; // smallest node of the right subtree TreeNode succ = root.right; while (succ.left != null) succ = succ.left; root.val = succ.val; root.right = delete(root.right, succ.val); } return root; } } TIME O(h) SPACE O(h) Recursive versions use the call stack. BST iterator BSTIterator.java: LeetCode 173 import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** * LeetCode 173 - BST Iterator: controlled inorder with a stack holding only the * left spine; next() is amortised O(1). */ public class BSTIterator { private final Deque stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); public BSTIterator(TreeNode root) { pushLeft(root); } Java 17+ public boolean hasNext() { return !stack.isEmpty(); } public int next() { TreeNode n = stack.pop(); // the right subtree's left spine comes next in order pushLeft(n.right); return n.val; } private void pushLeft(TreeNode n) { for (; n != null; n = n.left) stack.push(n); } } TIME next: O(1) amortised SPACE O(h) Each node is pushed and popped exactly once over n calls, so the average cost per next() is constant. Recover BST RecoverBST.java: LeetCode 99 /** * LeetCode 99 - Recover Binary Search Tree: two values were swapped; find them as * the inversions of the inorder sequence. */ public class RecoverBST { private TreeNode first, second, prev; public static void recoverTree(TreeNode root) { RecoverBST r = new RecoverBST(); r.inorder(root); int t = r.first.val; r.first.val = r.second.val; r.second.val = t; } private void inorder(TreeNode n) { if (n == null) return; inorder(n.left); if (prev != null && prev.val > n.val) { // first inversion: the larger element of the pair is misplaced if (first == null) first = prev; // last inversion: the smaller element is misplaced second = n; } prev = n; inorder(n.right); } } Java 17+ TIME O(n) SPACE O(h) Swap values , not nodes. PART VII · TREE PATTERNS 43 Tree Construction Rebuild trees from traversals, strings and sorted data. A. Pattern Overview Construction problems give you a description of a tree (two traversals, a serialized string, a sorted array) and ask for the tree. All of them are solved by the same recursion: pick the root, split the remaining data into a left part and a right part, recurse. What differs is how the root and the split are found. Input Root comes from Split comes from Cost Preorder + inorder (105) Next element of preorder Position of the root in inorder O(n) with a map Inorder + postorder (106) Last element of postorder (consume right to left) Position of the root in inorder O(n) with a map Serialized preorder with # (297) Next token The tokens themselves (nulls mark ends) O(n) Sorted array / list (108, 109) Middle element Left half / right half O(n) Array, max is root (654) Maximum of the range Elements left / right of it O(n) with a monotonic stack KEY IDEA Preorder alone (or postorder alone) does not determine a tree , nor does inorder alone. Preorder + inorder does, provided the values are distinct . Preorder + postorder determines it only when every internal node has two children (otherwise left-only and right-only are ambiguous). A preorder with explicit null markers is self-sufficient. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Construct a binary tree from …" traversal arrays, or "serialize and deserialize". "Height-balanced BST from a sorted array / list" : always the middle. "The root is the maximum / the first / the last" of a range. Two traversals of the same tree: one gives roots, the other gives sizes of the left and right parts. ONE-LINE TEST Whenever a problem hands you an inorder sequence, the inorder index of the root is the size of the left subtree. That one fact solves four problems in this chapter. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Preorder + inorder Preorder lists the root first; inorder places the root between its left and right subtrees. So pre[0] is the root; its position m in inorder splits the window into in[lo..m−1] (left) and in[m+1..hi] (right). The preorder pointer simply advances: after the root comes the whole left subtree, then the right one. Build the left subtree before the right so the pointer is in the right place. Traversal Sequence Preorder 3 9 20 15 7 Inorder 9 3 15 20 7 Depth Root = next preorder Window Split Sub-windows 0 3 in[0..4] root at in[1] left in[0..0], right in[2..4] 1 9 in[0..0] root at in[0] left in[0..-1], right in[1..0] 1 20 in[2..4] root at in[3] left in[2..2], right in[4..4] 2 15 in[2..2] root at in[2] left in[2..1], right in[3..2] 2 7 in[4..4] root at in[4] left in[4..3], right in[5..4] An empty window such as in[0..-1] means "no child" and returns null . Result: the tree [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] . Figure 81. The rebuilt tree; each node was created in preorder. TIP Build a value → inorder index map first. Scanning inorder for the root at every call makes the algorithm O(n²) on a skewed tree; the map makes the split O(1) . Inorder + postorder Postorder lists the root last . Walk it from the right; the order of roots is root, right subtree, then left subtree, so recurse into the right child first. Everything else is identical. Serialize and deserialize Write a preorder walk and emit # for each null . This single sequence is unambiguous: reading it back, the next token is the root, then recursively the whole left subtree, then the whole right subtree; a # ends a branch. Tree (level order) Serialized (preorder with #) [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5] 1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,# Level-order serialization (LeetCode's own format) also works with a queue; preorder is shorter to code. Values are separated by commas, so negative numbers are safe; never use a digit-only separator-free format. Sorted array to a height-balanced BST Choose the middle element as the root so both halves differ by at most one element; recurse on each half. The depth is ⌊ log ₂ n ⌋ + 1 . For a sorted linked list you cannot index the middle in O(1) . Instead build the left half first, consuming the list in order, so the list pointer always sits at the inorder position of the next root: O(n) time, O(log n) stack. Maximum Binary Tree The maximum of the array is the root; the part left of it builds the left subtree, the part right of it the right. Naively this is O(n²) for a sorted array. A monotonic stack (Chapter 7) does it in O(n) : keep a decreasing stack of nodes; a new value pops smaller nodes, which become its left child, and then becomes the right child of the new stack top. PART VII · TREE PATTERNS 44 Tree DP Return a small state per subtree and combine it at the parent. A. Pattern Overview Tree DP is dynamic programming where the subproblems are subtrees . There is no table to index: the recursion order (postorder) guarantees both children are solved before the parent, and each node is computed once , so the total cost is O(n) . The craft is choosing the state a subtree reports to its parent. State shape Meaning Problems Two values (take, skip) Best with / without using this node House Robber III (337) One value + global Return the best downward arm; keep the best bent path in a global Max Path Sum (124), Diameter (543), Longest Univalue Path (687) Small enum A node's status: not covered / camera / covered Binary Tree Cameras (968) Excess / balance Coins or flow that must cross the edge to the parent Distribute Coins (979) Direction pair Longest zigzag starting left / right Longest ZigZag Path (1372) Parameter down Ancestor maximum, running sum Count Good Nodes (1448) KEY IDEA The state must make the parent's decision independent of the subtree's internals. Ask: what is the least the parent needs to know? House Robber III needs only "best if I took the child" and "best if I didn't", not which grandchildren were robbed. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Optimise over a tree with a local constraint : no two adjacent nodes chosen, cover every node, maximise a path. "Path" between two arbitrary nodes with a sum or length objective: bend + arm. Each node's decision depends on its children's decisions and nothing else. Greedy on a tree (cameras, coins): a postorder pass that fixes the leaves first. The brute force explores subsets or paths, and a node's best value is the same each time it is reached. ONE-LINE TEST "Maximum / minimum / count, over a tree, with a rule linking a node to its neighbours" means a postorder pass that returns a tuple. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations House Robber III: two states per node Houses form a tree; robbing a node forbids robbing its children. Each node returns (rob, skip) : rob = node.val + left.skip + right.skip (children must be skipped). skip = max(left.rob, left.skip) + max(right.rob, right.skip) (children are free to be either). Maximum Path Sum: arms and bends A path may start and end anywhere. At each node: the best arm going down is node.val + max(0, left, right) , which is what we return, because a path continuing upward uses only one side. The best bent path through the node is node.val + max(0, left) + max(0, right) , which updates a global. Negative arms are clipped to 0 (we simply do not extend them). Binary Tree Cameras: a three-state greedy A camera covers its parent, itself and its children. Greedy from the bottom: never put a camera on a leaf (its parent covers more). Each node reports one of 0 not covered, 1 has a camera, 2 covered (no camera). Rules, given children states l , r (a null is treated as 2 , covered): Condition This node Cameras l == 0 or r == 0 (a child is exposed) 1: place a camera +1 l == 1 or r == 1 (a child has a camera) 2: covered 0 Both children covered, no camera 0: exposed, asks the parent 0 Node left right State and reason cameras 0 covered covered not covered: children covered, not watching → exposed 0 Node left right State and reason cameras 0 covered covered not covered: children covered, not watching → exposed 0 0 not covered not covered camera: a child is exposed → camera here 1 0 camera covered covered: a child has a camera → covered 1 If the root ends up exposed (state 0) add one more camera. Here the total is 1. Distribute Coins: excess flows along edges Every node must end with exactly one coin. Define excess(node) = node.coins + excess(left) + excess(right) − 1 : positive means coins must move up across the edge to the parent, negative means coins must come down . Each unit crossing costs one move, so add |excess(left)| + |excess(right)| at every node. The total is exact because every edge is crossed only by the net flow. Other shapes Longest Univalue Path clips the arm to 0 when the child's value differs. Longest ZigZag Path returns (startsLeft, startsRight) lengths. Count Good Nodes passes the maximum ancestor value down. D. Java Implementation All seven tree-DP solvers TreeDP.java: LeetCode 337, 124, 687, 968, 979, 1372, 1448 /** * Tree DP: each call returns a small summary of its subtree, and the parent * combines the summaries. * 337 House Robber III, 124 Maximum Path Sum, 687 Longest Univalue Path, 968 * Cameras, 979 Distribute Coins, Java 17+ * 1372 Longest ZigZag Path, 1448 Count Good Nodes (the last one pushes information * down instead of up). */ public class TreeDP { // ---- 337: summary = {best if this node is robbed, best if it is skipped} public static int houseRobberIII(TreeNode root) { int[] r = rob(root); return Math.max(r[0], r[1]); } private static int[] rob(TreeNode n) { if (n == null) return new int[]{0, 0}; int[] l = rob(n.left), r = rob(n.right); // children must be skipped int robbed = n.val + l[1] + r[1]; // children are free to be either int skipped = Math.max(l[0], l[1]) + Math.max(r[0], r[1]); return new int[]{robbed, skipped}; } // ---- 124: summary = best downward path starting at this node; the answer // bends at some node public static int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) { int[] best = {Integer.MIN_VALUE}; gain(root, best); return best[0]; } private static int gain(TreeNode n, int[] best) { if (n == null) return 0; // a negative arm is better dropped int left = Math.max(0, gain(n.left, best)); int right = Math.max(0, gain(n.right, best)); // path bending at n best[0] = Math.max(best[0], n.val + left + right); // only one arm continues to the parent return n.val + Math.max(left, right); } // ---- 687: length in edges of the longest path whose nodes all share one value public static int longestUnivaluePath(TreeNode root) { int[] best = {0}; univalue(root, best); return best[0]; } private static int univalue(TreeNode n, int[] best) { if (n == null) return 0; int l = univalue(n.left, best), r = univalue(n.right, best); int left = (n.left != null && n.left.val == n.val) ? l + 1 : 0; int right = (n.right != null && n.right.val == n.val) ? r + 1 : 0; best[0] = Math.max(best[0], left + right); return Math.max(left, right); } // ---- 968: states 0 = not covered, 1 = has a camera, 2 = covered without a // camera public static int minCameras(TreeNode root) { int[] cameras = {0}; int state = cover(root, cameras); // an uncovered root needs its own camera return cameras[0] + (state == 0 ? 1 : 0); } private static int cover(TreeNode n, int[] cameras) { // null counts as covered if (n == null) return 2; int l = cover(n.left, cameras), r = cover(n.right, cameras); // a child is exposed: put a camera here if (l == 0 || r == 0) { cameras[0]++; return 1; } // a child's camera covers this node if (l == 1 || r == 1) return 2; // both children covered but not watching: stay uncovered return 0; } // ---- 979: every node must end with one coin; moves = total |excess| crossing // each edge public static int distributeCoins(TreeNode root) { int[] moves = {0}; excess(root, moves); return moves[0]; } private static int excess(TreeNode n, int[] moves) { if (n == null) return 0; int e = excess(n.left, moves) + excess(n.right, moves) + n.val - 1; // |e| coins cross the edge above n moves[0] += Math.abs(e); return e; } // ---- 1372: summary = longest zigzag path starting here, going left first / // right first public static int longestZigZag(TreeNode root) { int[] best = {0}; zig(root, best); return best[0]; } private static int[] zig(TreeNode n, int[] best) { if (n == null) return new int[]{-1, -1}; int[] l = zig(n.left, best), r = zig(n.right, best); // step left, then the path must turn right int goLeft = l[1] + 1; int goRight = r[0] + 1; best[0] = Math.max(best[0], Math.max(goLeft, goRight)); return new int[]{goLeft, goRight}; } // ---- 1448: a node is good if no ancestor is larger (information flows down) public static int goodNodes(TreeNode root) { return good(root, Integer.MIN_VALUE); } private static int good(TreeNode n, int maxSoFar) { if (n == null) return 0; int here = n.val >= maxSoFar ? 1 : 0; int next = Math.max(maxSoFar, n.val); return here + good(n.left, next) + good(n.right, next); } } TIME O(n) each SPACE O(h) Each method is one postorder (or preorder for goodNodes ) pass. Pairs are returned as int[2] ; long sums are not needed under LeetCode's constraints but would be for adversarial inputs. F. Detailed Dry Run Section C contains four generated traces; each lists nodes in postorder . To audit the cameras table by hand: the two leaves report covered to their parents only through null children, so the leaf nodes themselves are exposed (state 0). The parent of two exposed leaves must place a camera (+1 → 1 camera) and reports state 1; the root sees a child with a camera and is covered, so no extra camera is needed: total 1. For max path sum, check the root row: left gain 9 , right gain 35 (the arm 20 + 15 ), bent path −10 + 9 + 35 = 34 , less than the current best 42. G. Variations of the Pattern Rerooting When the answer is needed for every node as root (Sum of Distances in Tree , 834), do one DP down to compute subtree values, then a second pass rerooting from parent to child. It is O(n) instead of O(n²) . DP on general trees Tree Diameter (1245) and Minimum Height Trees (310) run on undirected trees stored as adjacency lists; the DFS carries a parent to avoid walking back. Knapsack on trees Tree knapsack merges child tables of size ≤ k ( O(n·k) total with size bounds): used when the constraint is "choose at most k nodes". Counting Unique BSTs (96), All Possible Full Binary Trees (894): the count at size n is a convolution of counts at smaller sizes (Catalan-type recurrences). Game / interval flavour Binary Tree Coloring Game (1145): compare the three component sizes around the opponent's first move. H. PART VII · TREE PATTERNS 45 LCA and Binary Lifting Meet in the middle: lowest common ancestors and k-th ancestors. A. Pattern Overview The lowest common ancestor (LCA) of nodes p and q is the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant). It underlies tree distances ( dist(p,q) = depth(p) + depth(q) − 2·depth(lca) ), path queries and many "nearest shared ancestor" questions. Three tools cover almost every case: Situation Technique Per query Preprocessing One query, binary tree (236) Postorder: the node where both sides report a hit O(n) None One query, BST (235) Descend while p and q are on the same side O(h) None Many queries, static tree Binary lifting table up[j][v] O(log n) O(n log n) k-th ancestor queries (1483) Jump by the set bits of k O(log k) O(n log n) Offline queries, very many Tarjan offline LCA (union-find), or Euler tour + RMQ O( α ) / O(1) O(n) KEY IDEA Binary lifting stores the 2ʲ-th ancestor of every node. Because every integer is a sum of distinct powers of two, any k-th ancestor is reached in at most log ₂ k jumps, and an LCA is found by lifting the deeper node, then jumping both nodes while their ancestors still differ. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Lowest / nearest common ancestor" , "closest shared parent", "merge point of two paths up the tree". "Distance between two nodes in a tree" : LCA plus depths. "The k-th ancestor" , with many queries: binary lifting. "Smallest subtree containing all the deepest leaves" (1123): LCA of a set, computed bottom-up. Parent array input ( parent[i] ) with up to 5·10⁴ queries: the lifting table is the intended tool. ONE-LINE TEST Single query: recurse. Many queries on a fixed tree: precompute depths and up[][] . BST: use the values, no table needed. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations LCA in a binary tree: the node where the two reports meet Return the node itself if it is p or q ; otherwise ask both children. If both return non-null, p and q are in different subtrees and this node is the LCA. If only one is non-null, pass it up (it is either the LCA already found, or the single target). Figure 83. A node is its own descendant: LCA(5, 4) = 5. Node Children report Returns 5 hit 5 null null — null null — 0 one side: none — null null — Node Children report Returns null null — 8 one side: none — 1 one side: none — 3 one side: 5 5 The search stops descending as soon as it hits p = 5 , so 5 's subtree is never explored for q ; the other branch returns nothing and the root passes 5 up. Answer 5. TIP This relies on both nodes existing in the tree. If one may be absent (LeetCode 1644), count how many targets were seen and verify both before trusting the result. LCA in a BST: the first split point Start at the root. If both values are smaller, go left; if both are larger, go right. The first node where they split (or equal one of them) is the LCA. This is O(h) and iterative with O(1) space. Smallest subtree with all deepest nodes Return (depth, node) from each subtree. If both sides have equal depth, the current node is the LCA of the deepest leaves below it; otherwise keep the deeper side's answer. Binary lifting: the table Let up[0][v] be the parent ( −1 for the root) and up[j][v] = up[j−1][ up[j−1][v] ] . Example parent array [-1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3] : Figure 84. Nodes are labelled by their index; node 0 is the root. Node up[0] (2^0) up[1] (2^1) up[2] (2^2) 0 -1 -1 -1 1 0 -1 -1 2 0 -1 -1 Node up[0] (2^0) up[1] (2^1) up[2] (2^2) 3 1 0 -1 4 1 0 -1 5 2 0 -1 6 3 1 -1 7 3 1 -1 -1 means "no such ancestor". Node 6's ancestors: 3 (one step), 1 (two steps), 0 (three steps). The table gives up[1][6] = 1 directly. k-th ancestor and LCA queries k-th ancestor: for each set bit j of k , replace v by up[j][v] . For k = 3 = 0b11 from node 6: up[0][6] = 3 , then up[1][3] = 0 . Answer 0. LCA(u, v): (1) make u the deeper node; (2) lift it by depth[u] − depth[v] ; (3) if now u == v , done; (4) for j from high to low, if up[j][u] != up[j][v] , jump both; (5) the answer is the common parent up[0][u] . Step 4 works because the "ancestors still differ" predicate is monotone: all jumps that stay below the LCA are allowed, all that reach or pass it are not, exactly like binary search on the answer. Example LCA(6, 4) : depths 3 and 2; lift 6 by 1 to node 3; 3 ≠ 4; at every level the ancestors of 3 and 4 are equal ( -1 , -1 , then 1 and 1 ), so no jump is taken; the answer is up[0][3] = 1 . D. Java Implementation LCA of a binary tree, of a BST, and of the deepest leaves LowestCommonAncestor.java: LeetCode 236, 235, 1123 /** LCA in a binary tree (236), in a BST (235), and of the deepest leaves (1123). */ public class LowestCommonAncestor { /** * 236: if p and q are in different subtrees the current node is the LCA; * otherwise the answer is in the one non-null result. */ public static TreeNode binaryTree(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) { if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root; TreeNode left = binaryTree(root.left, p, q); TreeNode right = binaryTree(root.right, p, q); if (left != null && right != null) return root; return left != null ? left : right; } /** * 235: walk down while p and q are on the same side of the node; the first * split point is the LCA. */ public static TreeNode bst(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) { while (root != null) { if (p.val root.val && q.val > root.val) root = root.right; else return root; } return null; } /** * 1123: the deepest subtree whose two sides are equally deep; returns {depth, * node}. */ public static TreeNode deepestLeaves(TreeNode root) { return deepest(root).node; } private record Result(int depth, TreeNode node) {} private static Result deepest(TreeNode n) { if (n == null) return new Result(0, null); Result l = deepest(n.left), r = deepest(n.right); if (l.depth == r.depth) return new Result(l.depth + 1, n); Result deeper = l.depth > r.depth ? l : r; return new Result(deeper.depth + 1, deeper.node); } } Java 17+ TIME O(n) / O(h) / O(n) SPACE O(h) Reference equality ( root == p ) identifies the nodes; use values only for the BST. Preprocessing O(n * log n), each query O(log n). */ public class BinaryLifting { private final int[][] up; private final int[] depth; private final int levels; public BinaryLifting(int[] parent) { int n = parent.length; int lg = 1; while ((1 chain = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>(); int cur = v; while (cur != -1 && depth[cur] == -1) { chain.push(cur); cur = parent[cur]; } int d = cur == -1 ? -1 : depth[cur]; while (!chain.isEmpty()) depth[chain.pop()] = ++d; } /** * k-th ancestor of v, or -1 if it does not exist: jump by the set bits of k. */ public int kthAncestor(int v, int k) { for (int j = 0; j > j & 1) == 1) v = up[j][v]; return k >= (1 = 0; j--) Java 17+ // jump while the ancestors still differ if (up[j][u] != up[j][v]) { u = up[j][u]; v = up[j][v]; } return up[0][u]; } public int depth(int v) { return depth[v]; } } TIME Build O(n log n); query O(log n) SPACE O(n log n) Depths are computed iteratively, so a 100 000-node chain does not overflow the stack. kthAncestor returns −1 when k exceeds the depth. The lifting table is the full precomputation for 8 nodes (3 levels). To check a jump yourself: LCA(6, 7) have equal depth 3, neither is an ancestor of the other; at j = 2 and j = 1 the ancestors are equal ( -1 and 1 ), at j = 0 the parents are 3 and 3 , which are equal, so no jump happens and the answer is up[0][6] = 3 . G. Variations of the Pattern Distance and paths Distance between two nodes (1740), Find Distance in a Binary Tree, Step-by-Step Directions (2096): LCA plus depths or the two root paths. Weighted and path aggregates Store, next to each up[j][v] , an aggregate (max edge, sum) of the 2ʲ edges covered. Then path queries ( Minimum Edge on a Path, Kruskal reconstruction ) cost O(log n) . LCA of many nodes LCA of Deepest Leaves, LCA of a set of nodes (1676): the answer is the LCA of the two extremes in Euler order, or a recursion with counts. With parent pointers LCA III (1650): the two-pointer trick; climb each pointer to the other's start when it reaches the root. They meet at the LCA, exactly as in intersection of two linked lists (Chapter 21). Offline and Euler tour For up to ~10⁶ queries, an Euler tour with a sparse table gives O(1) per LCA. Tarjan's offline algorithm uses union-find. Both are beyond a typical interview but worth naming. H. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 46 Graph Representation Pick the right storage first; every graph algorithm follows from it. A. Pattern Overview A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices and a set of edges between them. Trees, grids, linked lists, state machines, dependency lists, road maps and social networks are all graphs; the first step in a graph problem is to name the vertices and the edges , and the second is to store them so the algorithm you need is cheap. A matrix costs n² memory: 10⁵ vertices would need 10¹⁰ cells. Use it only when n is small or the graph is dense and you need O(1) edge lookups. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Input is a list of pairs ( edges[i] = [a, b] ), prerequisites, trust relations, equations, accounts , or flights : build an adjacency list. Input is a matrix isConnected[i][j] : it already is the adjacency matrix. Input is a grid or a board of states : the graph is implicit; neighbours are computed (Chapter 55). Statement says "connected", "reachable", "dependency", "network", "friends of friends", "minimum number of moves". A degree question ("who is trusted by everyone", "which node is the centre") needs only counters, not a graph at all. ONE-LINE TEST Before choosing an algorithm answer four questions: directed? weighted? may it contain cycles? how large are n and m ? C. Core Intuition with Illustrations One graph, three storages The sample graph has 7 vertices and 6 undirected edges; vertices 5 and 6 form a separate component. Figure 85. A sample undirected graph with two components. Adjacency list Vertex Neighbours 0 [1, 2] 1 [0, 3] 2 [0, 3] 3 [1, 2, 4] 4 [3] 5 [6] 6 [5] Adjacency matrix 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 0 . 1 1 . . . . 1 1 . . 1 . . . 2 1 . . 1 . . . 3 . 1 1 . 1 . . 4 . . . 1 . . . 5 . . . . . . 1 6 . . . . . 1 . An undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix. A directed one does not. Storing int weights in the matrix needs a sentinel for "no edge" ( 0 is a legal weight in many problems). CSR (compressed sparse row) Array Contents start [0, 2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12] to [1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 6, 5] The neighbours of u are to[start[u] .. start[u + 1] − 1] . Two flat int[] arrays hold the whole graph: no Integer boxing, no per-vertex list objects. Competitive programmers and low-latency services use it; interviews rarely require it. Degrees answer some questions without any traversal Find the Town Judge (997): the judge has in-degree n − 1 and out-degree 0, so score[v] = in − out equals n − 1 only for the judge. Find Center of Star Graph (1791): the centre appears in every edge, so two edges are enough. Minimum Vertices to Reach All Nodes (1557): the answer is every vertex with in-degree 0 (in a DAG nothing else can reach them). PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 47 BFS and DFS The two traversals: breadth finds shortest paths, depth explores structure. A. Pattern Overview Every graph algorithm in this part is a traversal with some extra bookkeeping. A traversal visits every vertex reachable from a source exactly once, and costs O(n + m) with an adjacency list. The only difference between the two is the container that holds the frontier: BFS DFS Container Queue (FIFO) Stack (LIFO), or the call stack Visits in order of Distance from the source (layers) Going as deep as possible, then backtracking Finds Shortest path in an unweighted graph Any path; structure (cycles, order, components) Memory O(width) : can be O(n) O(depth) : can be O(n) Typical uses Fewest moves, levels, nearest, multi-source Components, cycles, topological order, bridges, backtracking KEY IDEA Mark a vertex visited when you add it to the frontier , not when you remove it. Marking on removal lets the same vertex be enqueued many times (still correct for reachability, but a BFS then does O(m) extra queue work and breaks the distance bookkeeping on weighted or multi-source variants). B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Minimum number of steps / moves / transformations" on unweighted transitions: BFS. "Is there a path" / "can we reach" : either; DFS is shorter to write, BFS safer for deep graphs. "Return all paths" : DFS with backtracking (Chapter 31). "Shortest sequence" over words, locks, genes, puzzle boards: BFS on an implicit state graph. "Distance from a node", "nodes at distance k", "time to infect everyone" : BFS depth. ONE-LINE TEST Unit-cost edges and the word minimum mean BFS. A weighted minimum means Dijkstra (Chapter 53). All solutions means DFS with backtracking. C. An explicit stack with a per-vertex next-neighbour pointer reproduces the recursive order exactly and cannot overflow. Why BFS gives shortest paths BFS maintains an invariant: the queue holds vertices at distance d followed by vertices at distance d + 1 , never more than one level apart. Dequeueing in order therefore discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance. With weights this breaks (a one-edge path of cost 100 beats nothing but loses to two edges of cost 1); use Dijkstra, or 0-1 BFS when weights are only 0 and 1. Depth can reach n: see the iterative one. */ public static List dfsOrder(List > g, int s) { List order = new ArrayList<>(); dfs(g, s, new boolean[g.size()], order); return order; } private static void dfs(List > g, int u, boolean[] seen, List order) { seen[u] = true; order.add(u); for (int v : g.get(u)) if (!seen[v]) dfs(g, v, seen, order); } /** Iterative DFS with the same visiting order as the recursive version. */ public static List dfsOrderIterative(List > g, int s) { List order = new ArrayList<>(); boolean[] seen = new boolean[g.size()]; Deque stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); int[] next = new int[g.size()]; // next neighbour to try stack.push(s); seen[s] = true; order.add(s); while (!stack.isEmpty()) { int u = stack.peek(); if (next[u] == g.get(u).size()) { stack.pop(); continue; } int v = g.get(u).get(next[u]++); if (!seen[v]) { seen[v] = true; order.add(v); stack.push(v); } } return order; } /** LeetCode 1971: is there a path from source to destination? */ public static boolean validPath(int n, int[][] edges, int source, int dest) { List > g = GraphRepresentation.adjList(n, edges, false); return bfsDistances(g, source)[dest] >= 0; } /** LeetCode 797: all paths from 0 to n-1 in a DAG (backtracking on a path). */ public static List > allPathsSourceTarget(int[][] graph) { List > out = new ArrayList<>(); List path = new ArrayList<>(); path.add(0); walk(graph, 0, path, out); return out; } private static void walk(int[][] g, int u, List path, List > out) { if (u == g.length - 1) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; } for (int v : g[u]) { path.add(v); walk(g, v, path, out); path.remove(path.size() - 1); } } } TIME O(n + m) SPACE O(n) allPathsSourceTarget is output-bound: a DAG with 2^k paths costs 2^k to list. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 49 Cycle Detection Undirected: a seen vertex that is not the arrival edge. Directed: a gray vertex. A. Pattern Overview A cycle is a path that returns to its start. Detecting one is the gateway to "is the dependency list valid?", "is this graph a tree?" and "which nodes are safe?". The rule depends on direction: Graph Cycle test Why Undirected DFS / BFS meets a visited vertex through an edge other than the one it arrived by ; or m > n − c ; or Union-Find sees both ends already connected Any second route to a visited vertex closes a loop Directed DFS meets a vertex that is still on the recursion stack (gray): a back edge ; or Kahn's algorithm cannot remove every vertex A visited vertex that has finished only gives a forward or cross edge Functional graph (each Floyd / Brent, or walk with step stamps Rho shape: tail then cycle node has one out-edge) (Chapter 21) KEY IDEA Undirected and directed are not the same problem. In an undirected graph the edge u – v makes v see u again immediately, so you must ignore the arrival edge . In a directed graph a visited vertex is only a problem if it is on the current path: visited-and-finished vertices are harmless. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Can all courses be finished", "valid build order", "deadlock" : directed cycle detection. "Is this graph a tree" : connected, n − 1 edges, no cycle. "Find the redundant edge" : first edge that closes a cycle (Union-Find, Chapter 52). "Safe states", "nodes that never enter a cycle" : three-colour DFS or reversed Kahn. "Detect a loop in a 2D grid" : undirected cycle on an implicit graph; ignore the cell you came from. Pattern Overview A topological order of a directed graph lists the vertices so that for every edge u → v , u appears before v . It exists if and only if the graph is a DAG (acyclic). Proof: for an edge u → v , v finishes before u (no back edges exist in a DAG), so u appears earlier in the reversed list. B. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 51 Kahn's Algorithm Peel off vertices with no prerequisites, level by level, using a queue. A. Pattern Overview Kahn's algorithm is the BFS version of topological sorting. Count each vertex's in-degree (unmet prerequisites). Put every vertex with in-degree 0 in a queue. Repeatedly remove one, append it to the answer, and decrement its out-neighbours' in-degrees, enqueueing any that reach 0. If the answer ends with fewer than n vertices, the leftover vertices lie on or behind a cycle. Kahn's algorithm: the whole template int[] indeg = new int[n]; for (List out : g) for (int v : out) indeg[v]++; Deque queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); for (int v = 0; v order = new ArrayList<>(); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int u = queue.poll(); order.add(u); for (int v : g.get(u)) if (--indeg[v] == 0) queue.add(v); } return order.size() == n ? order : List.of(); // else: a cycle Java 17+ Variation Change to the template Gives Levels / rounds Freeze queue.size() per round (like tree BFS) Minimum semesters, parallel scheduling Lexicographically smallest PriorityQueue instead of a queue Smallest valid sequence order Unique order check Fail if the queue ever holds more than one vertex Sequence reconstruction DP on the DAG finish[v] = max(finish[v], finish[u] + cost[v]) Longest path, earliest finish Reverse graph Run on reversed edges, peel off terminal nodes Eventual safe nodes Leaf peeling (undirected) In-degree = degree; start from degree-1 vertices Minimum Height Trees KEY IDEA Kahn needs no recursion and detects cycles for free. It is the production-safe topological sort: no StackOverflowError on a 10⁵-vertex chain, and its level structure answers "how many rounds" directly. B. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 52 Union-Find (DSU) Merge sets and ask "same set?" in almost constant time. A. Pattern Overview Union-Find (disjoint set union, DSU) maintains a partition of n elements under two operations: union(a, b) merges the sets of a and b ; find(a) returns a representative of a 's set. Each set is stored as a tree of parent pointers; the root is the representative. Two optimisations make both operations O( α (n)) , effectively constant ( α is the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for any real input): Optimisation What it does Effect Path compression / halving While walking up in find , point nodes closer to the root Flattens trees for later queries Union by size or rank Attach the smaller tree under the larger root Keeps height O(log n) Both together Amortised O( α (n)) per operation KEY IDEA Union-Find only merges. It answers "are they connected now?" for edges arriving online, but cannot delete an edge. For deletions, process offline in reverse (turn deletions into insertions). B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Are X and Y connected?" with edges, equalities, friendships or swaps given as a list or arriving over time. "Merge groups" of items that share an attribute (accounts, emails, equivalent strings). "Which edge creates a cycle" / "redundant connection" : the first union that returns false. "Number of components after each operation" (islands appearing one by one). Equality constraints ( a == b , a != b ) and equivalence classes. Kruskal's MST needs a fast cycle test (Chapter 54). ONE-LINE TEST Symmetric relations that only ever join things, and queries "same group?" → Union-Find. If you must also split groups, think offline-reverse or a different structure. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Forest of parent pointers Start with n singletons: parent[i] = i . find follows parents to a root. union links one root under another. Here is the sample run on 5 elements. Operation Effect parent[] size[] union(0, 1) attach root 1 under 0 [0, 0, 2, 3, 4] [2, 1, 1, 1, 1] union(2, 3) attach root 3 under 2 [0, 0, 2, 2, 4] [2, 1, 2, 1, 1] union(1, 2) attach root 2 under 0 [0, 0, 0, 2, 4] [4, 1, 2, 1, 1] union(0, 3) same root 0: cycle / redundant [0, 0, 0, 0, 4] [4, 1, 2, 1, 1] Figure 92. Arrows point from a vertex to its parent; the root has no outgoing arrow. The last operation union(0, 3) finds the same root (0) for both, so it is redundant : in Redundant Connection this is the edge to return. Final parent[] = [0, 0, 0, 0, 4] ; 4 stays a singleton. Why path halving works while (parent[x] != x) { parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]; } makes every other node on the path point to its grandparent. It needs no recursion, no stack and no second pass, and gives the same amortised bound as full compression. Union by size Attaching the smaller tree under the larger keeps the height at most log ₂ n . Store size[root] too: sizeOf(x) becomes O( α ) , and you can track the largest group ( Making a Large Island, Largest Component Size). PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 53 Shortest Path Algorithms BFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall: pick by weights and scale. A. Pattern Overview The shortest-path problem asks for the minimum total weight of a path between vertices. Four algorithms cover almost every case; the choice depends on edge weights (all equal, non-negative, possibly negative) and on how many sources you need. Algorithm Handles Time Space Use when BFS Unit weights, one source O(n + m) O(n) Moves, hops, grid steps 0-1 BFS Weights 0 or 1, one source O(n + m) O(n) Obstacle removal, flip-cost paths Dijkstra Non-negative weights, one source O((n + m) log n) O(n + m) Roads, latency, probabilities Bellman-Ford Negative weights, one source, detects negative cycles O(n · m) O(n) Negative edges; at most k edges Floyd-Warshall All pairs, negative edges (no negative cycle) O(n³) O(n²) n ≤ ~400 , all-pairs queries DAG DP Any weights, DAG, one source O(n + m) O(n) Topological order exists (Ch. 50) KEY IDEA Dijkstra's invariant: when a vertex is popped from the min-heap, its distance is final, because every other route must pass through a vertex still in the heap with distance ≥ the popped one, and edges cannot make it shorter. One negative edge breaks this , so Dijkstra cannot be used; switch to Bellman-Ford. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Minimum cost / time / distance" between nodes with weights : Dijkstra. "Minimum number of moves" with equal costs: BFS (Chapter 47). "At most k stops / edges" : Bellman-Ford with k + 1 rounds, or Dijkstra on (node, stops) . "Negative weights", "arbitrage", "detect a negative cycle" : Bellman-Ford. "For every pair" , small n (a few hundred): Floyd-Warshall. "Maximise a product of probabilities" or "minimise the maximum edge" : Dijkstra with a changed combine rule. ONE-LINE TEST Read the weights first: equal → BFS; 0/1 → 0-1 BFS; non-negative → Dijkstra; negative → Bellman-Ford; all pairs and tiny n → Floyd-Warshall. C. At most k stops Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (787): run Bellman-Ford for exactly k + 1 rounds, relaxing from a copy of the previous round's distances (otherwise a round can use more than one new edge). Plain Dijkstra fails here because the cheapest path may use too many stops, and a more expensive path with fewer stops can still be needed. Changing what "distance" means Path with Maximum Probability : use a max-heap and multiply (valid because probabilities are in [0, 1] , so extending a path never helps). Path With Minimum Effort (1631): the cost of a path is its maximum step; max(cur, step) replaces + . The rule is: the combine operation must be monotone (extending a path never makes it better). D. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 54 Minimum Spanning Tree Connect everything as cheaply as possible: Kruskal sorts, Prim grows. A. Pattern Overview A spanning tree of a connected undirected graph is a subset of n − 1 edges that connects all vertices without a cycle. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree of least total weight. It models "connect all sites with the least cable", and underlies clustering and approximation algorithms. Property Statement Cut property For any cut of the vertices, the lightest edge crossing it belongs to some MST Cycle property unique maximum) The heaviest edge on any cycle is not needed (it belongs to no MST if it is the Uniqueness If all weights are distinct, the MST is unique Edges Exactly n − 1 ; a disconnected graph has a minimum spanning forest Both greedy algorithms are Because of the cut property correct Kruskal Prim Idea Sort edges; take each that joins two different components Grow one tree; always add the cheapest edge leaving it Data structure Union-Find (Chapter 52) Min-heap (or array scan) Time O(m log m) O(m log n) ; O(n²) with an array Best for Sparse graphs, edge-list input Dense graphs, implicit complete graphs KEY IDEA Greedy works here because of the cut property. At every step the algorithm adds the lightest edge that crosses some cut, which is always safe. (This is why greedy fails for shortest paths with negative edges or for the travelling salesman problem: they lack such a property.) B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Connect all nodes / cities / points with minimum total cost". "Minimum cable / road / pipe length" and every node must be reachable. Cost of an edge is given, the answer is a total, not a path. "Minimise the maximum edge" to connect two nodes: the minimax path lies on the MST. "Clusters" : remove the k − 1 heaviest MST edges to get k groups (single-linkage clustering). A complete graph on points with Manhattan or Euclidean distances: dense Prim, O(n²) . ONE-LINE TEST "Connect everything" + "minimum total" = MST. "Shortest route from A to B" = shortest path. Do not confuse them: the MST does not give shortest paths. C. Prim starts at vertex 0 and repeatedly pops the cheapest edge leaving the tree; stale entries to vertices already inside are discarded. Dense graphs: Prim in O(n²) For Min Cost to Connect All Points (1584) the graph is complete with n²/2 edges. Never build the edge list ( n = 1000 gives 500 000 edges and a sort). Keep dist[v] = cheapest edge into the tree, and each round scan for the minimum: O(n²) time, O(n) memory. Why the cycle property is the Kruskal rejection rule When Kruskal examines edge e = (u, v) and u , v are already connected, all edges on that path are no heavier than e (they were examined earlier). So e is the heaviest edge on a cycle and is safe to discard. Minimax paths The path between two vertices in the MST minimises the largest edge weight among all paths between them. That is how Path With Minimum Effort can also be solved, and it is the key to "minimum bottleneck" queries. D. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 55 Grid-Based Graph Problems A grid is an implicit graph: cells are vertices, neighbours are computed. A. Pattern Overview Many "graph" problems arrive as a matrix. Each cell is a vertex; its edges go to the 4 (or 8) adjacent cells that satisfy a rule. Never build the adjacency list : generate neighbours on demand with direction arrays. Everything from Chapters 47 to 53 applies: components (islands), BFS (shortest path), Dijkstra (weighted cells), Union-Find (online land). Perimeter without a traversal Each land cell contributes 4 sides; every pair of adjacent land cells hides 2 sides. Number of Enclaves: land that cannot reach the border. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 56 Multi-Source BFS Start the queue with every source at once: distance to the nearest one. A. Pattern Overview Ordinary BFS starts from one vertex. Multi-source BFS starts from a set of sources, all at distance 0, by putting every one of them in the queue before the loop begins. The first time a vertex is reached, its distance is the distance to the nearest source. It is equivalent to adding a virtual super-source connected to every real source by a 0-cost edge. Multi-source BFS: the whole template Java 17+ Deque queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); for (int r = 0; r Question Sources Result Minutes until all oranges rot (994) All rotten oranges Number of BFS rounds Distance of each cell to the nearest 0 (542) All zeros dist[][] Water cell farthest from land (1162) All land cells Largest dist Distance to the nearest gate (286) All gates dist[][] Join two islands (934) All cells of one island Rounds until the other island is touched Safest path in a grid (2812) All thieves Safeness map, then a path search KEY IDEA Reverse the direction of the search. "For every cell, distance to the nearest X" would need one BFS per cell ( O(mn · mn) ). Run one BFS from all the X cells outwards instead ( O(mn) ): on an undirected graph the distance is symmetric. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Distance of each cell to the nearest …" (zero, gate, land, building). Simultaneous spreading: fire, infection, rot, flood, rumour: "every minute", "all at the same time". "Minimum time for everything to be affected" : the number of BFS rounds. "Farthest / safest from all hazards" : compute the distance map first, then optimise on it. Several starting points but a single shared goal ("shortest bridge", "nearest exit among many"). ONE-LINE TEST Many sources, unit edges, "nearest" or "time to spread": put all sources in the queue at distance 0. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Rotting oranges, minute by minute 2 rotten, 1 fresh, 0 empty. Each BFS round (one minute) turns every fresh orange adjacent to a rotten one rotten. Freezing queue.size() at the start of a round keeps the minutes apart. Figure 98. Rotting spreads one layer per minute (red = rotten, amber = fresh, blank = empty). All fresh oranges are rotten after 4 minutes. If a fresh orange were walled off by empty cells, fresh would stay positive and the answer is −1 . Distance to the nearest zero Figure 99. Two sources at (1,1) and (3,2) : every cell receives its distance to the closest one. Why one queue is enough The queue invariant of BFS holds even with many sources: it contains vertices at distance d followed by vertices at distance d + 1 . A vertex is first reached through the closest source, so its stored distance is the minimum over all sources. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 57 Bipartite Graph Two-colour the graph; an odd cycle is the only obstruction. A. Pattern Overview A graph is bipartite if its vertices split into two sets A and B so that every edge joins A to B . Equivalently: it can be two-coloured , or it has no odd-length cycle . The test is a BFS or DFS that assigns each neighbour the opposite colour and fails on the first edge whose endpoints share a colour. O(V + E) . BFS layers alternate colours, so the only way to fail is an edge inside one layer or between layers of equal parity: that edge closes an odd cycle. B. Kuhn's algorithm tries each left vertex and searches an augmenting path (alternating unmatched / matched edges); O(V · E) . Hopcroft–Karp batches augmentations into BFS phases for O(E √ V) . König's theorem: in bipartite graphs, max matching = min vertex cover. D. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 58 Strongly Connected Components Maximal groups of vertices that can all reach each other. A. Pattern Overview In a directed graph, a strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of vertices in which every vertex can reach every other. Contract each SCC to one node and the result, the condensation , is always a DAG. Two linear-time algorithms find the SCCs: Tarjan (one DFS with low-links and a stack) and Kosaraju (DFS on the graph, then DFS on the reversed graph in decreasing finish order). Concept Meaning Strongly connected u reaches v and v reaches u SCC Maximal strongly connected vertex set (an equivalence class) Condensation DAG One node per SCC, edges between SCCs; no cycles Source / sink SCC No incoming / no outgoing edges in the condensation disc[u] , low[u] Discovery time; smallest disc reachable via tree edges + one back/cross edge to the stack HOW OFTEN Honest note: SCC rarely appears in LeetCode (Critical Connections is the undirected cousin of Chapter 59). It is, however, a standard senior-level tool: dependency cycles in build systems, deadlock detection, 2-SAT, and condensing a graph before DP. Learn the idea well; do not over-invest in memorising code. B. "Minimum edges to make the graph strongly connected" : count source and sink SCCs. A DP over a graph that has cycles: condense first, then DP on the DAG. Deadlock / cyclic dependency reports that must list the whole group, not just detect one cycle. Implication graphs (2-SAT): variable and its negation in the same SCC means unsatisfiable. ONE-LINE TEST Directed + "everyone in the group can reach everyone else" = SCC. Directed + "is there a cycle" = Chapter 49 (colours or Kahn) is enough. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Three SCCs and a DAG between them Figure 102. Same colour = same SCC. Cycles 0→1→2→0, 3→4→5→3 and 6↔7; edges 2→3 and 6→5 cross between components. Component edges {0,1,2} → {3,4,5} and {6,7} → {3,4,5} form a DAG: no path can return, otherwise the components would merge. Tarjan's low-link DFS assigns disc[u] in visit order. low[u] is the smallest disc reachable from u 's subtree using tree edges plus one edge to a vertex still on the stack . When low[u] == disc[u] , u is the root of an SCC: pop the stack down to u ; those vertices form the component. The "still on the stack" test is what separates cross edges to finished SCCs (ignored) from back edges into the current one. Root closes disc low SCC popped 3 3 3 [3, 4, 5] 0 0 0 [0, 1, 2] 6 6 6 [6, 7] Kosaraju in two passes Pass 1: DFS on G , push vertices in finish order. Pass 2: process vertices in reverse finish order on the transposed graph G ᵀ ; each DFS tree is exactly one SCC. Why: the vertex finishing last belongs to a source SCC of G , which is a sink SCC of G ᵀ , so its DFS in G ᵀ cannot escape the component. Condensation and counting sources To make a graph strongly connected by adding the fewest edges, count SCCs with in-degree 0 ( s ) and out-degree 0 ( t ) in the condensation: the answer is max(s, t) (when there is more than one SCC). Functional graphs: a lighter special case When every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge ( Longest Cycle in a Graph , 2360; Maximum Employees to Be Invited , 2127), each component has at most one cycle; you can find cycles with timestamps or Kahn's algorithm without full SCC machinery. PART VIII · GRAPH PATTERNS 59 Bridges and Articulation Points Edges and vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. A. Pattern Overview In an undirected connected graph, a bridge (cut edge) is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph; an articulation point (cut vertex) is a vertex whose removal does. Both fall out of one DFS that records disc[u] (discovery time) and low[u] (the earliest discovery time reachable from u 's subtree using at most one back edge). Time O(V + E) .
