PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 60 Top K Elements Keep only the k best seen so far: a bounded heap, or quickselect. A. Pattern Overview Many problems ask for the k largest, k smallest, k closest or k most frequent items, or for the k-th item in sorted order. Sorting answers all of them in O(n log n) , but you rarely need the whole order. A bounded heap of size k keeps only the current best k candidates and costs O(n log k) time and O(k) space; quickselect finds the k-th element in expected O(n) . KEY IDEA Use the opposite heap. To keep the k largest , use a min-heap : the root is the weakest member of the current top k, so it is the one to evict when a better item arrives. To keep the k smallest , use a max-heap. Choosing the same-direction heap is the classic mistake. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "k-th largest / smallest" , "top k", "k closest", "k most frequent", "k weakest". A stream ("after each insertion, return the k-th largest") where you cannot sort the future. k is much smaller than n , or the constraints hint at n up to 10⁵–10⁶ with O(n log k) expected. "Repeatedly take the largest / smallest, modify it, put it back" (Last Stone Weight, halve the array): a heap simulates the process. Only a partial order is needed: you do not care how items below the k-th are arranged. ONE-LINE TEST "Best k out of n" with k � n or a stream: bounded heap. "Just the k-th value" of a static array: quickselect. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations The heap as a tree stored in an array A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored level by level in an array: the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 , the parent is (i − 1) / 2 . In a min-heap every node is ≤ its children, so the root is the minimum. offer and poll sift an element up or down one root-to-leaf path: O(log n) . peek is O(1) . Figure 104. The same seven values as a tree; the root (teal) is the minimum. Figure 105. Array layout of that heap. PITFALL A PriorityQueue 's iterator, toString() and toArray() are in heap order, not sorted order. Only repeated poll() returns elements in order. Printing a heap and "seeing" it unsorted is expected. Why a size-k min-heap holds the k largest After processing a prefix, the heap holds the k largest values of that prefix. A new value x either beats the root (the k-th largest so far), in which case the root is evicted and x takes a place in the top k, or it does not, and it is discarded immediately. The root is always the k-th largest so far. Quickselect: partition, then keep only one side Quicksort recurses on both sides of the pivot; quickselect recurses on the one side that contains the target index. The expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n) . A 3-way partition ( < pivot , == pivot , > pivot ) is essential with duplicates, and a random pivot avoids the O(n²) worst case on sorted input. Streams: the heap is the state KthLargest keeps a min-heap of exactly k values. add(x) costs O(log k) and the answer is always heap.peek() . PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 61 Two Heaps Split the data at the median: a max-heap below, a min-heap above. A. Pattern Overview The two-heaps pattern keeps a collection split into a lower half in a max-heap and an upper half in a min-heap . Every element in the lower half is ≤ every element in the upper half, and the heaps differ in size by at most one. The median is read from the two roots in O(1) ; each insertion costs O(log n) . Any problem asking for the median (or any fixed percentile) of a changing collection is a candidate. Running median: the whole pattern Java 17+ PriorityQueue lo = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()); // max-heap PriorityQueue hi = new PriorityQueue<>(); // min-heap void addNum(int num) { lo.offer(num); hi.offer(lo.poll()); // 1. route through lo: keeps lo lo.size()) lo.offer(hi.poll()); // 2. rebalance: |lo| = |hi| or |hi| + 1 } double median() { return lo.size() > hi.size() ? lo.peek() : ((long) lo.peek() + hi.peek()) / 2.0; } KEY IDEA Two invariants, always: (1) max(lo) ≤ min(hi) ; (2) |lo| = |hi| or |lo| = |hi| + 1 . Inserting through the other heap first guarantees (1) without any comparison; a single size check restores (2). B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Median" of a stream, a sliding window, or a changing set. Balance a collection into two halves and query the boundary between them. "Choose the best project / task now, then unlock more" (IPO): one structure of locked items sorted by a threshold, one heap of available items sorted by value. Core Intuition with Illustrations Why the median sits at the boundary Sorted order is [small half | large half] . The median is the largest of the small half (odd count) or the average of the two boundary elements (even count). A max-heap exposes the largest of the small half; a min-heap exposes the smallest of the large half. Nothing else in either half matters for the median, which is why heaps (partial order) are enough and a fully sorted structure is unnecessary. PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 62 K-Way Merge Merge k sorted sources by always taking the smallest front element. A. Pattern Overview Merging two sorted sequences needs two pointers. Merging k sorted sequences needs to find the smallest of k front elements at every step. A min-heap holding one "front" per source answers that in O(log k) , so merging N total elements costs O(N log k) time and O(k) extra space. The same machine finds the k-th smallest of many sorted rows, the smallest pairs from two sorted arrays, and the smallest range that touches every list. Pop the smallest, then push the successor of the same source . The heap size never exceeds k , so each operation is O(log k) , independent of how long the lists are. B. "Smallest range covering one element from each list". External sorting, log merging, database merge joins: merge many sorted runs on disk. Each pop emits the global minimum and pushes the next element of the list it came from. Why it is correct At every step the smallest not-yet-emitted element is the front of some list (lists are sorted), and every list front is in the heap. So the heap minimum is the global minimum of the remaining elements. Emitting it and exposing its successor preserves that invariant. Merging linked lists reuses the nodes For ListNode inputs the heap holds the nodes themselves , ordered by val . Polling a node, linking it to the output tail and offering its next merges everything in place , with O(1) extra nodes. Remember to skip null heads. A matrix is k sorted lists in disguise In a row-sorted matrix, each row is a sorted list. For the k-th smallest, seed the heap with the first element of the first min(n, k) rows and pop k times, each time pushing the right neighbour (378). Time O(k log min(n, k)) . If the matrix is also column-sorted, binary search on the value is O(n log(max − min)) and uses no heap. Smallest pairs: an implicit sorted matrix Pairs (a[i], b[j]) form a matrix whose rows i are sorted by j (because b is sorted). Seed with (i, 0) for the first k indices of a ; popping (i, j) pushes (i, j + 1) . We never build all |a| · |b| pairs (373). Smallest range covering all lists Keep one element per list in the heap and track their maximum . The window [heap minimum, max] covers every list. Record it, then advance the list that supplied the minimum; stop when a list runs out (632). D. PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 63 Scheduling with Priority Queue Greedy choices made, and reconsidered, with a heap of what is available. A. Pattern Overview Many scheduling and resource problems have the same skeleton: sweep over time (or a sorted order); at each step add what became available to a priority queue; then take the best available item. A second flavour defers a decision and undoes it later ("use a ladder now, and if I run out, retroactively swap the smallest climb to bricks"). The heap holds exactly the choices you may still revise. When a greedy choice can be revisited cheaply, make the optimistic choice, push it in a heap, and undo the least valuable commitment only when a constraint breaks. The heap root is the best candidate to undo. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Tasks with start (enqueue) times and durations or deadlines and a rule for picking the next one. "Maximise the number of courses / jobs / events" under deadlines: heap of durations, drop the longest. Two resources, one scarce (ladders vs bricks, fuel stops vs distance): defer the use of the scarce resource. "Pick at most k" with a score that depends on the minimum (or a threshold) of the chosen set : sort by the threshold, keep a size-k heap. Simulation of a machine that repeatedly chooses the "next best" item. ONE-LINE TEST Time or threshold sweep plus "best available" or "undo the worst": sorted input + PriorityQueue . C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Furthest building: ladders absorb the biggest climbs Heights [4, 2, 7, 6, 9, 14, 12] , 5 bricks, 1 ladder. Every positive climb enters a min-heap of ladder-covered climbs . When the heap has more entries than ladders, the smallest climb is moved from a ladder to bricks. Climbs are processed left to right but the final assignment is as if we had known all climbs in advance: the largest ones get the ladders. Why the exchange is safe At any moment the set of climbs covered by ladders should be the ladders largest climbs seen so far (a ladder is worth most on a tall climb). The heap maintains exactly that set. If it overflows, evicting its smallest member is optimal by an exchange argument: swapping a smaller climb onto bricks never uses more bricks. CHAPTER SUMMARY Scheduling with a priority queue: sweep over time or a sorted key, add newly available items, take the best; or make an optimistic choice and undo the cheapest-to-undo one when a constraint breaks. Furthest Building: ladders belong on the largest climbs, so keep a min-heap of ladder climbs and spill the smallest to bricks. CPU / IPO: sort by enqueue (or capital), heap by duration (or profit); jump over idle time. Courses III / Refuel: retroactive undo with a max-heap: drop the longest course, spend the biggest passed fuel. Performance / Hire K: sort by the threshold quantity, keep a size-k heap of the best values; multiply in long .

Any solution with c intervals cannot reach beyond the greedy reach , because every interval it could use starts within the previous reach (otherwise there would be a gap) and the greedy already picked the furthest end among them. By induction the greedy reaches at least as far with every c , so it needs no more intervals than any other solution. A gap means failure If no interval starting within reach ends beyond reach , the next point cannot be covered: return -1 . PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 65 Activity Selection Sort by finish time; always take the activity that ends first. A. Pattern Overview Given activities with start and end times, choose the largest set that do not overlap . The greedy rule is simple and surprisingly strong: sort by end time and take every activity whose start is at or after the end of the last one taken. It is the textbook greedy algorithm, and its proof (an exchange argument) is the template for most greedy proofs in this book. Touching endpoints (end 4, start 4) are compatible. Exchange argument Let g be the activity with the earliest finish time. Take any optimal solution S ; let a be its first activity. Since g finishes no later than a , replacing a with g keeps S valid (nothing else in S starts before a ends, hence not before g ends) and the same size. So some optimal solution contains g . Remove g and every activity overlapping it, and the rest is the same problem on a smaller instance: induction finishes the proof. Pattern Overview The meeting-rooms family asks two questions about a list of [start, end) intervals: can one person attend all of them (no overlap), and how many rooms are needed (the maximum number of meetings in progress at the same instant). The heap's size is the number of rooms allocated; it never shrinks below the number of live meetings. Why the heap works Process meetings by start time. The heap holds one end time per occupied room. The smallest end time is the room that frees up first. If it is ≤ the new start, reuse it (pop, then push the new end); otherwise a new room is needed (push). The heap size after processing is the number of rooms in use. Sweep line without a heap Sort all starts and all ends separately. Walk the starts; for each start, first retire every meeting whose end is ≤ that start (ties: ends first, because [a, b) and [b, c) do not overlap), then count the new meeting. Track the maximum count. No heap and no objects, only two sorted int[] . Events form: +1 and −1 The sweep line generalises: emit an event (time, +1) at each start and (time, −1) at each end, sort by time ( −1 before +1 on ties), and keep a running sum. The maximum prefix sum is the peak. With weights ( Car Pooling ) the ±1 becomes ±passengers . Rooms with identities (2402) When meetings must take the lowest-numbered free room , and a delayed meeting keeps its duration, use two heaps: free rooms ordered by index and busy rooms ordered by (end time, index) . Before each meeting, release every busy room that has ended; if no room is free, take the busy room that ends first and delay the meeting. D. PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 67 Jump Game Track the furthest reach; each BFS level is one more jump. A. Pattern Overview In a jump game you stand at index 0 of an array and each cell says how far (or in which ways) you may jump. The classic questions are can I reach the end? (55) and what is the fewest number of jumps? (45). Both have an O(n) greedy solution that maintains one number, the furthest index reachable so far , and the second reads it as an implicit BFS whose levels are jumps. Variants with irregular moves (backwards jumps, teleports to equal values, windows) fall back to explicit BFS or sliding-window DP. The two greedy loops int far = 0; // Jump Game: can we reach the end? for (int i = 0; i far) return false; // stranded: index i is unreachable far = Math.max(far, i + nums[i]); } return true; int jumps = 0, levelEnd = 0; // Jump Game II: fewest jumps for (int i = 0; i Java 17+ Problem Moves Method Time Jump Game (55) Forward 1..nums[i] Furthest reach O(n) Jump Game II (45) Forward 1..nums[i] Greedy = implicit BFS by levels O(n) Jump Game III (1306) ±arr[i] BFS / DFS over indices O(n) Jump Game IV (1345) ±1 , or any equal value BFS; clear each value group once O(n) Jump Game VI (1696) Forward 1..k , maximise score DP + monotonic deque ( JumpGameVI.java ) O(n) Jump Game VII (1871) Forward [minJump, maxJump] , only on '0' Sliding window count of reachable O(n) KEY IDEA Reachability is contiguous. If you can reach index far , you can reach every index ≤ far too, because a jump may be shorter than nums[i] . So one number (the furthest reach) describes the entire reachable set. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals An array of maximum jump lengths and a question about reaching the end or the fewest jumps. "Reach the last index" with moves that go forward by up to some value. Layers of reachability: all indices reachable in 1 jump, then 2 jumps, and so on (BFS by levels). Backward moves or teleports (equal values, ±arr[i] ): explicit BFS with a visited array. A sliding window of allowed jump lengths ( minJump..maxJump ): sliding window counter or deque DP. ONE-LINE TEST Forward jumps up to nums[i] : greedy furthest reach. Arbitrary jump rules: BFS on indices. Score-maximising jumps with a window k : DP + deque. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Furthest reach, scanned once nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] . At index 0 the reach is 2; index 1 extends it to 4 (the last index); the loop can stop. If the reach ever lags behind the scan ( i > far ), index i and everything after it is unreachable. i nums[i] furthest Note 0 2 2 reach 2 1 3 4 reach 4 2 1 4 reach 4 3 1 4 reach 4 4 4 8 reach 8 Figure 110. The reachable prefix grows as the scan advances. A failing case [3, 2, 1, 0, 4] : every jump from indices 0 to 2 reaches at most index 3, where nums[3] = 0 traps you. At i = 4 , far = 3 < 4 : return false . The zero is a barrier only if nothing before it can jump past it. Fewest jumps: BFS by levels without a queue Level 0 is {0} . Level 1 is every index reachable by one jump from level 0, i.e. 1..nums[0] . Level 2 is everything reachable from level-1 indices, and so on. Because reachability is contiguous, each level is an interval (levelEnd_prev, levelEnd] . Scan the current level, compute the furthest index any cell in it reaches, and when the scan hits the level's end, count a jump and move the boundary to that furthest index. i nums[i] furthest level end Note 0 2 2 2 jump 1: next level ends at 2 1 3 4 2 2 1 4 4 jump 2: next level ends at 4 3 1 4 4 [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] needs 2 jumps (0 → 1 → 4). Why jumps need to stop one before the last index The loop runs to n − 2 : once the boundary reaches the last index no further jump is needed, and counting at index n − 1 would add a spurious jump when levelEnd == n − 1 . Backward and teleport jumps need a visited array Jump Game III allows i ± arr[i] ; the goal is any index with value 0. A BFS or DFS with a visited array is O(n) . Jump Game IV adds teleports to every index with the same value. The classic trap is O(n²) : visit a value group once , then delete it from the map so later cells with that value do not re-scan the group. Window of allowed jump lengths In Jump Game VII ( s[j] == '0' , jump length in [minJump, maxJump] ) index i is reachable if some reachable j lies in [i − maxJump, i − minJump] . Maintain a counter of reachable indices inside that sliding window: add i − minJump when it becomes eligible, remove i − maxJump − 1 when it leaves. O(n) with no inner loop. D. PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 68 Gas Station Circular tours, two-pass constraints and one-scan feasibility. A. Pattern Overview Gas Station is the model problem for a family of greedy arguments built on running totals: when a prefix of the scan becomes infeasible, you can discard all starting points in that prefix at once. Related problems ( Candy, Lemonade Change, Hand of Straights ) share the flavour: make the locally forced choice, never look back, and prove it with a short exchange or counting argument. Gas Station: one pass long total = 0, tank = 0; int start = 0; for (int i = 0; i = 0 ? start : -1; Java 17+ Problem Greedy fact Time Gas Station (134) Total ≥ 0 ⇒ a start exists; a failure at i kills every start in [start, i] O(n) Candy (135) Two passes: satisfy the left neighbour, then the right neighbour with max O(n) Lemonade Change (860) For a 20-dollar bill give 10 + 5 before 5 + 5 + 5 O(n) Hand of Straights (846) The smallest card must start a group O(n log n) Maximum Sum Circular Subarray Best is max(maxSub, total − minSub) O(n) (918) KEY IDEA A failing prefix eliminates all its starts. If starting at s first fails at i , then starting at any s' ∈ (s, i] also fails: each of those prefixes had a non-negative tank on arrival (otherwise the failure would have occurred earlier), so beginning with an empty tank is no better. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals A circular array and the question "from which index can you complete the loop?". Running balance must stay non-negative (fuel, cash, inventory). Total ≥ 0 means feasible somewhere: the question is only where to start. Each element must be better than a neighbour (ratings, heights): two directional passes. The tank column is the running balance since the last restart; total is the whole-circuit balance. Why one candidate suffices Two facts. (1) If total ≥ 0 , the candidate chosen by the scan (the index after the last failure) completes the circuit: the suffix from start to n − 1 has non-negative balance (it never failed), and the prefix before it has total balance total − suffix , which is a deficit at most the suffix surplus, because total ≥ 0 . (2) Every earlier start was eliminated by a failure. So the candidate is the unique answer (the problem guarantees uniqueness; otherwise it is an answer). Prefix-sum view Let P[i] be the prefix sum of gas − cost . The correct start is the index right after the minimum prefix sum : starting there turns every partial sum into P[i] − P[min] ≥ 0 . This is the same computation as the greedy, expressed with an argmin . Candy: two passes, one constraint each Each child has ≥ 1 candy and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour needs more candy than that neighbour. A left-to-right pass enforces the left constraint; a right-to-left pass enforces the right constraint using max so the left result is not destroyed. Figure 111. Ratings [1,0,2,2,3,1] need 9 candies in total. Lemonade change: prefer the bills you will need least Customers pay 5, 10 or 20 for a 5-dollar lemonade. A 5 needs no change, a 10 needs one 5, and a 20 needs 15: either 10 + 5 or 5 + 5 + 5 . Give 10 + 5 first because fives are useful for every future 10 and 20, while tens are useful only for 20s. Keeping fives is never worse. Hand of Straights: the smallest card has no choice Whatever the arrangement, the smallest remaining card must be the start of its group (nothing smaller is left to precede it). Remove first, first + 1, ..., first + groupSize − 1 ; if any is missing, fail. A TreeMap keeps the counts sorted. D. PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 69 Task Scheduler Cooldowns: the most frequent task decides the length. A. Pattern Overview Given tasks (letters) and a cooldown n , the same task must be separated by at least n other slots, and the CPU may idle. What is the least time to finish? Two solutions: a closed formula driven by the most frequent task, and a simulation with a max-heap of remaining counts plus a cooldown queue. The same machinery rearranges strings so equal letters are k apart (Reorganize String, Rearrange String k Distance Apart). Task Scheduler in O(n): the formula Java 17+ int [] freq = new int [ 26 ]; 1 2 int maxFreq = 0 ; for ( char t : tasks) maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, ++freq[t - 'A' ]); 3 4 int tied = 0 ; for ( int f : freq) if (f == maxFreq) tied++; // tasks sharing the maximum 5 6 long frame = ( long ) (maxFreq - 1 ) * (n + 1 ) + tied; // (maxFreq - 1) full frames + last row return ( int ) Math.max(tasks.length, frame); // never fewer slots than tasks 7 Problem Constraint Greedy Time Task Scheduler (621) Same task n slots apart Most frequent first; formula or heap O(n) / O(T log 26) Reorganize String (767) No two equal neighbours ( k = Max-heap of counts, hold the O(n log 26) 2 ) previous letter back Rearrange String k Distance Equal letters ≥ k apart Max-heap + waiting queue of size k O(n log 26) (358) Task Scheduler II (2365) Tasks in order; space days Jump to last + space + 1 O(n) between equal types Minimum Rounds (2244) Finish tasks in groups of 2 or 3 ⌈ count / 3 ⌉ per type, -1 if count is 1 O(n) KEY IDEA The busiest task is the bottleneck. If task A appears m times, between its m copies there are m − 1 gaps of at least n slots each. Everything else is packed into those gaps; only if the gaps overflow does the answer become the number of tasks. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Cooldown", "at least k apart", "no two adjacent equal" in a scheduling or arrangement problem. The answer depends on the most frequent item and on how many items tie for the maximum. Counts, not order, matter (letters are interchangeable except for their type). Idle time may be inserted and you minimise the total length. "Return any valid arrangement or empty string" : feasibility is maxFreq ≤ ⌈ (len + k − 1) / k ⌉ -style. ONE-LINE TEST Equal items must be spaced apart: count frequencies and place the most frequent first (heap of counts), or use the frame formula. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Frames of n + 1 slots Tasks AAABBB , cooldown n = 2 . The most frequent tasks A and B (3 each) define m − 1 = 2 frames of n + 1 = 3 slots, plus a final row holding one copy of each tied task: Figure 112. Two frames of three slots plus a last row of two tied tasks; _ marks idle. Formula: (maxFreq − 1) · (n + 1) + tied = (3 − 1) · 3 + 2 = 8 slots (idle slots included); simulation gives 8. When the formula is too small With many different tasks the gaps overflow and no idle time is needed: the answer is just the number of tasks. Example: AAABBBCCCDDD with n = 2 has frame length (3 − 1) · 3 + 4 = 10 < 12 , so the answer is 12. That is why the code returns max(tasks.length, frame) . The simulation Each time slot: move a task from the cooldown queue back into the heap if its cooldown ended, then run the task with the highest remaining count, put it in the queue with ready-time time + n + 1 , or idle if the heap is empty but the queue is not. Running the highest count first is what keeps the busiest tasks from being starved. Reorganize and k-distance as the same machine Reorganize String is the k = 2 case: after using a letter, hold it out for one step. Rearrange String k Distance Apart holds it out for k − 1 steps using a queue; if the heap empties before all letters are placed, the arrangement is impossible. A quick feasibility check for k = 2 is maxFreq ≤ (len + 1) / 2 . Task Scheduler II and Minimum Rounds: counting shortcuts Task Scheduler II (tasks in a fixed order) only needs lastDay[type] : if the current day is within space of the last run, jump to last + space + 1 . Minimum Rounds (2244) is a pure counting greedy: a type with c tasks needs ⌈ c / 3 ⌉ rounds (use as many triples as possible, and c mod 3 ∈ {1, 2} is absorbed by one extra round); c = 1 is impossible. Java Implementation Task Scheduler (formula and simulation), k-distance, Scheduler II, minimum rounds TaskScheduler.java: LeetCode 621, 358, 2365, 2244 import java.util.*; /** * Ch 69: cooldown scheduling; LeetCode 621, 358, 2365, 2244 (767 is * ReorganizeString). */ public class TaskScheduler { /** LeetCode 621 in O(n): idle slots are forced by the most frequent task(s). */ public static int leastInterval(char[] tasks, int n) { int[] freq = new int[26]; int maxFreq = 0; for (char t : tasks) maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, ++freq[t - 'A']); int tied = 0; for (int f : freq) if (f == maxFreq) tied++; // frames of n + 1 slots long frame = (long) (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + tied; // never fewer than the tasks return (int) Math.max(tasks.length, frame); } /** LeetCode 621 by simulation: max-heap of counts plus a cooldown queue. */ public static int leastIntervalSimulation(char[] tasks, int n) { int[] freq = new int[26]; for (char t : tasks) freq[t - 'A']++; PriorityQueue ready = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()); for (int f : freq) if (f > 0) ready.offer(f); // {count left, time it is ready} Deque cooling = new ArrayDeque<>(); int time = 0; while (!ready.isEmpty() || !cooling.isEmpty()) { time++; if (!cooling.isEmpty() && cooling.peekFirst()[1] == time) ready.offer(cooling.poll()[0]); if (!ready.isEmpty()) { // run the most frequent task int left = ready.poll() - 1; if (left > 0) cooling.add(new int[] {left, time + n + 1}); } } return time; } /** * LeetCode 358: rearrange so equal letters are at least k apart; "" if * impossible. Greedy: place the most frequent available letter each step. */ public static String rearrangeKDistance(String s, int k) { if (k heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[1] != b[1] ? Integer.compare(b[1], a[1]) : Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])); for (int c = 0; c 0) heap.offer(new int[] {c, freq[c]}); StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(); Deque wait = new ArrayDeque<>(); while (!heap.isEmpty()) { int[] cur = heap.poll(); Java 17+ out.append((char) ('a' + cur[0])); cur[1]--; wait.add(cur); // k steps passed: usable again if (wait.size() >= k) { int[] back = wait.poll(); if (back[1] > 0) heap.offer(back); } } return out.length() == s.length() ? out.toString() : ""; } /** * LeetCode 2365: tasks run in order; same type needs `space` days between runs. */ public static long taskSchedulerII(int[] tasks, int space) { Map lastDay = new HashMap<>(); long day = 0; for (int t : tasks) { day++; Long last = lastDay.get(t); // wait it out if (last != null && day count = new HashMap<>(); for (int t : tasks) count.merge(t, 1, Integer::sum); int rounds = 0; for (int c : count.values()) { if (c == 1) return -1; // ceil(c / 3): leftovers fit as 2s rounds += (c + 2) / 3; } return rounds; } } TIME O(T) SPACE O(1) The formula is O(T) time and a 26-entry array. PART IX · HEAP AND GREEDY PATTERNS 70 Huffman Coding Repeatedly merge the two lightest: optimal prefix codes. A. Pattern Overview Huffman coding assigns shorter bit strings to more frequent symbols so that the total encoded length is minimal among all prefix codes (no code is a prefix of another, so decoding needs no separators). The algorithm is the canonical heap-driven greedy: put every symbol in a min-heap by weight , repeatedly merge the two lightest trees into one whose weight is their sum, and read the codes from the root-to-leaf paths (left = 0, right = 1). Huffman: the whole algorithm PriorityQueue heap = new PriorityQueue<>(byWeight); for (symbol : symbols) heap.offer(leaf(symbol)); while (heap.size() > 1) { Node a = heap.poll(), b = heap.poll(); // the two lightest trees heap.offer(new Node(a.weight + b.weight, a, b)); // merge: cost a.weight + b.weight } Node root = heap.poll(); // codes = paths from the root Java 17+ Same engine, different story What is merged Cost Huffman coding Symbol frequencies Total bits Σ freq · depth Connect Sticks (1167) Sticks, cost = sum of the two lengths Total merge cost Optimal merge pattern (files) Files, cost = size of the merged file Total I/O Minimum Time to Build Blocks (1199) Blocks, merge time = split + max Variant with max instead of sum Fill Cups (2335), Last Stone (1046) Take two largest, reduce A max-heap cousin KEY IDEA The total cost of merging equals the weighted path length of the merge tree. Every merge adds the combined weight once, and a leaf's weight is added once per ancestor, i.e. once per level of depth. Minimising total merge cost is minimising Σ weight · depth . B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Minimum total cost to combine all items" where combining two items costs their sum and produces a new item. Variable-length encoding / compression with known frequencies. Merge files / sticks / ropes pairwise with cost proportional to size. Cost structure is additive over merges and the order of merging is free. "Always combine the two smallest" feels natural: a heap plus a loop. ONE-LINE TEST Repeatedly combine two items, cost = their sum, order is free: always merge the two smallest (min-heap). C. Then c:12 and b:13 : 25. Then 14 and d:16 : 30. Then 25 and 30 : 55. Finally a:45 and 55 : 100. Merge the two lightest New node Weight Running cost added f(5) + e(9) N6 14 14 c(12) + b(13) N7 25 25 N6(14) + d(16) N8 30 30 N7(25) + N8(30) N9 55 55 a(45) + N9(55) N10 100 100 Figure 113. Leaves show the symbol and, below it, its frequency; edge labels are the bits. Symbol Frequency Code Bits a 45 0 1 b 13 101 3 c 12 100 3 d 16 111 3 e 9 1101 4 f 5 1100 4 Total encoded length: 45·1 + 13·3 + 12·3 + 16·3 + 9·4 + 5·4 = 224 bits per 100 symbols, versus 300 for a fixed 3-bit code: a 25% saving. The exact bit strings depend on tie-breaking; the cost does not. Why prefix-free codes are a tree Place symbols at the leaves of a binary tree. A code is the path from the root. No leaf is an ancestor of another, so no code is a prefix of another. Decoding walks the tree bit by bit and restarts at the root on reaching a leaf. Why the greedy is optimal The two lightest symbols x, y can be siblings at the deepest level of some optimal tree: if they were shallower than another symbol z at max depth, swapping x with z cannot increase the cost ( weight(x) ≤ weight(z) and depth decreases for z ). (2) Merging them into one symbol of weight w(x) + w(y) gives a smaller instance whose optimal cost plus w(x) + w(y) is the original optimum. Induction on the number of symbols finishes the proof. Kraft's inequality A prefix code with lengths �₁ … �ₙ exists iff Σ 2^(− �ᵢ ) ≤ 1 . Huffman codes are complete: the sum equals exactly 1 (every internal node has two children). The test suite checks this for every random alphabet. Decoding and the single-symbol case Decode by walking from the root; each leaf emits a symbol. With one distinct symbol the tree is a single leaf with an empty path; the implementation assigns the code 0 so every symbol still costs one bit. Cost-only problems: no tree needed Connect Sticks only needs the total merge cost: poll two, add their sum to the answer, push the sum. Use long : with many large sticks the cost exceeds int quickly. CHAPTER SUMMARY Huffman coding: merge the two lightest trees until one remains; codes are the root-to-leaf paths; the result minimises Σ freq · depth among prefix codes. Why it works: the two lightest symbols can be deepest siblings in some optimal tree (exchange argument); merging them gives a smaller instance of the same problem. Cost view: the total merge cost equals the weighted path length, so Connect Sticks needs only a min-heap and a long total. Codes are prefix-free (symbols at leaves) and complete (Kraft sum = 1); a single symbol gets the code 0 . Where merging is restricted to neighbours ( Minimum Cost to Merge Stones ), the greedy fails and DP takes over.

PART X · INTERVAL PATTERNS 71 Merge Intervals Sort by start, then fold every overlapping neighbour into one run. A. Pattern Overview Merge Intervals collapses a pile of possibly overlapping intervals into the smallest set of disjoint ones that covers exactly the same points. It is the foundation of the whole interval family: once the intervals are sorted by start, overlap can only happen between neighbours , so one left-to-right pass with a current run is enough. The cost is the sort: O(n log n) time, O(n) output space. Core Intuition with Illustrations Why sorting by start is enough Suppose the intervals are sorted by start and A comes before B before C . If C overlaps A , then C.start <= A.end ; but B.start <= C.start , so B.start <= A.end and B overlaps A too. Overlap is transitive along the sorted order , which is why a single run that remembers only its maximum end is correct. A worked example Intervals [1,3] [8,10] [2,6] [15,18] [17,20] . After sorting by start: [1,3] [2,6] [8,10] [15,18] [17,20] . The result is [1,6] [8,10] [15,20] . Figure 114. Sorted by start: three clusters of overlap. Figure 115. Merged: three disjoint runs. Gaps are the complement Run the same loop but emit the gap between the current run's end and the next start whenever the next start is larger. Online version: a stream of integers (352) Store disjoint closed intervals in a TreeMap<start, end> . For a new value v , look at floorEntry(v) (an interval starting at or before v ) and at the interval that starts at v + 1 . Four cases: inside an existing interval (ignore), joins only the left one (extend its end), joins only the right one (move its start down), joins both (fuse into one), or stands alone. D. CHAPTER SUMMARY Sort by start, then keep one run: overlap is transitive along the sorted order, so next.start <= run.end is the whole test. Pattern Overview The list is already sorted and disjoint , so there is no reason to sort again. Inserting a new interval splits the list into three contiguous blocks: intervals that end before the new one, intervals that overlap it (absorbed into one), and intervals that start after it. [1,2] ends at 2, before 4: before . [3,5] , [6,7] , [8,10] all start at or before 8 and (since the list is sorted) each overlaps the growing union: absorbed into [3,10] . Interval Phase Output so far New interval [1,2] before: 2 < 4 [[1,2]] [4,8] [3,5] overlap: 3 <= 8, absorb [[1,2]] [3,8] [6,7] overlap: 6 <= 8, absorb [[1,2]] [3,8] [8,10] overlap: 8 <= 8, absorb [[1,2]] [3,10] emit merged interval [[1,2], [3,10]] - [12,16] after: copy [[1,2], [3,10], [12,16]] - Result: [1,2] [3,10] [12,16] . Why the conditions are exactly those An interval is before iff end < lo ; with closed intervals, end == lo means they touch and must merge, hence strict < . An interval overlaps iff start <= hi . Because the list is sorted, once one interval fails the first test and passes the second, every following interval up to the first that fails the second also overlaps. Binary-search variant When the list has a million intervals and the new one is tiny, scanning wastes work. Binary-search the first interval whose end is >= lo and the first interval whose start is > hi . Everything between them is merged with the new interval; copy the prefix, the merged interval, and the suffix. Searching is O(log n) ; building the output array is still O(n) for an array (a LinkedList or a balanced tree avoids the copy). A persistent range set (Range Module) Maintain half-open ranges [l, r) in a TreeMap<l, r> with the invariant that stored ranges are disjoint and never touch . addRange looks at the range starting at or before l , then absorbs every range starting in [l, r] . removeRange trims or splits the ranges it hits (keeping the left remainder [s, l) and the right remainder [r, e) ). queryRange(l, r) is a single floorEntry(l) test: its end must be >= r . Pattern Overview Once intervals are sorted and disjoint , whole-list operations run in linear time with two pointers : intersect two lists, subtract an interval from a list, or union two lists. PART X · INTERVAL PATTERNS 74 Sweep Line Algorithm Turn intervals into +1 / -1 events and sweep left to right. A. Pattern Overview The sweep line replaces a messy picture of overlapping intervals with an ordered list of events : every interval contributes a start event and an end event. Sort the events by coordinate, walk through them once, and maintain a small piece of state (a counter, a sum, a multiset). Whatever you need to know about "the moment right now" is available at each event. Cost: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the walk. Events in a TreeMap, running sum TreeMap delta = new TreeMap<>(); for (int[] iv : intervals) { delta.merge(iv[0], +1, Integer::sum); // start event delta.merge(iv[1], -1, Integer::sum); // end event } int live = 0, peak = 0; for (int d : delta.values()) { live += d; peak = Math.max(peak, live); } Java 17+ Question State kept during the sweep Examples Maximum simultaneous intervals A counter ( +1 / -1 ) Meeting Rooms II, platforms, max population (1854) Total weight at each moment A running sum Car Pooling, painting segments (1943) Maximum value among live A multiset or heap Skyline (Chapter 75) intervals Covered length or area A coverage count per cell Rectangle Area II (Chapter 75) Which intervals are live A set of ids Overlap reports, interval graph colouring KEY IDEA Only the endpoints matter. Between two consecutive event coordinates nothing changes, so the sweep needs to look at 2n positions, not at every point of the number line. B. The skeleton is identical: create events, sort them with a careful tie rule, apply each event to the structure, and read the answer at the points where it changes. The data structure is the whole difficulty. Core Intuition with Illustrations The skyline problem Buildings [left, right, height] : [2,9,10] [3,7,15] [5,12,12] [15,20,10] [19,24,8] . The skyline is the list of key points (x, height) where the outline's height changes. Result: (2,10) (3,15) (7,12) (12,0) (15,10) (20,8) (24,0) . Figure 118. Five buildings and their skyline. Why those events and that order A left edge is stored as {x, -h} and a right edge as {x, +h} . Sorting by (x, value) then gives, at one x : taller starts first (most negative), then starts of shorter buildings, then shorter ends before taller ends . This avoids emitting a spurious key point when one building ends exactly where another begins, and avoids dips below the true outline. x Event Live heights Max Key point 2 start h=10 [0, 10] 10 (2, 10) 3 start h=15 [0, 10, 15] 15 (3, 15) 5 start h=12 [0, 10, 12, 15] 15 - 7 end h=15 [0, 10, 12] 12 (7, 12) 9 end h=10 [0, 12] 12 - 12 end h=12 [0] 0 (12, 0) 15 start h=10 [0, 10] 10 (15, 10) 19 start h=8 [0, 8, 10] 10 - 20 end h=10 [0, 8] 8 (20, 8) 24 end h=8 [0] 0 (24, 0) Why a multiset Two buildings can share a height. Removing the height of one building must not remove the height of the other, so the structure stores counts . A TreeMap<height, count> gives lastKey() in O(log n) . (A max-heap with lazy deletion also works; Chapter 61's lazy removal idea.) CHAPTER SUMMARY Richer sweeps keep a richer structure: a multiset of heights for the skyline, a coverage array over compressed y-gaps for the union area. Skyline: events {x, -h} / {x, h} , sorted by (x, value) ; emit (x, max) only when the maximum changes; seed the multiset with the ground. Area: between consecutive x events the covered length is constant; area += covered * dx ; use long and reduce at the end. Perfect Rectangle: areas must add up and only the four outer corners may appear an odd number of times. A segment tree upgrades the area sweep to O(n log n) ; the simple array version is enough for n <= 200 .

PART X · INTERVAL PATTERNS 76 Offline Interval Queries Sort the queries too: answer them in one sweep, then restore order. A. Pattern Overview Many interval problems ask a question about a point for many points : how many flowers bloom at time t ?, what is the smallest interval containing q ?, which room is closest to my preference? Answering each query from scratch costs O(n) . The offline trick: because all queries are known in advance, sort them (remembering their original indices), sweep once over intervals and queries together, and keep just enough state to answer each query as the sweep reaches it. Then write each answer back at its original index. Typical cost: O((n + q) log (n + q)) . Sort the queries so the set of relevant intervals only grows (or only shrinks); then incremental structures replace per-query scans. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "For each query, find …" with up to 10^5 intervals and 10^5 queries. Queries are given all at once (an array), not one by one. The answer for a query depends on intervals that contain or precede a point. Constraints that make O(nq) impossible but allow O(n log n) . A natural monotonic order exists (by value, by threshold), so the relevant set grows or shrinks. ONE-LINE TEST Many point queries over fixed intervals: sort both, sweep once, store each answer at its original index. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Counting with two sorted arrays (2251) A flower blooming over the closed interval [s, e] is in bloom at t iff s <= t <= e . Count flowers that started by t ( s <= t ) minus those that ended before t ( e < t ). Those that ended before t have also started before t , so the difference is exactly the in-bloom count. Two sorted arrays and two binary searches per query. Flowers [1,6] [3,7] [9,12] [4,13] : sorted starts [1, 3, 4, 9] , sorted ends [6, 7, 12, 13] . Time t starts <= t ends < t In bloom 2 1 0 1 3 2 0 2 7 3 1 2 11 4 2 2 Smallest interval containing a point (1851) Intervals [1,4] [2,4] [3,6] [4,4] , queries [2,3,4,5] . Sort queries ascending. For each query, push every interval that has started ( start <= q ) into a min-heap ordered by size; pop heap tops that already ended ( end < q ); the top is the answer. Expired intervals are removed lazily: they only matter when they reach the top. Figure 120. Four intervals and four queries. Query Heap after adding and expiring Answer 2 heap (size,end): [(3,4), (4,4)] 3 3 heap (size,end): [(3,4), (4,4), (4,6)] 3 4 heap (size,end): [(1,4), (3,4), (4,4), (4,6)] 1 5 heap (size,end): [(4,6)] 4 Answers [3, 3, 1, 4] , written back to the original query positions. Why sorting the queries makes the heap valid With queries ascending, an interval that has ended before the current query has ended before every later query too: dropping it is permanent. And an interval that has started stays started. The heap therefore only needs to support add and remove-top-if-expired , never arbitrary deletion. Closest room (1847): sort by the threshold, descending Each query wants a room with size >= minSize whose id is closest to the preference. If we process queries by decreasing minSize , the set of eligible rooms only grows : add rooms into a TreeSet<id> as the threshold drops, then answer with floor(pref) and ceiling(pref) , choosing the closer (ties: the smaller id). Prefix maximum plus binary search (2070) For maximum beauty among items priced <= q , sort items by price, build a prefix maximum of beauties, and binary-search the last price <= q . The prefix maximum plays the role of the heap: a running summary of everything that has started. D. CHAPTER SUMMARY Offline processing: when all queries are known, sort them (by index array) and sweep once; write answers back to their original positions. Counting containment: #starts <= t minus #ends < t with two sorted arrays and binary search. Best interval for a point: sorted queries, a min-heap keyed by the criterion, and lazy removal of expired tops. Threshold queries: sort so the eligible set only grows (rooms by size descending) and use an ordered set for closest-match lookups. Closed intervals: expired means end < q , not <= ; this is the usual off-by-one.

PART X · INTERVAL PATTERNS 77 Calendar and Booking Problems Online booking: keep intervals in a TreeMap and test two neighbours. A. Pattern Overview Calendar problems are online versions of the interval patterns: bookings arrive one at a time and each must be answered immediately. Three questions cover the family: can I book without any overlap (My Calendar I), can I book without a triple booking (My Calendar II), and what is the maximum number of simultaneous bookings so far (My Calendar III). A TreeMap of start to end (or time to delta ) answers each in O(log n) or O(n) without sorting again. A related problem, Count Integers in Intervals , keeps a merged set and a running total. That is why one lowerEntry and one ceilingKey suffice. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals A class with book(start, end) that must answer on every call. "Double booking", "triple booking", "k-booking". Overlap limits : at most one, at most two, the maximum so far. Room, seat, or slot reservation systems with intervals. Dynamic sets of ranges (add, count covered) where the number of operations is large. ONE-LINE TEST book(start, end) called many times: sorted map, test the neighbours (or keep deltas). C. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 78 Introduction to DP and State Modeling Define a state, write the transition, fix the base case, order the work. A. Pattern Overview Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by combining answers to smaller instances of the same problem , each solved once. It applies when two properties hold: overlapping subproblems (the same smaller question is asked many times) and optimal substructure (an optimal answer is built from optimal answers to smaller questions). Every DP solution is described by four decisions, in this order: the state (what a subproblem is), the transition (how a state is computed from smaller states), the base cases (states answered directly) and the evaluation order (so that dependencies are ready). Decision Question to ask Fibonacci example Climbing cost example State What do I need to know to answer the rest? n i : the step I am standing on Transition How does a state reduce to smaller ones? f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + c[i-1], dp[i-2] + c[i-2]) Base cases Which states need no recursion? f(0) = 0 , f(1) = 1 dp[0] = dp[1] = 0 Order Which states must exist first? Increasing n Increasing i Answer Which state holds the result? f(n) dp[n] KEY IDEA A DP is a recursion whose parameters are small enough to enumerate. If the number of distinct states times the work per state is polynomial, memoising the recursion turns an exponential algorithm into a polynomial one. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Count the number of ways" to reach a target, tile a board, decode a string. "Minimum / maximum" over choices where each choice leaves a smaller version of the same problem. "Is it possible" with a budget (sum, capacity, length). A greedy choice that fails on a counter-example , while brute force is exponential. A recursion that recomputes the same arguments : draw its call tree and look for repeated nodes. The input size is small in one or two dimensions ( n <= 1000 , n * m <= 10^6 ), which allows a table. ONE-LINE TEST Ask: what is the smallest piece of information I must remember to finish the problem? That piece is the state. C. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 79 Memoization vs Tabulation Top-down caches what is asked; bottom-up fills everything in order. A. Pattern Overview Both styles compute the same recurrence. Memoization (top-down) writes the natural recursion and caches results; only the states the question reaches are computed. Tabulation (bottom-up) loops over states in dependency order and fills a table; every state is computed, but there is no recursion and the loop can be compressed to rolling rows. Choosing between them is an engineering decision about reachable states, stack depth and space , not a different algorithm. Memoization (top-down) Tabulation (bottom-up) Shape Recursion + cache Loops + table States computed Only reachable ones All states in the range Order Chosen by the recursion You must find a valid order Stack depth Up to the longest dependency chain None Space optimisation Hard Easy (rolling rows) Overhead Call + hash or array lookup Plain array access Best for Sparse state spaces, tricky orders Dense tables, large n , production KEY IDEA Write the recursion first, then decide. The recursion proves the recurrence is right; the table is an optimisation of how it is evaluated. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals You have a recurrence but not an obvious loop order : start top-down. Only a fraction of the states matter (a target far from the base): memoisation skips the rest. n up to 10^5 or more with a linear chain : bottom-up, or the recursion overflows the stack. You need only the previous row : bottom-up with rolling arrays. Transitions jump irregularly (word break, partitions): memo with a HashMap can be simpler than a full table. ONE-LINE TEST Dense and deep: tabulate. Sparse or awkward order: memoise. C. CHAPTER SUMMARY Memoisation caches a recursion and visits only reachable states; tabulation fills all states in dependency order. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 80 1D Dynamic Programming One index, a handful of earlier cells: take-or-skip, counts and prefix feasibility. A. Pattern Overview In one-dimensional DP the state is a single index : dp[i] answers the problem for the first i items (or for the item ending at i ). The transition looks back a fixed number of steps (House Robber, Climbing Stairs) or scans back over a set of allowed lengths (Word Break, Integer Break). Four families cover most problems: take-or-skip, counting ways, prefix feasibility, and best split of a number. Family Transition Examples Take or skip dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + v[i]) House Robber (198), Delete and Earn (740) Counting dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] under conditions Climbing Stairs (70), Decode Ways (91) Prefix feasibility dp[i] = OR dp[j] and ok(j, i) Word Break (139) Best split dp[n] = max dp[k] * dp[n-k] Integer Break (343) Circular variant Run twice on two linear slices House Robber II (213) KEY IDEA Ask what the last element did. Either it is part of the answer (take it, then look back past its neighbours) or it is not (inherit the previous answer). Those two cases are the transition. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals A sequence of items with a constraint between neighbours : no two adjacent, steps of size 1 or 2, a code of one or two digits. "Maximum sum with no two adjacent" or its disguises (delete-and-earn). "Number of ways to decode / reach" : counts that add over disjoint last moves. "Can the string be segmented" : boolean over prefixes. A greedy local choice that a counter-example breaks. ONE-LINE TEST A single array, each answer needs only earlier answers: 1D DP. C. CHAPTER SUMMARY 1D DP keeps one index. Ask what the last element did: it is used (look back) or not (inherit). Take-or-skip is two variables; counting adds disjoint last moves; feasibility ORs over allowed last pieces. Reductions (Delete and Earn) and splits (circular Robber) reuse the linear solution. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 81 2D Dynamic Programming (Grids) Cell (r, c) is built from its neighbours above and to the left. A. Pattern Overview In grid DP the state is a cell (r, c) . The value is the answer for the path or sub-rectangle that ends at that cell, and the transition looks at the cell above and the cell to the left (or the three upper-left neighbours for squares). Filling row by row, left to right, guarantees every dependency is ready. Space drops from O(m n) to O(n) by keeping only the previous row. Most grid DPs describe the path that ends at a cell and run forward. Dungeon Game describes the requirement that starts at a cell and runs backward, because the health needed now depends on what lies ahead. B. Obstacles, costs or health attached to cells. Both m and n are moderate (up to a few thousand). Free movement in four directions is not this pattern (use BFS or Dijkstra), unless values strictly increase (Chapter 88). Pattern Overview The knapsack family answers: from these items, which can I pick to hit a budget? The state is (items considered, budget used) . Four variants cover almost every interview problem, and they differ only in how often an item may be used and what is asked (feasible, best value, count). Downwards, dp[w - wt] still holds the value before this item (use once). Upwards, dp[w - wt] may already include this item (use many times). B. Pattern Overview A subsequence keeps order but may skip characters. The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) of two sequences is the longest sequence that is a subsequence of both. The state dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the prefixes a[0..i) and b[0..j) . LCS is the template for a whole family: edit-like distances, shortest common supersequence, minimum deletions to make strings equal, and longest common substring (with a reset). Green cells are matches taken from the diagonal; the red arrows trace the answer back from the corner. Figure 133. LCS table. Bold green cells are matched characters. Walking back from dp[7][6] = 4 : if the characters match, record the character and go diagonally; otherwise move toward the larger neighbour. One answer is BCBA ; other subsequences of length 4 (such as BDAB ) are equally valid. Why a match can be taken greedily If a[i-1] == b[j-1] , any LCS can be rearranged to use this pair: if the optimum does not match the last characters, replacing its last matched pair with them leaves the length unchanged. So dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 , no need to consider the two drops. Deletion distance and supersequences Keep the LCS; delete everything else: m + n - 2 LCS . Merge instead: every LCS character is written once, the rest of both strings once each, giving m + n - LCS . For abac and cab the LCS is ab (length 2), so the shortest supersequence has length 4 + 3 - 2 = 5 , e.g. "cabac" . Pattern Overview The Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) is the longest subsequence whose values strictly increase. Two solutions matter: the O(n^2) DP ( dp[i] is the LIS ending at i ) and the O(n log patience-sorting method, where tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1 . The pattern extends to counting the LISes, rebuilding one, nesting envelopes, and divisibility chains. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 87 DP on Trees General trees: root once, combine children, and re-root for all-nodes answers. A. Pattern Overview Chapter 44 solved DP on binary trees. This chapter handles general trees (any number of children, given as an edge list). The state is a node v plus, when needed, a small flag; the value summarises the subtree of v . A post-order pass combines children into the parent in O(n) . Two extensions appear in interviews: re-rooting (compute an answer for every node as root in O(n) total) and tree knapsack (allocate a budget among children). Technique State Combine step Examples Subtree aggregate size[v] , height[v] Sum or max over children Subtree sizes, depth Take / skip take[v] , skip[v] take += skip[c] ; skip += max(take[c], skip[c]) House Robber III (337), independent set Best path through a down[v] plus a global best Two longest child chains meet at v Tree Diameter (1245), node Binary Tree Max Path Sum Re-rooting down[v] , then ans[v] from the parent ans[c] = ans[p] - size[c] + (n - size[c]) Sum of Distances in Tree (834) Tree knapsack dp[v][k] : best using k nodes Merge child tables like a knapsack Choose k nodes with constraints KEY IDEA Process children before parents. Do it with recursion (watch the depth), or iteratively: compute a BFS/DFS order from the root and walk it in reverse. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals An undirected edge list with n - 1 edges , no cycles: a tree. "Maximum weight set with no two adjacent nodes." "Diameter", "longest path", "time to collect all apples". "For every node, compute ..." (sum of distances, farthest node): re-rooting. "Choose at most k nodes / edges" under tree constraints: tree knapsack. ONE-LINE TEST Tree + optimise over a connected or independent set: post-order DP. "For every root": re-root. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Rooting the tree Pick node 0 as root. The parent array and a BFS order let you process nodes children-first without recursion. The sample tree has edges 0-1, 0-2, 2-3, 2-4, 2-5 . Figure 140. The sample tree. Maximum weight independent set take[v] is the best total in the subtree of v if v is chosen; skip[v] if it is not. A chosen node forces its children out; an unchosen node lets each child take its better option. With weights [3,2,5,4,1,6] : Node (leaves first) weight take[v] skip[v] best in subtree 5 6 6 0 6 4 1 1 0 1 Node (leaves first) weight take[v] skip[v] best in subtree 3 4 4 0 4 2 5 5 11 11 1 2 2 0 2 0 3 14 13 14 Best total 14 (verified against all 2^6 subsets in the test suite). Re-rooting: sum of distances to all other nodes One pass up the tree computes size[v] and down[v] (sum of distances to nodes inside the subtree). The root's answer is down[0] . Moving the root from parent p to child c , the size[c] nodes below c get 1 closer and the other n - size[c] nodes get 1 farther: The re-rooting step 1 ans[c] = ans[p] - size[c] + (n - size[c]); Java 17+ Node size[v] down[v] ans[v]: parent - size + (n - size) Answer 0 6 8 = down[0] = 8 8 1 1 0 8-1+5=12 12 2 4 3 8-4+2=6 6 3 1 0 6-1+5=10 10 4 1 0 6-1+5=10 10 5 1 0 6-1+5=10 10 WHY RE-ROOT A naive solution runs a BFS from every node: O(n^2) . Re-rooting reuses the parent's answer and does O(1) work per edge, so the whole problem is O(n) . Diameter and best path through a node For each node, the longest path with that node as its highest point is best1 + best2 , the two largest child chains (each + 1 for the edge to the child). Track the maximum over all nodes. For unweighted trees this is the diameter; for weighted trees add edge weights. Time to collect all apples (1443) The walk must return to the root, so every edge on a path to an apple is traversed twice. cost[v] = sum over children c of (cost[c] + 2) if the child subtree contains an apple (it has one itself or cost[c] > 0 ). One post-order pass. Tree knapsack dp[v][k] is the best value choosing k nodes in the subtree of v (connected to v if required). Merging a child is a knapsack convolution; with the sizes bounded by the subtree sizes, the total work is O(n^2) rather than O(n^3) : every pair of nodes is combined at most once, at their lowest common ancestor. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 88 DP on Graphs A DP needs an acyclic order: topological order, sorted values, or Dijkstra's settling order. A. Pattern Overview Dynamic programming works on any structure whose states can be ordered so that dependencies come first . In a graph that order is a topological order of a DAG. Three situations cover most interview problems: DP on an explicit DAG (longest path, number of paths, course scheduling), DP on an implicit DAG (a grid where values strictly increase, so edges always point to larger values), and DP on a shortest-path graph (count shortest paths, restricted paths) where Dijkstra's settling order supplies the order. Setting Order Examples Explicit DAG Kahn's algorithm or DFS finishing order Longest path in a DAG, Parallel Courses (1136), count paths Implicit DAG on a grid Cells sorted by value (or memoised DFS) Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix (329) Shortest-path DAG Dijkstra's settling order Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination (1976), Restricted Paths (1786) Graph with cycles Condense SCCs first (Chapter 58) or reject DP on the condensation DAG KEY IDEA If there is a cycle, no DP order exists. Detect it (Kahn leaves nodes unprocessed) or collapse strongly connected components before running the DP. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Prerequisites, dependencies, build order : a DAG. "Longest / shortest / number of paths" in a directed acyclic graph. Moves allowed only to strictly larger (or smaller) values on a grid or graph. "Number of shortest paths" : count along the shortest-path DAG. "Minimum semesters / time with prerequisites" : longest chain. ONE-LINE TEST Directed, acyclic (or made acyclic by a value ordering): process nodes in topological order and relax. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Longest path and path counts in a DAG The DAG has edges 0->1, 0->2, 1->3, 2->3, 3->4, 2->5, 5->4 . Process nodes in topological order; for every edge u -> v set longest[v] = max(longest[v], longest[u] + 1) and paths[v] += paths[u] . Figure 141. A small DAG. Node (topological order) Edges out longest path ending here paths from 0 0 -> 1, 2 0 1 1 -> 3 1 1 2 -> 3, 5 1 1 3 -> 4 2 2 5 -> 4 2 1 Node (topological order) Edges out longest path ending here paths from 0 4 -> none 3 3 Longest path length is 3 (e.g. 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 ) and there are 3 distinct paths from 0 to 4. Parallel Courses (1136) and minimum semesters Courses with prerequisites: each semester you can take every course whose prerequisites are done, so the minimum number of semesters is the number of layers in Kahn's algorithm (the longest chain). If Kahn processes fewer than n courses there is a cycle: return -1 . Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix (329) Moves go to adjacent cells with strictly larger values, so the move graph is acyclic by construction. Sort cells by value (or memoise a DFS) and set dp[cell] = 1 + max(dp[smaller neighbour]) . For [[9,9,4],[6,6,8],[2,1,1]] : Cell (in increasing value) Value dp (longest path ending here) (2,1) 1 1 (2,2) 1 1 (2,0) 2 2 (0,2) 4 1 (1,0) 6 3 (1,1) 6 2 (1,2) 8 3 (0,0) 9 4 (0,1) 9 3 The longest path is 1 -> 2 -> 6 -> 9 , length 4. Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination (1976) Run Dijkstra and keep ways[v] . When a strictly shorter distance to v is found, reset ways[v] = ways[u] ; when an equal distance is found, add ways[v] += ways[u] . Dijkstra settles nodes in non-decreasing distance order, so ways[u] is final when u is settled. The sample has 7 nodes and 10 roads; the shortest distance to node 6 is 7 and there are 4 shortest paths. Node settled dist ways (final at settling) 0 0 1 1 2 1 2 5 1 3 5 1 Node settled dist ways (final at settling) 4 5 1 5 6 2 6 7 4 WATCH FOR ZERO WEIGHTS Zero-weight edges break the 'final when settled' argument for equal-distance nodes. LeetCode 1976 guarantees positive times; with zero-weight edges process ties in topological order of the shortest-path DAG. Restricted Paths (1786) Compute dist[v] to the target n with Dijkstra, then count paths from 1 to n that move only to nodes with strictly smaller dist . That condition makes the walk acyclic; process nodes in increasing dist and add ways[u] along each edge to a smaller-distance neighbour, modulo 10^9 + 7 . D. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 89 State Machine DP Name the states, draw the allowed transitions, and keep one value per state. A. Pattern Overview Some problems are best seen as a finite automaton : at each step you are in one of a few states (holding a stock, in cooldown, painted red), and each step moves you along an allowed transition that earns or costs something. The DP keeps one value per state and updates all of them from the previous step's values. Part I covered the basic stock problems with greedy and Kadane-style passes; this chapter gives the general framework that also handles cooldowns, fees and at most k transactions, plus colouring problems with a neighbour constraint. Problem States Key transition Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with hold , sold , rest hold = max(hold, rest - p) ; sold = hold + Cooldown (309) p ; rest = max(rest, sold_prev) With Transaction Fee (714) hold , cash cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee) At Most Two Transactions (123) buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2 Chain four values At Most K Transactions (188) hold[t] , free[t] hold[t] = max(hold[t], free[t-1] - p) Paint House (256) Colour of the last house cost + min(other two) Paint House II (265) Colour of the last house, k colours Use the smallest and second smallest of the previous row KEY IDEA Draw the automaton first. Every edge becomes one line of the update; the starting state gets the base value and the answer is the best of the final states that are legal to end in. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals A day-by-day process with modes (holding or not, cooling down, on or off). "At most k transactions", "cooldown", "fee per transaction". A constraint between consecutive choices : different colours for neighbours, no two consecutive identical actions. A small number of modes (2 to 5) so that the state per step is a vector, not a table. Greedy fails because the best action today depends on the mode you want to be in tomorrow. ONE-LINE TEST Sequence + a handful of modes + allowed transitions: keep one value per mode. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations The cooldown automaton After selling you must rest one day before buying again. Three states: hold (own a share), sold (just sold today), rest (own nothing and free to buy). From Action To Value change Update line rest Buy hold - p hold = max(hold, rest - p) hold Do nothing hold 0 (kept by the max above) hold Sell sold + p sold = hold + p sold Cooldown day rest 0 rest = max(rest, prevSold) rest Do nothing rest 0 (kept by the max above) Each day, compute the new values from the old ones. Prices [1,2,3,0,2] : Price hold sold rest 1 -1 -inf 0 2 -1 1 0 3 -1 2 1 0 1 -1 2 2 1 3 2 Answer max(sold, rest) = 3 (buy 1, sell 2, cooldown, buy 0, sell 2). At most k transactions Let hold[t] be the best profit while holding a share during the t -th transaction, and free[t] the best profit after finishing t transactions. Update per price p : hold[t] = max(hold[t], free[t-1] - p) ; free[t] = max(free[t], hold[t] + p) . For k = 2 , prices [3,3,5,0,0,3,1,4] : Price hold[1..k] free[1..k] 3 [-3, -3] [0, 0] 3 [-3, -3] [0, 0] 5 [-3, -3] [2, 2] 0 [0, 2] [2, 2] 0 [0, 2] [2, 2] 3 [0, 2] [3, 5] 1 [0, 2] [3, 5] 4 [0, 2] [4, 6] Answer free[2] = 6 (buy 0, sell 3, buy 1, sell 4). SHORTCUT When k >= n / 2 transactions are never the limit; the answer is the sum of all positive day-to-day gains (Stock II). Check this first to avoid an O(n k) table for huge k . Transaction fee (714) Two states are enough: cash (no share) and hold . Pay the fee when selling: cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee) ; hold = max(hold, cash - p) . For prices [1,3,2,8,4,9] and fee 2 the best is 8 (buy 1, sell 8 minus fee 2 gives 5; buy 4, sell 9 minus fee 2 gives 3). Paint House (256) Neighbouring houses must differ in colour. Keep the best cost of painting the prefix with the last house in each colour: red' = cost[red] + min(green, blue) and so on. For costs [[17,2,17],[16,16,5],[14,3,19]]: House cost if red cost if green cost if blue 0 17 2 17 1 18 33 7 2 21 10 37 Answer min(last row) = 10 (green, blue, green: 2 + 5 + 3). Paint House II (265): k colours in O(nk) Naively each house takes O(k^2) . Keep only the smallest and second smallest values of the previous row: a colour can use the smallest unless it was that colour's own, in which case it uses the second smallest. That is O(n k) overall. D. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 90 Bitmask DP Encode a subset in an integer: 2^n states, n <= 20, and a bit trick per transition. A. Pattern Overview When the state must remember which items out of a small set have been used , encode that set as a bitmask: bit i is 1 if item i is taken. The mask is an int , so dp[mask] or dp[mask][last] is a plain array of size 2^n (times n ). With n <= 20 that is about a million masks, which is fast enough; with n <= 16 you can afford an extra dimension of n . Operation Java Meaning Test bit i (mask >> i & 1) == 1 Is item i in the set? Set bit i mask | (1 << i) Add item i Clear bit i mask & ~(1 << i) Remove item i Toggle bit i mask ^ (1 << i) Flip membership Full set (1 << n) - 1 All n items Lowest set bit mask & -mask Isolate one item Count bits Integer.bitCount(mask) Size of the set Iterate submasks for (s = mask; s > 0; s = (s - 1) & mask) All non-empty subsets of mask KEY IDEA Bitmask DP is DP where the state is a set. Process masks in increasing numeric order: any submask of mask is numerically smaller, so dependencies are ready. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals n <= 20 (or <= 16 ) items, and an order or assignment matters. "Visit every node exactly once" (Travelling Salesman, Hamiltonian paths). "Partition into k groups of equal sum", "assign n tasks to n workers". "Shortest path that visits all nodes" in a small graph. Counting hat assignments or permutations with constraints. ONE-LINE TEST Tiny n (<= 20) and a subset must be remembered: dp[mask] . C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Travelling Salesman (Held-Karp) dp[mask][last] is the cheapest cost of a path that starts at city 0, visits exactly the cities in mask and ends at last . Extend by an unvisited city next : dp[mask | 1<<next][next] = min(dp[mask][last] + d[last][next]) . For the four-city matrix [[0,10,15,20],[10,0,35,25],[15,35,0,30],[20,25,30,0]] (masks printed with city 3 on the left): Visited mask (city 3..0) Last city Cheapest path cost 0011 1 10 0101 2 15 0111 1 50 0111 2 45 1001 3 20 1011 1 45 1011 3 35 1101 2 50 1101 3 45 1111 1 70 1111 2 65 1111 3 75 Closing the tour from the full mask 1111 : min over last of dp[1111][last] + d[last][0] = 80 (tour 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 0 : 10 + 25 + 30 + 15). WHY IT WORKS Brute force tries (n-1)! orders. Held-Karp needs 2^n * n states and n transitions each: O(2^n n^2) . For n = 20 that is about 4 * 10^8 basic steps instead of 10^17 . Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes (847) The path may start anywhere and revisit nodes and edges, so run BFS over states (mask, node) . Start from all (1 << i, i) simultaneously at distance 0; the first time the mask is full, the distance is the answer. For the star graph [[1,2,3],[0],[0],[0]] the answer is 4 ( 1 -> 0 -> 2 -> 0 -> 3 ). Figure 142. States are (set of visited nodes, current node). Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (698) dp[mask] is the sum of the chosen elements modulo target ( target = total / k ), or -1 if the mask is unreachable. Adding element i to mask is allowed if the running partial sum does not exceed target . If dp[full] == 0 the elements split into k buckets. For [4,3,2,3,5,2,1] and k = 4 : total 20, target 5 (buckets {5} , {1,4} , {2,3} , {2,3} ). Quantity Value Total 20 Target per bucket 5 Masks 2^7 = 128 Reachable full mask dp[127] = 0 (feasible) Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats (1434) and assignment Flip the viewpoint to keep the mask small: iterate over hats (up to 40) and let the mask be the set of people (up to 10) who already have a hat. dp[h][mask] = number of ways using the first h hats. Choosing the side with the smaller count is the main modelling decision. The same idea gives the minimum-cost assignment ( n workers, n tasks): dp[mask] over tasks done, the worker index is bitCount(mask) . Submask enumeration Some transitions split a set into two parts: dp[mask] = best over submasks s of dp[s] + dp[mask ^ s] . Iterating all submasks of all masks costs O(3^n) , which is acceptable up to n = 16 or so. D. Brute Force to Optimal Solution Problem Brute force Bitmask DP TSP O(n!) O(2^n n^2) Shortest path visiting all nodes Try every walk, exponential BFS over (mask, node) : O(2^n n) states Partition into k subsets O(k^n) assignments O(2^n n) Min-cost assignment O(n!) O(2^n n) Subset split recurrences - O(3^n) via submask loops For larger n the Hungarian algorithm (assignment, O(n^3) ) and heuristics (TSP) take over; bitmask DP is the exact method for tiny sets. PART XI · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERNS 91 DP Space Optimization Keep only the rows you still need: rolling arrays, in-place updates and Hirschberg. A. Pattern Overview Most table DPs read only a small window of previous states. Space optimisation keeps just that window: the previous row, the previous two values, or a single array updated in a careful direction. Time stays the same; memory drops from O(m n) to O(n) , or from O(n) to O(1) . The price is that you can no longer walk back through the table to rebuild the answer, which is where Hirschberg's algorithm helps. Dependency pattern Keep Technique Examples dp[i] from dp[i-1] , dp[i-2] Two or three variables Rolling variables Fibonacci, House Robber dp[i][j] from row i-1 only Two rows Two-row swap LCS, edit distance, unique paths dp[i][j] from dp[i-1][j] , dp[i][j-1] , One row + one saved In-place single row LCS, edit distance dp[i-1][j-1] diagonal dp[i][w] from dp[i-1][w'] , w' <= w One row Iterate w downward 0/1 knapsack dp[l][r] from shorter ranges Diagonals or one row, i descending Row indexed by l , filled l downwards Longest Palindromic Subsequence Need the actual answer string Two halves Hirschberg LCS string in O(n) space KEY IDEA Draw the dependency arrows. The loop direction and what you must save before overwriting follow directly from which cells each cell reads. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals Memory limit or large dimensions ( 10^4 x 10^4 tables are 400 MB). A transition that reads only the previous row or column. An interviewer asks "can you reduce the space?" after the table solution. You only need the final value, not the path. You need the path in small memory: Hirschberg or checkpointing. ONE-LINE TEST Each cell reads only the previous row: keep two rows, then try one. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations LCS with two rows Row i of the LCS table reads row i-1 and its own left neighbour. Keep prev and cur , then swap. For abcde and ace : After dp row over b = 'ace' row 0 [0, 0, 0, 0] row 1 ('a') [0, 1, 1, 1] row 2 ('b') [0, 1, 1, 1] row 3 ('c') [0, 1, 2, 2] row 4 ('d') [0, 1, 2, 2] row 5 ('e') [0, 1, 2, 3] One row with a saved diagonal A single array dp[0..n] can hold row i . The cell dp[j] currently holds the up value ( dp[i-1][j] ); dp[j-1] already holds the left value ( dp[i][j-1] ). PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 92 Bit Manipulation Treat integers as sets of bits: masks, shifts, XOR cancellation and Kernighan. A. Pattern Overview An int is a 32-element boolean array that the CPU can read, test and change in one instruction. Bit manipulation uses that fact to replace loops, hash sets and lookup tables by a handful of operators: & , | , ^ , ~ , << , >> and >>> . Three ideas cover most problems: masks (test, set, clear, toggle one bit), XOR cancellation ( a ^ a = 0 , a ^ 0 = a ) and lowest-set-bit tricks ( n & (n - 1) and n & -n ). Operation Expression Meaning Test bit i (n >> i) & 1 1 if bit i is set Set bit i n | (1 << i) Force the bit to 1 Clear bit i n & ~(1 << i) Force the bit to 0 Toggle bit i n ^ (1 << i) Flip the bit Clear lowest set bit n & (n - 1) Kernighan step; also the power-of-two test Isolate lowest set bit n & -n Two's complement keeps only that bit All ones below bit k (1 << k) - 1 Mask of k low bits KEY IDEA Know your shift. >> is arithmetic (sign-extending); >>> is logical. Use >>> whenever the value may be negative and you want to walk its 32 bits. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Without extra space" or "constant space" on a counting or uniqueness problem (XOR cancellation). Powers of two appear in the statement, or the answer needs log loops over bit positions. Set membership over at most 20-30 items (a bitmask is a set; Chapter 90). Pairwise bit comparison (Hamming distance): handle each bit column independently. Parity, flags, permissions, compact state in a single integer. ONE-LINE TEST Each bit position is independent, or equal values must cancel: think masks and XOR. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Kernighan: clear the lowest set bit Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and every zero below it to 1. ANDing with the original therefore deletes exactly that one bit. Repeating it popcount(n) times counts the bits in O(popcount) , not O(32) . CHAPTER SUMMARY Integers are bit arrays; masks test, set, clear and toggle single bits in O(1) . n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, which gives popcount and the power-of-two test; n & -n isolates it. PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 94 Trie (Prefix Tree) Share common prefixes in a tree so insert, lookup and prefix queries cost O(length). A.
