PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 95 XOR Trie (Binary Trie) Store numbers as bit paths and greedily walk the opposite bit to maximise XOR. A. Pattern Overview A binary trie inserts each number as its bit string from the most significant bit down. Because a higher bit outweighs all lower bits together, the best partner for x can be found greedily: at each level prefer the child with the opposite bit (it makes that bit of x ^ y equal to 1). Each query costs O(B) where B is the bit width, independent of the number of stored values. Query How the walk works Cost Max x ^ y over stored y At each bit take the opposite child if it exists, else the same child O(B) Count y with x ^ y < limit Compare the XOR prefix against limit 's bits; count whole subtrees that are already smaller O(B) Max x ^ y with y <= m (offline) Sort queries by m , insert values <= m as you go O((n + q) B + sort) Pairs with XOR in [low, high] count(< high + 1) - count(< low) over earlier elements O(n B) KEY IDEA Max XOR is a greedy over bits : the top bit dominates, so decide it first and never revisit. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "Maximum XOR" of a pair, a subarray (via prefix XOR), or a path (via root-to-node XOR). A constraint on the partner ( y <= m , index order, an interval) that rules out a plain sort. Counting pairs whose XOR is below a bound. Values below 2^30 , so a trie has at most 30 levels. Queries arriving offline, which lets you sort them and build the trie incrementally. ONE-LINE TEST XOR optimisation plus a pair or subarray: prefix XORs and a binary trie. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Greedy opposite-bit walk With 5-bit numbers {3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8} , the best partner of 5 = 00101 is 25 = 11001 : the walk picks the opposite bit at every level where it can. x binary best x ^ y binary 3 00011 26 11010 10 01010 19 10011 5 00101 28 11100 25 11001 28 11100 2 00010 27 11011 8 01000 17 10001 The maximum over all x is 28 (from 5 ^ 25 ). Why greedy is correct Suppose a stored number offers the opposite bit at position i . Any pair that sets bit i of the XOR beats every pair that does not, by at least 2^i , which exceeds the total of all lower bits (2^i - 1) . So committing to the opposite child never loses. Counting pairs below a limit Walk x and limit together. At a level where limit 's bit is 1: all stored values that make this XOR bit 0 (same child as x ) are strictly smaller, so add that child's subtree count and continue into the opposite child. Where limit 's bit is 0: the XOR bit must be 0, so continue into the same child. Level bit of limit XOR bit we need Action 1 0 gives a smaller value count += cnt(sameChild) ; follow oppositeChild 0 must be 0 Follow sameChild Run out of bits XOR equals limit Not counted (strict less) Offline with a cap on the partner For max(x ^ y) with y <= m , sort numbers ascending and queries by m . Before answering a query, insert every number <= m . If the trie is empty the answer is -1 . TRAP Prefix XORs convert subarray problems to pair problems: xor(l..r) = p[r+1] ^ p[l] . Remember to insert the empty prefix 0 first. D. PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 96 Segment Tree Answer range queries and point or range updates in O(log n) with a tree of intervals. A. Pattern Overview A segment tree stores, for every node, a summary (sum, min, max, gcd, count) of an interval of the array. The root covers everything; children cover the two halves. Any range [l, r] decomposes into at most 2 log n nodes, and changing one element recomputes only the log n ancestors. With lazy propagation , adding a value to a whole range is also O(log n) . Core Intuition with Illustrations The tree and a query For [2, 5, 1, 4, 9, 3] each node shows its sum and range. A query for [1, 4] touches three nodes, amber: [1] , [2] and [3, 4] (total 5 + 1 + 13 = 19 ). Everything else is either outside the range or already covered by a bigger node. Figure 145. A range is covered by at most two nodes per level. The bottom-up (iterative) layout Store leaves at t[n..2n-1] and set t[i] = t[2i] + t[2i+1] . For a query [l, r] put pointers lo = l + n , hi = r + 1 + n . While lo < hi : if lo is odd it is a right child, so take it and move right; if hi is odd take t[hi - 1] ; then climb with lo >>= 1 , hi >>= 1 . About 10 lines, no recursion. Pointers (after step) Action Sum lo=8 hi=10 take t[7] = 5; take t[10] = 9 14 lo=4 hi=4 take t[4] = 5 19 Point update Write the leaf, then recompute each ancestor from its two children. Updating index 2 to 7 in the array above: Node New value Recomputed from 8 7 leaf 4 11 t[8] + t[9] 2 23 t[4] + t[5] 1 30 t[2] + t[3] Lazy propagation for range updates To add v to [l, r] store at each fully covered node an unpushed tag lazy and update its aggregate right away ( sum += v x length , max += v ). PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 97 Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) Prefix sums with updates in a dozen lines, driven by the lowest set bit of the index. A. Pattern Overview A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree, BIT) supports point update and prefix sum in O(log n) using one array and two loops. Index i (1-based) stores the sum of the lowbit(i) = i & -i elements ending at i . A prefix query hops down by removing the lowest set bit; an update hops up by adding it. Counting problems become easy: store a frequency array and ask how many values are <= x . PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 98 Sparse Table and Range Queries O(1) range minimum, maximum and gcd on static data using overlapping power-of-two blocks. A. Pattern Overview A sparse table precomputes the answer for every interval whose length is a power of two: st[k][i] summarises a[i .. i + 2^k - 1] . It is built in O(n log n) by doubling ( st[k][i] = op(st[k-1][i], st[k-1][i + 2^(k-1)]) ). For an idempotent operation ( op(x, x) = x : min, max, gcd, AND, OR), any query [l, r] is answered by two overlapping blocks, so the overlap does no harm and the query is O(1) . PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 99 Quickselect and Selection Algorithms Find the k-th element in expected O(n) by partitioning and discarding the half you don't need. A. Pattern Overview Quickselect finds the k -th smallest element without sorting. Partition around a pivot; the pivot lands at its final sorted position p . If p == k you are done; otherwise recurse into only one side. The work shrinks geometrically ( n + n/2 + n/4 + ... ), so the expected time is O(n) , against O(n log n) for sorting and O(n log k) for a heap. Approach Time Space Modifies input Best when Sort, then index O(n log n) O(1) to O(n) Yes Many different k Min/max-heap of size k O(n log k) O(k) No Streams , small k Quickselect (random pivot) O(n) expected , O(n^2) worst O(1) Yes (reorders) One query on an in-memory array Median of medians O(n) worst case O(1) Yes Adversarial inputs, theory Counting / bucket O(n + V) O(V) No Small value range KEY IDEA Quickselect is quicksort that ignores one half . Everything you know about partitioning, duplicates and pivot choice carries over. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "k-th largest / smallest", "median", "top k in any order" on an array in memory. Output order does not matter (K Closest Points), so full sorting is wasted effort. You are asked to beat O(n log n) for selection. Wiggle sort, partition around the median, minimum moves to equalise (the median minimises absolute deviations). Data does not fit a heap-friendly stream model: the full array is available. ONE-LINE TEST Need only the k-th element or the best k unordered: partition, don't sort. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Three-way partition (Dutch national flag) Maintain three zones inside a[lo..hi] : < pivot , == pivot , > pivot . Pointers lt , i , gt : if a[i] < pivot swap it into the left zone, if a[i] > pivot swap it into the right zone, else step. After the pass the middle zone [lt, gt] is final. Handling equal keys as one zone is what keeps arrays of duplicates O(n) instead of O(n^2) . Selecting the 5th smallest of [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4] kthSmallest(a, 4) (0-based). The Java code draws a random pivot; the trace below picks the middle element so the run is reproducible. Range Pivot Equal zone [lt, gt] Array after partition Decision [0..5] 1 [0, 0] [1, 2, 5, 6, 4, 3] k > 0: go right [1..5] 6 [5, 5] [1, 2, 5, 4, 3, 6] k < 5: go left [1..4] 5 [4, 4] [1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6] k in [4, 4]: found The answer is 5 (the 2nd largest of six, LeetCode 215 with k = 2 ). Each round discards at least the pivot's zone. Why it is expected linear A random pivot lands in the middle half of the sorted order with probability 1/2, shrinking the range to at most 3n/4 . The expected total work is a geometric series bounded by ~ 4n comparisons (more precisely <= 3.4 n for the median). The worst case O(n^2) requires consistently terrible pivots, and randomisation makes that vanishingly unlikely. Median of medians: worst-case linear Split into groups of 5, take each group's median, recursively select the median of those medians as the pivot. At least 3n/10 elements are guaranteed on each side, giving T(n) <= T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n) = O(n) . The constant is large, so it is rarely used in practice, but it is the answer to "can you do it in worst-case linear time?". Selection on keys other than values K Closest Points compares distances , but partitions the point objects. Use squared distances in long to avoid sqrt and overflow. The result is any set of k closest points, not sorted. CHOOSING Heap versus quickselect: if the interviewer says "data stream" or "cannot modify the array" choose a heap. If they say "optimal average time", quickselect. D. PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 100 Reservoir Sampling and Random Sampling Pick uniformly from data you can't count in advance: streams, weights and shuffles. A. Pattern Overview Random-sampling questions test whether you can make an exactly uniform choice with limited memory or information. Reservoir sampling picks k items uniformly from a stream of unknown length in one pass and O(k) space. Related patterns: the Fisher-Yates shuffle (uniform permutation), weighted sampling by prefix sums and binary search, and rejection sampling to build one random source from another. For the i -th item (1-based), replace the kept item with probability 1/i . Item i ends up selected if it is chosen at step i and survives every later step j (survival probability 1 - 1/j = (j-1)/j ). The product telescopes to 1/n : Item i Chosen then survives Probability 1 1/1 x 1/2 x 2/3 x 3/4 x 4/5 1/5 2 1/2 x 2/3 x 3/4 x 4/5 1/5 3 1/3 x 3/4 x 4/5 1/5 4 1/4 x 4/5 1/5 5 1/5 x 1 1/5 Reservoir sampling with k items Fill the reservoir with the first k items. PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 101 KMP and the Prefix Function Never move backwards in the text: reuse what a partial match already told you. A. Pattern Overview Naive substring search restarts at the next text position after every mismatch, costing O(n m) . Knuth-Morris-Pratt observes that after matching k characters, the pattern itself says which shorter prefix is still a valid partial match. That information is the prefix function pi[i] : the length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..i] that is also a suffix of it (a border). With pi , search is O(n + m) and the text pointer never goes backwards. Core Intuition with Illustrations The prefix function For abababca : pi tells how far the match can fall back. At each step, if the next character differs, follow the border chain k = pi[k-1] until a character matches or k = 0 . i s[i] Fall-backs pi[i] 1 b - 0 2 a - 1 3 b - 2 4 a - 3 5 b - 4 6 c k 4 -> 2; k 2 -> 0 0 7 a - 1 Result: pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 1] . The value 4 at index 5 means abab is both a prefix and a suffix of ababab . Searching: reuse the border Treat k as the number of pattern characters currently matched. On a mismatch, drop to pi[k-1] and retry; on a full match ( k == m ) record the hit and also drop to pi[m-1] so overlapping matches are found. The text index only increases. i text[i] k before k after Event 0 a 0 1 1 b 1 2 2 a 2 3 3 b 3 4 4 a 4 5 5 b 5 6 MATCH at 0 6 c 6 0 7 a 0 1 8 b 1 2 9 a 2 3 10 b 3 4 11 a 4 5 12 b 5 6 MATCH at 7 Matches at starts [0, 7] . The overlap ababab + ab + ab at the end shows why the fall-back after a full match matters. Figure 148. Falling back along the border keeps the matched part of the text and avoids re-reading it. Periods and repetition If p = pi[n-1] and n % (n - p) == 0 , the string is made of repetitions of its first n - p characters. abcabcabc : pi[8] = 6 , 9 - 6 = 3 , 9 % 3 == 0 , so period 3, three repeats. The smallest period (no divisibility needed) is simply n - pi[n-1] . Shortest palindrome by prepending Let t = s + '#' + reverse(s) . The last prefix-function value is the length of the longest palindromic prefix of s . Prepend the reverse of the remaining suffix: aacecaaa has longest palindromic prefix aacecaa (7), so prepend a to get aaacecaaa . Counting every prefix's occurrences Count cnt[pi[i]]++ for each i , then propagate from long to short ( cnt[pi[len-1]] += cnt[len] ) and add 1 for each prefix itself. Total O(n) . This is the same fact as "Sum of Scores of Built Strings" (Chapter 103). TRAP pi stores proper borders: pi[i] < i + 1 . Forgetting that the whole string is not its own border gives infinite loops or wrong periods. D. CHAPTER SUMMARY The prefix function pi[i] is the longest proper border of p[0..i] and is computed in O(m) with the same loop used for searching. Search follows borders instead of re-reading text, giving O(n + m) with the text pointer moving only forward. Periods, repetition, rotation and shortest-palindrome questions all reduce to pi of a well-chosen string. Fall back with pi[k - 1] , and fall back after a full match so overlapping hits are found. Use a separator character when concatenating strings, otherwise borders cross the boundary.

PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 102 Rabin-Karp and Rolling Hash Compare substrings by fingerprints that update in O(1) as the window slides. A. Pattern Overview A rolling hash maps a window of m characters to one number that can be updated in O(1) when the window slides by one character. Rabin-Karp compares the pattern's hash with each window's hash and verifies only the windows that match. Hash comparison is O(1) , so search is O(n + m) expected. The same idea powers binary search on the answer for longest repeated substring, duplicate detection, and substring equality queries via prefix hashes. Equal hashes mean "probably equal": verify, or choose a modulus so large that collisions are negligible. B. Compare many substrings for equality (palindromes in O(1) with forward and reverse hashes). Fixed-length window over a string or array that needs a canonical key (DNA windows, subarray patterns). Binary search on length is valid because "a repeat of length L exists" is monotone in L . Multi-pattern or 2D matching where KMP does not extend easily. PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 103 Z Algorithm For every position, how long is the match with the whole string's prefix? Answer in O(n). A. Pattern Overview The Z array of a string s has z[i] equal to the length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of s (with z[0] = n by convention). It is computed in O(n) by maintaining a Z-box [l, r) : the rightmost interval that matched a prefix. Positions inside the box copy information from the matching spot near the beginning, so characters are compared at most once outside it. PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 104 Manacher's Algorithm Every palindromic substring of a string in linear time, by reusing mirrored radii. A. Pattern Overview Palindromes are symmetric around a centre. Manacher's algorithm computes, for every centre, the radius of the largest palindrome around it, in O(n) total. It keeps the palindrome [l, r] that reaches farthest to the right. For a new centre i inside it, the mirror centre l + r i already knows a lower bound for the radius, so only characters beyond r need comparing. The longest is abaaba. Figure 149. The even centre between indices 2 and 3 gives the whole string. The mirror trick Let [l, r] be the rightmost palindrome seen. For a centre i inside it, its mirror is j = l + r i . The palindrome around j reappears around i , but it is clipped by the right edge: start from min(d1[j], r - i + 1) . If d1[j] fits strictly inside, no comparison is needed; otherwise extend character by character past r , which advances r . Every position is the right edge at most once, so extensions total O(n) . All other work per centre is O(1) . PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 105 Meet in the Middle Split the input in half, enumerate each half, and join the halves with sorting or hashing. A. Pattern Overview Some problems have a search space of 2^n with n around 30 to 40: too large to enumerate ( 2^40 ~ 10^12 ) but too small for a polynomial algorithm to apply. Meet in the middle splits the input into two halves of size n/2 , enumerates all 2^(n/2) subsets of each (about 10^6 for n = 40 ), and combines the two lists with a sort + two pointers, binary search or hash map. Time falls from O(2^n) to O(2^(n/2) * n) . Method Time Space Feasible n Brute force over subsets O(2^n n) O(1) ~25 Pseudo-polynomial DP (subset sum) O(n S) O(S) Small values only Meet in the middle O(2^(n/2) n) O(2^(n/2)) 30 to 40 , any values Branch and bound Exponential, data dependent O(n) Heuristic KEY IDEA The signature is small n (<= 40) combined with huge values or a target that rules out a sum-indexed DP . The constraints announce the technique. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals n <= 40 (or 36, 30, 2n with n <= 20). Values up to 10^9 or negative, so a DP over the sum is impossible. "Closest subsequence sum to a goal", "split into two equal-size groups", "count subsets with sum S". Two independent halves interact only through one aggregate (a sum, XOR, count). The answer needs the best pair (x from left, y from right) under a combining rule. ONE-LINE TEST n <= 40, values huge: enumerate two halves and join them. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Closest subset sum to a goal Enumerate all 2^h subset sums of the left half and of the right half; sort the right sums. For each left sum s we need a right sum closest to goal - s : binary search for it and check its neighbours. For a = [5, -7, 3, 5] , goal = 6 : Left sums sorted: [-7, -2, 0, 5] . Right sums sorted: [0, 3, 5, 8] . Left sum s Need goal - s Closest right sum Total Distance Best so far -7 13 8 1 5 5 -2 8 8 6 0 0 0 6 5 5 1 0 5 1 0 5 1 0 The minimum distance is 0 (left sum -2 plus right sum 8 : the whole array sums to exactly 6). Two pointers instead of binary search If both lists are sorted, walk i upward over the left sums and j downward over the right sums: when s_i + t_j > goal decrement j , otherwise increment i . This saves a log factor after the sorts. Equal-size split (Partition Array into Two Arrays to Minimise Sum Difference) The groups must have size exactly n out of 2n , so group left subsets by size : a left subset of size k must pair with a right subset of size n - k . For each k sort the right sums of that size and binary search for the value that makes 2(x + y) closest to the total. Left size k Right size Combine rule 0 n Binary search in right sums of size n 1 n - 1 Binary search in right sums of size n - 1 ... ... ... n 0 Only the empty right subset Counting subsets with a given sum Count right sums in a HashMap<Long, Integer> ; for each left sum s add map[target - s] . Counting runs in O(2^(n/2)) expected; sorting and binary search gives the same with a log factor and no hashing. Why two halves of equal size The cost is 2^a + 2^b + (join) ; with a + b = n it is minimised at a = b = n/2 . Unequal splits are useful only when the join step is expensive on one side. ENUMERATION Generate subset sums iteratively: sums = [0] ; for each element v , sums += [x + v for x in sums] . No recursion, and the list is built in O(2^h) . D. PART XII · ADVANCED ALGORITHMS 106 Merge Sort and Inversion Counting Count cross-pairs while merging: divide and conquer for order-based counting problems. A. Pattern Overview Merge sort splits an array, sorts each half and merges. At the merge step, both halves are already sorted , so a question of the form "how many pairs (i, j) , i in the left half and j in the right half, satisfy a condition between a[i] and a[j] ?" can be answered with one linear scan or a two-pointer sweep. Every pair is split exactly once, at the level where i and j first land in different halves, so the total cost is O(n log n) . Problem family Cross-pair condition Technique at the merge Inversions a[i] > a[j] When taking from the right, add the remaining left count Reverse pairs a[i] > 2 a[j] Separate two-pointer pass before merging Count of smaller numbers after self a[j] < a[i] for j > i Carry original indices, add to the left element's counter Count of range sum lower <= p[j] - p[i] <= upper Two pointers on sorted prefix sums Global vs local inversions Compare counts Or an O(n) shortcut for permutations KEY IDEA The merge step turns a quadratic cross-count into a linear one because sortedness makes the counts monotone : advancing in one half never decreases the matching prefix of the other. B. When to Recognize This Pattern Pattern Recognition Signals "For each element count how many later elements are smaller/larger" , or total such pairs. Pairs (i, j) with i < j and a relation between values (not between indices). Order statistics over prefix sums (Count of Range Sum). n up to 10^5 : O(n^2) fails, O(n log n) fits. The relation allows a sorted-order sweep (monotone in the sorted halves). ONE-LINE TEST Count pairs by index order and value relation: merge sort, or a Fenwick tree over ranks. C. Core Intuition with Illustrations Counting inversions during the merge Merge the sorted halves L and R . When L[i] <= R[j] take from the left. When R[j] < L[i] , then R[j] is smaller than all remaining left elements L[i..] (they are sorted), so it forms len(L) - i inversions with them. Add that and take R[j] . Merge Result Cross inversions [4] + [2] [2, 4] 1 [8] + [2, 4] [2, 4, 8] 2 [5] + [3] [3, 5] 1 [1] + [3, 5] [1, 3, 5] 0 [2, 4, 8] + [1, 3, 5] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8] 6 The total for [8, 4, 2, 1, 5, 3] is 10 inversions. Reverse pairs: count before merging The condition a[i] > 2 a[j] does not match the merge order, so count it in a separate pass over the two sorted halves: for each i in the left, advance j while a[i] > 2 a[j] ; since the left side is increasing, j never moves back. Then perform the ordinary merge. Use long for 2 a[j] . Count of smaller numbers after self: carry the indices Sort an array of indices by value. In the merge, whenever an element from the left half is placed, add the number of right-half elements already placed (they are smaller and were originally to its right). Store counts per original index. Count of range sum With prefix sums p , count pairs i < j such that lower <= p[j] - p[i] <= upper . In each merge, for each p[i] in the sorted left half find, using two moving pointers lo and hi in the right half, the range of p[j] with p[j] - p[i] >= lower (starting at lo ) and p[j] - p[i] > upper (ending at hi ). Add hi - lo . Global vs local inversions A permutation of 0..n-1 has every local inversion as a global one. Counts are equal exactly when no element is more than one position from its sorted place: check |a[i] - i| <= 1 in O(n) . Merge sort counting confirms it but is overkill. TRAP Count before or during the merge as each problem requires, but never after: once the halves are merged the left/right distinction is gone. D. CHAPTER SUMMARY Count cross-pairs while merging: sorted halves make the match count monotone, so the pass is linear. Inversions: when the right element wins, add the number of remaining left elements. Conditions that don't match the merge order (reverse pairs, range sums) get a separate two-pointer pass over the sorted halves. Carry indices to attribute counts to original positions (smaller after self). Use long for totals and for doubled values; a Fenwick tree is the shorter alternative.

PART XIII · MASTERCLASSES AND REFERENCE M1 Pattern Recognition Masterclass How to look at an unfamiliar problem and name the pattern before writing a line of code. Why recognition beats memorisation Parts I to XII taught 107 patterns one at a time. In an interview nobody announces the chapter. You get a paragraph of English, a few constraints and a clock. This masterclass is the missing step: a repeatable procedure that turns the statement and the constraints into a short list of candidate patterns , then uses cheap tests to choose between them. Every rule below is tied to the chapter where the pattern is taught and proved. PART XIII · MASTERCLASSES AND REFERENCE M2 Complexity Analysis Masterclass Big O, Omega and Theta, amortised cost, stack space, and a verified Java collections reference. What we are counting Complexity analysis answers one question: how does the cost grow as the input grows? We count basic steps (comparisons, array reads and writes, arithmetic) rather than seconds, because seconds depend on the machine, the JIT and the data, while growth rates do not. Constants matter in practice, but they cannot rescue a growth rate that is too steep: O(n²) on 10⁵ elements is 10¹⁰ steps whatever the hardware. Figure 156. Growth rates for n up to 16 (clipped at 260 operations). The exponential curves leave the page almost immediately. Big O, Omega and Theta The three symbols describe bounds on a function , not cases of an algorithm. This distinction is the most common source of confusion in interviews. Symbo l Meaning for f(n) Formal statement Read it as O(g) f grows no faster than g exists c, n0 : f(n) <= c · g(n) for all n >= n0 Upper bound Ω (g) f grows at least as fast as g exists c, n0 : f(n) >= c · g(n) for all n >= n0 Lower bound Θ (g) f grows exactly like g both O(g) and Ω (g) Tight bound Insertion sort illustrates the difference. Its worst case (reverse-sorted input) takes Θ (n²) steps; its best case (already sorted) takes Θ (n) . So "insertion sort is O(n²) " is true for every input, "insertion sort is Ω (n) " is true for every input, and "insertion sort is Θ (n²) " is true only if you say in the worst case . In interviews "the complexity" nearly always means the tight worst-case upper bound , written with O . COMMON MISCONCEPTION O is not "the worst case". The worst case is a scenario; O , Ω and Θ are bounds you can attach to the worst case, the best case or the average case separately. Amortised cost is the average cost per operation over any sequence of operations in the worst case : it is a guarantee about the whole sequence, with no randomness and no assumption about the input. That is different from average-case cost, which averages over a distribution of inputs. Example: appending to a dynamic array ArrayList.add writes into spare capacity in O(1) . When the array is full it allocates a bigger one and copies every element. With doubling , the copies for n appends are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^k < 2n , so the total work is below 3n writes and the amortised cost per append is O(1) . Figure 157. Cost of each append to a doubling array (bars) and the running average (line). Spikes at 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33 are the resizes; the average stays below 3. The instrumented CountingArray confirms this by counting writes: for 1,000,000 appends, a doubling array performs 2,048,575 writes (about 2.05 per append) and a 1.5x array performs 3,099,753 (about 3.10 per append) . The growth factor changes the constant, never the class. OpenJDK's ArrayList grows by about 1.5x; that is an implementation detail, not a documented guarantee. WHY GEOMETRIC GROWTH Growing by a fixed amount (say +10) is not amortised O(1) : the number of resizes is n / 10 , each copying up to n elements, so n appends cost Θ (n²) . Say "worst-case O(...) " to be unambiguous. Auxiliary space excludes the input; recursion depth counts, and Java does not eliminate tail calls. Amortised cost guarantees the average over any sequence: geometric growth makes dynamic-array appends O(1) , fixed growth does not. For objects, supply a Comparator . Build it with Comparator.comparingInt(...).thenComparing(...) , which is readable and cannot overflow. THE OVERFLOW TRAP Never write (a, b) -> a - b . For a = Integer.MAX_VALUE and b = -1 the subtraction overflows to a negative number, the comparator answers the wrong way, and the sort silently produces a wrong order (or TimSort throws "Comparison method violates its general contract"). Use Integer.compare(a, b) . The toolkit includes a function that detects exactly when subtraction breaks. PriorityQueue is a min-heap; reverse the comparator for a max-heap; there is no decrease-key, so use lazy deletion. ArrayDeque is both your stack and your queue; merge counts frequencies; records make clean pair keys. Compute midpoints as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 , accumulate sums in long , and use Math.floorMod and Math.addExact where signs or overflow matter. Buffered input and a flushed PrintWriter are the only fast I/O you need. A DSU and a trie are each about 40 lines: practise writing them without looking.

The first sixty seconds Restate the problem in your own words and confirm the input and output types. CHAPTER SUMMARY First minute: restate, ask about limits and edge cases, example, brute force, pattern, complexity, then code. Write the thirteen templates until your hands know them; compare with Integer.compare , compute midpoints safely. Announce edge cases by data type: empty, single, duplicates, negatives, overflow, disconnected, touching intervals. Know the forgotten algorithms by their one-line idea and their cost. Say your reasoning out loud: naming the signal and the test is what you are scored on.

Glossary Term Meaning Activity selection Choosing the largest set of non-overlapping intervals; solved by sorting by end time. Adjacency list A graph stored as one list of neighbours per vertex; O(V + E) memory. Amortised analysis Averaging the cost of operations over a whole sequence. A while inside a for is still O(n) if each element is processed a bounded number of times in total. Amortised analysis Bounding the average cost per operation over any worst-case sequence of operations; a guarantee about the sequence, not about random inputs. Amortised O(1) Constant cost per operation averaged over a sequence, although a single operation (such as a stack-to-stack transfer) may cost more. Anti-diagonal A diagonal running down-left; its cells share the value r + c . Argsort The indices that would sort an array, used when original positions must be kept. Arm and bend In path problems, the arm is the best downward path returned to the parent; the bend is the best path through the node, recorded in a global. Articulation point A vertex whose removal disconnects an undirected graph. Auxiliary space Extra memory used beyond the input (and usually the returned output). Auxiliary space Memory an algorithm allocates beyond its input, including recursion stack frames. Back edge In a DFS of a directed graph, an edge to an ancestor still on the recursion stack; it proves a cycle. Backtracking Recursive search that builds a solution step by step, abandoning (undoing) a choice when it cannot lead to a solution. Balanced tree A tree in which every node's subtree heights differ by at most one. Base case An input answered directly, without recursion; it guarantees termination. Bellman-Ford Shortest paths by V − 1 rounds of relaxing every edge; tolerates negative weights and detects negative cycles. Big O, Omega, Theta Upper, lower and tight asymptotic bounds on a function; separate from the best, worst and average case they may describe. Binary (XOR) trie A trie over the bits of integers, most significant first; walking opposite bits finds the maximum XOR partner. Binary lifting Precomputing the 2^j-th ancestor of every node so that k-th ancestors and LCAs are answered in O(log n) . Binary search tree A binary tree in which every key in a node's left subtree is smaller, and every key in its (BST) right subtree larger, than the node's key. Bipartite graph A graph whose vertices split into two sets with every edge between them; equivalently, no odd cycle. Term Meaning Bitmask An integer whose bits represent membership of elements in a subset. Bitonic array An array that strictly increases to a single peak and then strictly decreases (a mountain). Bounded heap A heap capped at k entries by evicting its root when it grows past k; keeps the k best items in O(n log k) . Boyer-Moore voting A one-pass algorithm that keeps a candidate and a count; different elements cancel, so a strict majority always survives. Bracket A range [lo, hi] known to contain the answer; exponential search first builds it by doubling. Bridge An edge whose removal disconnects an undirected graph. Bucket sort by An array indexed by frequency (1..n) whose cells list the values with that count; frequency scanning it from high to low gives values by descending frequency in O(n). Canonical key A representation where two items are equivalent exactly when their keys are equal (sorted letters, reduced slope, count signature). Chaining Collision handling in which each hash bucket holds a linked list (or tree) of entries. Choose / explore / The three-step body of every backtracking loop: apply a choice, recurse, then restore unchoose the state exactly. Closed interval An interval [a, b] that includes both endpoints; [1,2] and [2,3] share the point 2. Condensation The DAG obtained by contracting each strongly connected component to a single node. Cooldown A required number of slots between two runs of the same task; the most frequent task determines the minimum schedule length. Coordinate Replacing sparse coordinates by their ranks so they can index an array. compression Cross product (2D) (b - a) x (c - a) ; its sign tells whether a, b, c turn left, right or are collinear. Cut property The lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST; it justifies Kruskal and Prim. DAG Directed acyclic graph; exactly the graphs that have a topological order. Diameter The number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes; the path bends at its highest node. Difference array Array of adjacent differences; makes range additions O(1). Inverse of the prefix sum. Dijkstra's algorithm Greedy single-source shortest paths for non-negative weights using a priority queue. Disjoint-interval Stored intervals never overlap or touch, so a new interval can only conflict with its two invariant nearest neighbours. Dominance Element a is dominated by b if a can never be a better answer than b from now on; dominated elements are discarded (monotonic deque). Dummy (sentinel) node A placeholder node placed before the head so that every real node has a predecessor; removes head-specific special cases. Error log A short record of each missed problem and the signal that was overlooked, used to drive spaced revision. Term Meaning Euler tour A depth-first walk that records a node on every entry and return; with a sparse table it answers LCA queries in O(1) . Event (sweep) A coordinate at which something starts or ends; the sweep line processes events in sorted order. Exchange argument Proof technique: show that swapping or discarding an element cannot worsen the optimum. Justifies two-pointer moves. Exchange argument A proof that swaps an optimal solution's choice for the greedy one without making it worse, showing the greedy choice is safe. Exchange argument A greedy proof: swap an optimal solution's first choice for the greedy choice without making it worse. Expand around centre Grow l--, r++ from each of the 2n − 1 centres while the characters match; finds palindromes in O(n²) time, O(1) space. Expected-closer stack A stack holding the closing bracket each open bracket requires; the next closer must equal the top. Factorial number A mixed-radix system with place values (n−1)!, (n−2)!, …, 1! ; it maps a rank k to the system k-th permutation. Feasibility check The function feasible(x) evaluated by binary search on the answer, usually a greedy scan. Feasibility predicate A yes/no test feasible(x) on a candidate answer; binary search on the answer needs it to be monotone. Fenwick tree (BIT) A binary indexed tree: cell i stores the aggregate of the i & -i elements ending at i ; prefix queries and point updates in O(log n) . Term Meaning Fisher-Yates shuffle The unbiased in-place shuffle that swaps position i with a uniformly random position in i..n-1 . Floyd's cycle detection Tortoise-and-hare: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; they meet inside a cycle, and restarting one pointer at the head finds the cycle entrance. Floyd-Warshall All-pairs shortest paths by dynamic programming over intermediate vertices, O(V³) . Functional graph A graph in which every node has exactly one outgoing edge ( i -> nums[i] ); it contains cycles, so Floyd applies. Gray code A sequence of binary numbers in which consecutive values differ in exactly one bit; g(i) = i ^ (i >> 1) . Greedy choice A locally best decision that is proved to be part of some optimal solution, so it never needs to be revisited. Half-open interval An interval [a, b) that includes a but not b ; [1,2) and [2,3) do not overlap. Head insertion Repeatedly moving the node after cur to just after a fixed before node; reverses a segment without a reconnection step. Heap A complete binary tree stored in an array in which every node is ordered against its children; the root is the minimum (min-heap) or maximum (max-heap). Term Meaning Held-Karp The O(2^n n^2) bitmask DP for the travelling salesman problem: dp[mask][last] is the cheapest path over a set of cities. Hirschberg's algorithm A divide-and-conquer method that recovers an LCS or alignment in linear space by finding where an optimal path crosses the middle row. Home index The array position where a value belongs in cyclic sort ( v - 1 for values 1..n). Huffman coding A greedy algorithm that merges the two lightest trees repeatedly to build an optimal prefix code. Idempotent operation An operation with op(x, x) = x (min, max, gcd, AND, OR); overlapping ranges do no harm, which sparse tables exploit. Inorder successor The smallest key greater than a given key; the leftmost node of the right subtree, or the last ancestor from which the walk went left. Interval cover Choosing the fewest intervals whose union covers a target range; solved by always extending the furthest reach. Interval graph A graph whose vertices are intervals, adjacent when they overlap; its chromatic number equals its largest clique, the peak overlap. Invariant A statement that holds before and after every loop iteration; the basis of correctness proofs. Inversion A pair of positions i < j with a[i] > a[j] ; the count measures how far an array is from sorted. k-way merge Merging k sorted sequences by always taking the smallest current head, using a min-heap or pairwise merging in O(N log k) . K-way merge Merging k sorted sources by keeping one front element per source in a min-heap; O(N log k) for N elements. Kahn's algorithm Topological sort that repeatedly removes vertices of in-degree 0; a short result signals a cycle. Kernighan's trick n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so a loop of that step counts set bits in O(popcount) . Key point (skyline) A pair (x, height) at which the outline's height changes. Kraft inequality A prefix code with codeword lengths l1..ln exists if and only if the sum of 2^(-li) is at most 1; equal to 1 for a complete code. Lazy deletion Marking an element as removed and discarding it only when it reaches the top of the heap; avoids the O(n) cost of removing from the middle. Lazy deletion Leaving stale entries in a heap and discarding them when they reach the top, instead of an O(n) removal. Lazy propagation Storing a pending update at a segment-tree node and pushing it to the children only when they are visited. Lazy tag A pending update stored on one element and applied only when that element is next read or removed (CustomStack increments). Lexicographic order Dictionary order: compare element by element from the left. Load factor Entries divided by buckets; java.util.HashMap resizes at 0.75. Term Meaning Low-link low[u] : the smallest discovery time reachable from u 's DFS subtree using at most one back edge; the basis of Tarjan's algorithms. Lower / upper bound First index with nums[i] >= t (lower) or nums[i] > t (upper); the occurrences of t are [lower, upper) . Lowest common The deepest node that has both given nodes as descendants (a node is its own ancestor (LCA) descendant). LRU / LFU Least Recently Used / Least Frequently Used: cache eviction policies by recency and by access count (ties by recency). Manacher's algorithm A linear-time method that finds the radius of the longest palindrome at every centre by reusing mirrored radii. Meet in the middle Splitting the input into two halves, enumerating each half and joining the results, to turn 2^n into about 2^(n/2) . Memoisation Caching the result of a call by its arguments so repeated calls return immediately (top-down dynamic programming). minFreq In an LFU cache, the lowest frequency that currently has a non-empty bucket; the eviction bucket. Minimum spanning tree A subset of edges connecting all vertices with the least total weight and no cycle. Modular inverse A number x with a x = 1 (mod m) ; replaces division under a modulus. Exists iff gcd(a, m) = 1 . Monotone / monotonic Always moving in one direction. A window condition is monotone if growing the window can only break (or only help) validity. Monotone predicate A yes/no test over an ordered range that changes answer at most once; the precondition for binary search on the answer. Monotonic stack / A stack or deque kept in sorted order by popping elements that violate the order before deque each push. Morris traversal Inorder or preorder walk in O(1) extra space by temporarily threading each predecessor's right pointer to its ancestor and removing the thread afterwards. Most constrained The slot with the fewest remaining candidates; branching on it first makes failures variable appear early. Multi-source BFS BFS started with several sources at distance 0, giving distance to the nearest one. Multiset A set that stores counts, so equal values can be added and removed independently; a TreeMap<value, count> . Negative cycle A cycle with negative total weight; shortest paths through it are undefined. Offline algorithm An algorithm that sees all its queries in advance and may reorder them; contrast with online. Online algorithm An algorithm that must answer each request as it arrives, without seeing later ones. Optimal substructure An optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its subproblems, so smaller optima can be combined. Overlapping The same smaller question is asked many times; the property that makes caching pay subproblems off. Term Meaning Path compression Re-pointing nodes on a find path closer to the root; path halving is the one-pass variant. Term Meaning Patience sorting Dealing cards onto piles with a decreasing-top rule; the number of piles equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence. Postfix (RPN) Reverse Polish notation: operands before operators, so evaluation needs only one operand stack and no parentheses. Power set The set of all subsets of a set; 2 ⁿ elements for n items. Prefix code A code in which no codeword is a prefix of another, so a bit stream can be decoded without separators. Prefix function / border pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also its suffix; such a prefix is called a border. Prefix sum P[i] = sum of the first i elements; range sums become P[r+1] - P[l] . Preorder / inorder / Tree traversal orders that visit the node before, between or after its two subtrees; the postorder inorder of a BST is sorted. Priority queue An abstract structure that returns the item with the highest priority; usually implemented with a binary heap, O(log n) per offer and poll . Pruning Skipping a branch because it provably cannot lead to a valid answer. Pseudo-polynomial Polynomial in the numeric value of an input (such as a knapsack capacity) but exponential in its bit length. Pseudo-polynomial Polynomial in the numeric value of an input (such as a knapsack capacity) but exponential in its bit length. Quickselect Selection by partitioning around a pivot and recursing into one side; finds the k-th element in expected O(n) . Quickselect Partitioning around a pivot and recursing into one side to find the k-th smallest element in expected O(n) time. Re-rooting Computing an answer for every node of a tree as root by reusing the parent's answer in O(1) per edge. Reader / writer pointers Same-direction two pointers: read scans, write marks the next output slot. Recursion tree A tree with one node per call; its size times the work per node is the cost of the recursion. Recursive descent Parsing by one function per precedence level, each calling the next-tighter level; parentheses recurse back to the top. Relaxation Improving a tentative distance dist[v] by going through u : dist[u] + w < dist[v] . Relinking Changing next pointers to reorder nodes without copying or moving values. Reservoir sampling Choosing k items uniformly from a stream of unknown length in one pass by replacing a random slot with probability k / i . Ring (circular list) A list whose tail points to the head; used to rotate by cutting at a computed node. Ring buffer A fixed array used circularly with a head index and a size; indices wrap with modulo. Term Meaning Rolling array Keeping only the most recent row(s) of a DP table when each row depends only on the previous one. Rolling hash A polynomial hash of a window that can be updated in O(1) when the window slides by one character. Segment tree A tree whose nodes store an aggregate (sum, min, max) of an interval; range queries and point updates run in O(log n) . Sentinel A dummy value (for example height 0 at the end) that forces a loop to flush pending state without a special case. Shunting-yard Dijkstra's algorithm that converts infix to postfix with an operator stack, popping operators of greater or equal precedence first. Sieve of Eratosthenes Listing primes up to n by crossing out multiples of each prime from its square, in O(n log log n) . Sliding window A contiguous range [left, right] whose summary is updated incrementally as it moves. Sparse table A table st[k][i] of answers for windows of length 2^k ; answers idempotent range queries in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing. Stabbing query Asking which intervals contain a given point. Stable sort A sort that keeps equal keys in their original relative order; counting sort achieves it by filling the output right to left. Stable sort A sort that keeps equal elements in their original order; List.sort and Arrays.sort(Object[]) are stable. Staircase search Walking a row-and-column-sorted matrix from a corner, discarding a row or column per step. State (DP) The smallest set of facts about the problem so far that determines the best way to finish; the index (or indices) of a DP table. State machine DP DP whose state is a small mode (holding, cooldown, colour) updated each step along allowed transitions. Stays ahead A greedy proof showing that after every step the greedy solution is at least as good as any other partial solution. Strongly connected A maximal set of vertices in a directed graph that all reach each other. component Subarray / substring A contiguous part of an array / string (as opposed to a subsequence , which may skip elements). Submask A subset of the bits of a mask; all non-empty submasks are enumerated with s = (s - 1) & mask . Swap-remove Delete from an array in O(1) by overwriting the element with the last one and shrinking the size; order is not preserved. Sweep line Processing sorted events (starts and ends) left to right while maintaining a running count or set of active intervals. Symmetry breaking Skipping choices equivalent to ones already tried (equal items, interchangeable buckets). Term Meaning Tabulation Bottom-up DP: fill a table in dependency order with loops instead of recursion. Tie-breaking rule The order in which events with equal coordinates are processed; ends first for half-open intervals, starts first for closed ones. Topological order A linear order of a DAG's vertices in which every edge points forward. Transition The rule that computes one DP state from smaller states; the recurrence relation. Transpose Swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] ; combined with a row reversal it rotates a square matrix by 90°. Tree DP Dynamic programming over subtrees: a postorder pass in which each node returns a small state computed from its children. Tree height / depth Height is the longest downward path from a node; depth is the distance from the root. Count in nodes or edges consistently. Tree serialization Encoding a tree as a string (for example preorder with # for null) so that it can be rebuilt exactly. Trie A prefix tree: a node per character, with word-end markers; used to prune grid searches by prefix. Two heaps A max-heap holding the lower half and a min-heap holding the upper half of a collection; the median is read from the roots. Union-Find (DSU) Structure maintaining disjoint sets with near-constant-time find and union . Upper mid lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2 : required when the loop assigns lo = mid , to guarantee progress. Wall (stack) A sentinel index such as -1 pushed first so that every pop has a left boundary, even when the stack would otherwise be empty. Term Meaning Weaving Placing each copied node directly after its original so that original.next locates the copy in O(1) . XOR cancellation a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a ; XOR-ing a collection removes every value that appears an even number of times. Z function z[i] is the length of the longest common prefix of s and the suffix s[i..] ; computed in O(n) with a Z-box.
